title: Thermal radiation effects on unsteady MHD dusty viscoelastic Couette flow through an inclined porous channel
authors: Syed Modassir Hussain, Bilal Ali, Sidra Jubair, Zokir Mamadiyarov, Shakhnoza Khojimatova, Bobur Mirzayev
abstract: This paper describes an analytical study of unsteady magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) Couette flow of a dusty second-grade viscoelastic fluid between two infinite inclined porous plates. The problem involves the combined influences of porous medium permeability, uniform suction/injection, rotation of the system, thermal radiation, and coupled heat and mass transfer. The fluid is electrically conducting with a transverse magnetic field, and the dust particles are coupled to the base fluid by Stokes drag forces. The porous channel is inclined, which causes a buoyancy force in the flow direction, thus affecting the momentum and heat transfer characteristics. The equations of motion for the fluid and dust particles are developed with suitable assumptions and scaled to obtain dimensionless equations. Periodic solutions for velocity, temperature, and concentration are derived using the Poincaré-Lighthill perturbation method. The results are presented to illustrate the effects of various dimensionless parameters such as the magnetic parameter, Darcy number, rotation parameter, viscoelastic parameter, radiation parameter, Peclet number, thermal Grashof number, mass Grashof number, and dust concentration parameter. The results show that the magnetic field intensity, rotation, dust concentration, and porous resistance reduce fluid and dust particle velocities. Buoyancy forces and permeability increase fluid velocity. Thermal radiation increases temperature profiles, and higher Peclet numbers decrease thermal diffusion. The skin friction, Nusselt number, and Sherwood number results illustrate the effects of porous resistance, electromagnetic damping, and convective transport. The results of this study will help in understanding the control of multiphase viscoelastic fluid transport in inclined porous media, which are applicable to thermal management systems, rotating machinery cooling, porous reactors, and particle-laden energy transport devices. For the parameter ranges considered, the Nusselt number varies by about 5% with the radiation parameter and the Sherwood number by about 1% with the Schmidt number.

title: A Fourier-Graph Neural Operator for Transient Isothermal Two-Phase Mold Filling Relevant to Metal Casting
authors: Edgard M. Minete, Mathis Immertreu, Fabian Teichmann, Sebastian Müller
abstract: In metal casting, mold-filling hydrodynamics strongly influence defect formation and final component quality. However, systematic exploration of gating configurations remains limited by the computational cost of repeated transient Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations. This study investigates whether a neural operator can provide faster short-horizon field predictions for parametrized mold-filling problems. We develop a non-autoregressive Fourier-Graph neural operator that extends the Geometry-Informed Neural Operator (GINO) framework to transient multi-field prediction through spatio-temporal latent construction, inlet and gating parameter conditioning, multi-field decoding, and causal rollout weighting. The model is evaluated on two controlled 2D isothermal water-air Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes (CHNS) datasets of increasing parametric complexity. For held-out parameter combinations within the sampled fixed-cavity design grid, the mean relative L 2 errors are 29.79% on DS 1 and 35.92 % on DS 2 . Matched-horizon inference is 90.55 × faster than CFD over 0.1 s and 40.52 × faster over 0.6 s. Qualitative comparisons show broad agreement in the velocity, pressure, and volume-fraction fields, although pressure transients and localized gradients remain challenging to resolve. Moreover, performance deteriorates under spatial or temporal subsampling and reduced training-data availability. Overall, the results demonstrate computational acceleration for controlled in-grid interpolation, while the field-wise relative L 2 errors make the current accuracy limitations explicit. The present model is not a stand-alone substitute for high-fidelity CFD in demanding settings and has not yet been validated on unseen cavity geometries. Nevertheless, with further development, neural operators of this type could support early-stage mold design by rapidly screening designs and reducing the number of final high-fidelity CFD evaluations.

title: Convectively Coupled Equatorial Waves in a Global Storm‐Resolving Model
authors: Sebastián Ortega, Hans Mikhail Segura, Víctor C. Mayta, Romain Fiévet, Angel Peinado, Junhong Lee, M. A. Giorgetta, Björn Stevens
abstract: Abstract We show how reducing the fall speeds of rain and ice leads to reduced biases of Convectively Coupled Equatorial Waves (CCEWs) in convection‐resolving configurations of the Icosahedral Non‐hydrostatic Model (ICON). In particular, reducing the fall speeds of rain and ice leads to stronger activity over the wavenumbers and frequencies associated with convectively coupled Kelvin waves, inertio‐gravity waves, mixed Rossby‐gravity waves, equatorial Rossby waves, and the Madden‐Julian oscillation, and to weaker activity of tropical depressions. The changes in CCEW activity are mediated by changes in the frequency of mesoscale convection profiles. Reducing the fall speeds increases the frequency of bottom‐heavy and top‐heavy mesoscale convection profiles and decreases the frequency of mid‐heavy mesoscale convection profiles. In turn, changes to the mesoscale convective profiles are reflected in the ability of the model to develop the tilt and top‐heaviness of CCEWs. Reductions in the fall speeds also increase precipitation over the warm pool region, possibly allowing for a stronger equatorial forcing of convectively coupled Kelvin waves. Our findings suggest that the representation of CCEWs within ICON agrees with their observed multiscale structure.

title: Estimating Twomey forcing sensitivity to aerosol plume spreading rates
authors: Lucas A. McMichael, Ehsan Erfani, Robert Wood, Knut von Salzen
abstract: Abstract. The amount of sunlight that reaches Earth's surface can be reduced by increasing cloud droplet number and decreasing droplet size (i.e., Twomey forcing), a central idea underpinning the Marine Cloud Brightening strategy. Cloud albedo depends nonlinearly on cloud droplet concentration, meaning the spatial extent of aerosol plumes could be an important constraint on the brightening potential. Horizontal spreading of aerosols can be simulated by Langevin particle models, which depend on turbulence characteristics and precipitation. The turbulence information that drives the particle model is derived from a library of realistic, 2-day LES cases, spanning northeast Pacific stratocumulus conditions. The 2-D reflectance fields from the LES are superimposed onto the 2-D perturbed aerosol concentrations to calculate the 2-D Twomey forcing response. The Day 1 and Day 2 LES regimes have distinct meteorological, aerosol, and turbulence characteristics associated with equatorward movement of the LES domain. Our results indicate that the Day 2 regime has substantially faster plume spreading than Day 1, with ensemble median differences exceeding 2 km hr-1. Despite these differences, Twomey forcing is insensitive to the natural variability in spreading rate. This study suggests that Twomey forcing is resilient to variations in meteorology, aerosols, and turbulence, with its efficacy governed primarily by aerosol lifetimes and assumptions surrounding cloud adjustments. Although the natural variation in spreading rate does not materially affect Twomey forcing, idealized plume spreading simulations suggest that current GCM assumptions of an infinitely fast spreading rate could lead to a 10-200% overestimation of cooling.

title: CFD Investigation of the Effect of Jet-Surface Distance on Thermal Performance in Inclined Jet Impingement Cooling
authors: Haydar Kepekçi
abstract: This study numerically investigates the influence of geometric parameters on heat transfer in inclined jet impingement cooling. Twenty configurations were analyzed for H/D ratios of 3–6 and jet inclination angles of 0°–60° at Re = 15,000. Two-dimensional steady turbulent simulations were performed using the SST k–ω model within a CFD framework. Results show that both the H/D ratio and inclination angle significantly affect thermal performance. The average Nusselt number increased from 4.09–4.49 at H/D = 3 to 5.05–6.83 at H/D = 6. The heat transfer coefficient rose from 19.82 W/m²K at H/D = 3 and 0° to 33.08 W/m²K at H/D = 6 and 60°. Enhanced turbulence and flow mixing improved heat transfer. The most favorable thermal performance among the investigated cases was observed at H/D = 5–6 and inclination angles of 45°–60°, providing useful guidance for the geometric optimization of inclined jet impingement cooling systems.

title: Introductory Chapter: The Future of Boundary Layer Control Techniques
authors: Zambri Harun
abstract: The thin layer of fluid flow near the surface that contains the shearing forces is a crucial aspect of fluid dynamics and aerodynamic optimization. The manipulation of this layer results in a change in the overall behavior, such as the lift and drag forces. This control mechanism is critical in various engineering applications, from enhancing the lift on aircraft wings to reducing drag on high-speed vehicles. This chapter summarizes the latest control mechanisms at both lab-scale and engineering application scales. Beyond the theories, the chapter also considers socio-economic benefits and perspectives.

title: World Embedding Benchmark
authors: Yiqi Liu, Ruifeng Yuan, Yang Wang, Long Li, Fengyu Cai, Hou Pong Chan, Jialin Yu, Hao Zhang, Chenghua Lin, Chenghao Xiao
abstract: Physical fidelity has received increasing attention in world models and video generation, yet how video representations encode physical information remains less understood. We introduce the World Embedding Benchmark, comprising 8,000 controlled simulation cases from 80 families spanning fluid mechanics, solid mechanics, dynamics, and optics & electromagnetism. Each case pairs a rendered video with simulation-derived physical annotations, supporting three complementary tasks: text-video retrieval, physical-property regression, and multiple-choice video-description pair classification. We use these tasks to distinguish cross-modal physical alignment from the recoverability of quantitative physical information. Evaluated pre-trained omnimodal embedding models show weak retrieval and near-chance within-family pair classification, while lightweight probes recover useful physical information from frozen video embeddings. Continual contrastive training with physics-specific video-text pairs improves retrieval and pair classification but degrades physical-property regression, revealing a trade-off between alignment and quantitative information recoverability. Finally, we use the embeddings to retrieve reference videos for retrieval-augmented generation with MiniMax-H3. Retrieved references improve the physical fidelity of generated videos, with stronger retrieval models yielding larger gains in our experiments. Together, these findings highlight the need to evaluate physical alignment and property recoverability jointly, and demonstrate the utility of physical representations for improving video generation.

title: A Kinetic Theory of the Gated Self-Evolving LLM Agent
authors: Haipeng Wang
abstract: We find traces of fluid dynamics in the self-evolution of an LLM agent, and give the kinetic theory that predicts them. Gated self-evolution is the loop in which an agent rewrites its own skills under a validation gate. Self-evolution research has treated the agent as the unit; we study instead the individual instances inside it. Here the agent is DSH-plugin-based: it runs in production on DeepSeek Harness (DSH), and its plugins satisfy four architectural properties (permutation symmetry, reversibility, acyclicity, typed contracts), which license treating these instances as identical hard spheres; the theory is accordingly scoped to DSH-class plugin populations. On this scope the paper builds three theory layers. The rigorous layer, independent of any analogy, comprises an any-time hitting-time certificate bounding the expected rounds to any prescribed improvement, a resolution law that prices held-out validation budgets, and a separation theorem: the daemon must stay outside the population, because merging evaluator with evaluated voids the certificate. The kinetic layer is a master equation over the plugin x version x task grid with four operators (collision, reaction, external field, gate), where collision is co-activation. Its moment hierarchy, the step that turns a gas into fluid equations, generates the falsifiable statistical signatures. Throughout, the fluid reading is a bounded analogy: momentum is not conserved, so no Navier-Stokes limit exists. The measured layer runs on a faithful minimal instance, a large library of four-parameter skill plugins retrieved one per episode with a co-activation probe, in a one-model, one-task-family WebShop environment; every element maps to the DSH loop by architectural role. Population fluctuation scaling is density-gated: invisible at sparse edit density, it emerges at the predicted rate under tripled density, as directional evidence.

title: Energy-efficient and uniform drying-oriented jet box optimization in textile manufacturing: a slit design with CFD-ML driven multi-objective optimization and full-scale experimental verification
authors: Shizhao Zhen, Di Zhou, Gaoyu Li, Rong Hua, Ming Wei, Chenjian Wang, Zhiping Mao, Huimin Chen
abstract: Uneven width-wise drying and high energy consumption of jet boxes in knitted fabric pre-drying, stemming from non-uniform airflow in traditional structures, degrade textile product quality and increase production cost. This study designs a centrosymmetric variable cross-section slit-type jet box via sixth-order Bezier curves. A hybrid surrogate model combining computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and machine learning (ML) is established to analyze the influence of structural parameters on airflow uniformity and energy utilization efficiency. This model enabled efficient multi-objective optimization, yielding Pareto-optimal solutions with a maximum relative error of less than 10 % compared to direct CFD simulations. Full-scale duct experiments verified the aerodynamic performance of the optimized jet-box structure, with deviations between simulated and measured values below 15 %. The optimized jet box exhibits a coefficient of variation (CV) of less than 0.16, ensuring uniform width-wise outlet airflow and indicating potential reduction in aerodynamic energy loss. This study establishes an innovative jet box optimization paradigm, providing a potential energy-efficient jet-box design strategy for textile drying equipment.

title: Machine learning-assisted axial fan blade optimization for electronics cooling
authors: Rujie Shi, Jing Yang, Zhiyuan Luo, Xuechun Li, Houyu Wei, Kang Zhu
abstract: In an air-cooling system for electronic devices, the axial fan critically determines energy use, heat dissipation, and noise. To address shrinking cooling spaces and noise challenges, this study integrated CFD methods with Bayesian optimization (BO) to design fan blades achieving high airflow with low noise. A CFD model combining the fan with a finned heat pipe cooler simulated CPU cooling scenarios, obtaining flow rate 𝑄 at 2000 rpm. Aerodynamic and acoustic simulations further provided pressure fluctuations and sound pressure level (SPL). Starting from a commercial blade profile, parameterization using blade wrap angle and quadratic functions reduced dimensionality. These parameters and 𝑄 formed a high-dimensional black-box function. Therefore, a Gaussian process regression (GPR) machine learning model was employed to rapidly identify the optimal Q combination from the explored data. Prototype experiments validated the CFD models. Results showed a 24% increase in Q compared to the original design, reducing CPU surface temperature by over 2 °C under a 280 W heat load. Among blades with >20% 𝑄 improvement, combinations exist where SPL match those of the prototype fan, achieving the optimization of conflicting parameters. Sensitivity analysis clarified the effect of each parameter on 𝑄 , static pressure rise 𝑃 , and SPL, guiding key parameter optimization for axial fans in electronic cooling.

title: Role of Mo in Enhancing the Elevated‐Temperature Strength of Steel Through Dislocation and Grain‐Boundary Stabilization
authors: Jinghua Cong, Haibin Zhu, Pengcheng Liu, Xueliang Shang, Yongzhe Yang, Xu Ji, Wenjie Fan, Xuemin Wang
abstract: Fire‐resistant structural steels must retain load‐bearing capacity under fire exposure, and their elevated‐temperature performance is governed not only by alloy design but also by the thermal stability of the microstructure. This work investigates the effects of Mo on the microstructural evolution, mechanical properties, and fire resistance of steels subjected to air‐cooling and water‐cooling. SEM observations reveal that Mo promotes a limited fraction of bainite under air‐cooling and refines the bainitic/martensitic lath structure under water‐cooling. Mechanical testing demonstrates that Mo enhances room‐temperature strength under both cooling conditions; however, its contribution to fire resistance is strongly microstructure‐dependent. In the air‐cooled steel, the yield‐strength retention at 600 °C remains essentially unchanged upon Mo addition, whereas in the bainitic/martensitic steel, the yield strength at 600 °C increases markedly from ~162.9 to ~254.4 MPa with the retention ratio rising from 0.29 to 0.38. TEM analysis after holding at 600 °C identifies coarse alloyed cementite along lath boundaries, without a high number density of fine Mo‐rich precipitates, indicating that precipitation strengthening is unlikely to dominate. EBSD characterization, prior austenite reconstruction, and boundary statistics confirm that Mo mitigates dislocation annihilation and preserves block/sub‐block boundary density during elevated‐temperature exposure, thereby enhancing resistance to recovery, coarsening, and softening.

title: State-of-the-art microfluidics technology for CO₂-foam flooding and geological CO₂ storage: A review
authors: Muhammad Raees Khan
abstract: Microfluidic technology has been a powerful tool for exploring CO₂-foam flooding and CO₂ sequestration at the microscale. Traditional methods, e.g., core flooding experiments, are prone to facing challenges in simulating fluid dynamics in porous media accurately; however, microfluidic platforms allow for direct observation and real-time evaluation of multiphase flow dynamics. This review evaluates cutting-edge microfluidic techniques, such as rock-on-a-chip and high-temperature high-pressure (HTHP) chips, with enhanced functionalities in simulating reservoir conditions. Additionally, advances in image processing and machine learning greatly promoted data analysis in microfluidics-driven experiments. The integration of microfluidics with digital rock physics and reservoir simulations offers a platform for the translation of laboratory findings into field-applicable operations. Besides advances in technology, this review considers the economic feasibility and environmental benefits of microfluidic operations in enhanced oil recovery (EOR) and carbon capture and storage (CCS). The results show that microfluidics can play a key role in optimizing CO₂ injection strategies, enhancing oil recovery, and ensuring the security of long-term CO₂ storage, and thus promoting energy efficiency as well as climate change mitigation.

title: Synergistic solidification of ternary hybrid nano-enhanced solar salt PCM using enclosure-mounted fins and internal cooling cylinders
authors: R. Saran Raj, P.S. Sushmitha, R. Harish
abstract: The low thermal conductivity of solar salt limits the heat extraction rate and discharge performance of latent heat thermal energy storage systems. This study numerically investigates the combined effect of enclosure-mounted fins and internal cooling cylinders in a ternary hybrid nano-enhanced solar salt phase change material on solidification. Three combinations of ternary hybrid nanoparticles, including SiO 2 + TiO 2 + Al 2 O 3 , SiO 2 + Al 2 O 3 + h-BN, and SiO 2 + h-BN + SWCNT, are considered to investigate their effects on heat transfer and solidification. The enthalpy–porosity method is used to model the solidification process, and the effects of fin number, nanoparticle type, and nanoparticle concentration on solidification are investigated. The simulations are restricted to a two-dimensional 10 mm × 10 mm square enclosure in which solidification occurs, assuming constant thermophysical properties and the absence of nanoparticle agglomeration and sedimentation. Melting and repeated charge–discharge cycles are not considered. These modelling simplifications may lead to deviations from practical systems involving temperature-dependent properties, three-dimensional effects, nanoparticle instabilities, and cyclic melting–solidification behaviour. It is found that the number of fins has a significant effect on the improvement of heat extraction rate and the enhancement of the heat transfer during the solidification. Compared with the case without fins, eight fins reduce the liquid fraction by 33.3%, indicating enhanced solidification. The increase in the volume fraction of nanoparticles improves the thermal conductivity of the phase change material and the removal of the latent heat. The SiO 2 + h-BN + SWCNT combination exhibits the best performance among the studied ternary hybrid nanoparticles since h-BN and SWCNT have a high thermal conductivity. The reductions in PCM temperature and solidification time with eight fins and SiO 2 + h-BN + SWCNT nanoparticles at 6 vol.% are 8.75% and 38.0%, respectively, compared with the pure solar salt PCM without fins. Within the investigated configuration and modelling conditions, the application of fins and ternary hybrid nanoparticles can considerably enhance the solidification of the nano-enhanced solar salt.

title: 3D vascular quantitation with application to computational modeling: a pre-clinical light sheet microscopy, high resolution ultrasound, nano-computed tomography comparison study
authors: Daibo Zhang, Stéphanie E. Lindsey
abstract: It is increasingly necessary to both study biology in 3D and obtain quantitative measurements. Not all 3D-reconstructions are created equal, particularly when using the anatomical model as a basis for force calculations, i.e. computational modeling. Here, we compare 3D anatomical reconstructions from two emerging imaging modalities: 4D ultrasound (4DUS) and light sheet fluorescent microscopy (LSFM) against our previous nano-computed tomography (nanoCT) cohort data, using the tortuous highly intricate pharyngeal arch artery system of the chick embryo as a test bed. We highlight modality-specific morphological image acquisition discrepancies and their influence on subsequent computational fluid dynamics results. Overall, LSFM accurately captured quantitative volumetric measurements of small rapidly-changing vascular morphologies while 4DUS systematically inflated small tortuous vessels. Differences in image-based morphology changes led to significant changes in computationally-obtained force magnitudes and flow patterns linked to vessel angle and tortuosity. This validates LSFM as a comparative preclinical vascular quantitative imaging tool and suggests that 4DUS needs extensive 3D anatomical validation for non cardiac chamber vessels.

title: CFD-Based Numerical Optimization of the Thermal Performance of PCM-Integrated Hollow Bricks: Combined Effects of Cavity Geometry and Phase-Change Temperature under Hot-Climate Conditions
authors: Jawaher Hamden, Fatma Kria, Sirine Chtourou, Frédéric Kuznik, Moez Hammami, Mounir Baccar
abstract: Abstract This study presents a two-dimensional transient CFD investigation of the thermal performance of hollow bricks incorporating air, glass wool, and phase change materials under the hot-climate conditions of Kairouan, Tunisia. Five brick geometries and three PCMs-RT26, RT30, and RT34 were evaluated over a 24-h thermal cycle using ANSYS Fluent R19. The numerical model, based on the enthalpy-porosity method, was validated against experimental data from the literature, with a maximum deviation below 3%. The solid brick exhibited the highest thermal load, with an energy demand of 191.78 Wh·m⁻², whereas the air- and glass-wool-filled bricks reduced this value to 84.90 and 73.80 Wh·m⁻², respectively. Among the investigated PCMs, RT30 achieved the best balance between latent-heat activation and thermal regulation, with an energy demand of 77.90 Wh·m⁻² and a maximum liquid fraction of 0.45. RT26 melted completely but activated too early, while RT34 reached a maximum liquid fraction of only 0.27 and increased energy demand to 96.50 Wh·m⁻². Increasing the cavity number from 8 to 12 reduced the transmitted heat flux by up to 57.65% under the investigated configurations. Overall, glass wool provided the lowest energy demand, while PCM performance depended strongly on the compatibility between its melting range, cavity geometry, and imposed thermal cycle.

title: Orbital angular momentum recognition method in ocean turbulent environment based on HOG-KELM
authors: Jing-Kai Wang, Zhe Wu, Yi-Ran Wang, Hai-Yang Yu
abstract: To address the problem of orbital angular momentum (OAM) recognition in ocean turbulent environments, a Kernel Extreme Learning Machine (KELM) recognition model based on Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) features has been proposed. In this model, HOG is employed to extract discriminative features from OAM beam intensity patterns, and KELM combined with a one-vs-one multi-class classification strategy is used to further improve the robustness and stability of OAM mode identification. The performance of the proposed HOG-KELM model is compared with three representative comparison methods. Experimental results show that the HOG-KELM model can accurately identify OAM beams under weak turbulence. Under weak, moderate, and strong ocean turbulence conditions, the evaluation metrics of HOG-KELM are superior to those of the comparison methods, demonstrating the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed model for OAM beam recognition under ocean turbulence disturbances.

title: Assessment of the Eddy Viscosity-Based Turbulence Models on the Solution of the Highly Separated/Attached Flow
authors: T. Tunay, Ahmet Remzi Erkoç
abstract: The present study investigated performance of different turbulence models based on the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations to solve the flow over a backward-facing step (BFS). Three different turbulence models, i.e., Spalart-Allmaras, Realizable k-↋ and SST k-ω turbulence models, were investigated for the flow over BFS. The investigations were performed for the Reynolds number of Reh = 9.6 x 103 based on step height, h, and the free stream velocity, U∞. The results, which are validated against the experimental data, showed that the Spalart–Allmaras model predicted the reattachment length, Xr, with an error of 9.52%. The Realizable k-↋ and SST k-ω models overpredicted the reattachment length, Xr, by 26.7% and 38.1%, respectively. Within the recirculation region, however, the SST k-ω provided the best prediction of the streamwise velocity, with a maximum difference of 5% from the experimental measurements. The largest local difference of 191% was obtained with the Spalart–Allmaras model at x/h = 1.

title: From Static Material Design to Predictive Open-Loop Control via Chemistry–Architecture Coupling in a Moving-Boundary Reaction–Diffusion Framework
authors: Andualem Belachew Workie
abstract: Bioactive silicate ceramics, wollastonite (CaSiO 3 ), diopside (CaMgSi 2 O 6 ), and apatite-wollastonite glassceramics constitute a unique class of bone-regeneration materials whose therapeutic action is intrinsically coupled to their own degradation.Yet the field continues to design these materials as static objects, optimizing initial composition, porosity and elastic modulus while evaluating outcomes at fixed endpoints, tacitly ignoring the central fact that the physicochemical microenvironment they create evolves continuously and irreversibly.We argue that this temporal evolution is not a side effect but the therapeutic mechanism itself, and that it can be engineered predictively.This work consolidates and mathematically hardens the emerging paradigm of spatiotemporal trajectory engineering: the pre-encoded, open-loop programming of a degrading scaffold's full physicochemical trajectory through coupled control of ceramic network chemistry and pore-network architecture.Three advances over prior treatments are delivered.First, the solid-state chemistry foundation is deepened: Q n speciation from 29 Si MAS-NMR is mapped onto hydration versus hydrolysis activation barriers; the incongruent dissolution cascade (cation exchange → silica-gel layer → hydroxycarbonate apatite nucleation) is formalized as a coupled surface-gel-layer-precipitation problem; and the autocatalytic OH --feedback loop that drives local pH spikes is quantified, together with surface-specific XPS O 1s BO/NBO deconvolution as the front-tracking metric.Second, the static reaction-diffusion model is upgraded to a moving-boundary erosion formulation: an explicit porosity-evolution law, a dynamically self-consistent effective diffusivity, and interstitial convective (Brinkman) transport are introduced, yielding a two-dimensional Damköhler-Péclet regime map that delineates four phenomenologically distinct trajectory regimes, reaction-limited, diffusion-limited, convective washout, and convection-amplified dosing, plus a coupled design corridor where trajectory classes diverge maximally.Third, biological admissibility is replaced from discrete endpoint thresholds to a continuous phase-indexed Regenerative Target Zone (RTZ) envelope incorporating M1-gating, M2-switch, and HCA-maturation kinetics; and the computational pipeline is extended with functional data analysis (fPCA, DTW), neural ordinary differential equations, physicsinformed neural networks, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo credible tubes, and Bayesian-optimal experimental design.The resulting framework is fully specified, falsifiable, and implementable with open-source tools and standard instrumentation.It reclassifies the design problem from optimizing a material to programming an evolving microenvironment, and because the temporal program is pre-encoded without biological sensing, it qualifies as a passive implant under current regulatory frameworks.

title: Worker exposure to particulate matter and volatile organic compounds during semiconductor failure analysis: assessment of local exhaust ventilation using field measurements and computational fluid dynamics
authors: Yongsoon Park, Moung-hun Choung, Ji-seck Oh, Haeng-sub Roh, Chankyu Kang
abstract: Manual wafer cutting during semiconductor failure analysis generates particulate matter (PM), volatile organic compounds (TVOCs), and process odors that may contribute to worker inhalation exposure. This study evaluated PM and TVOC exposure conditions during wafer cutting and examined how a hybrid containment workbench (HCW) modified airflow patterns that may influence contaminant movement toward the worker breathing zone. PM and TVOC measurements were used to characterize exposure conditions during wafer-cutting operations, while airflow measurements, steady-state CFD analysis, qualitative smoke visualization, and worker questionnaires were used to evaluate changes associated with HCW implementation. Airflow characteristics were analyzed using computational fluid dynamics (CFD), quantitatively compared with measured air velocities, and qualitatively evaluated using smoke visualization. Worker questionnaires assessed perceived odor and dust exposure before and after HCW installation. TVOC concentrations observed during patterned-wafer cutting (0.12–0.15 mg/m³) were higher than those observed during bare-wafer cutting (0.02–0.03 mg/m³). CFD-predicted air velocities showed relative errors of 5.3–18.2% compared with the experimentally measured velocities. The HCW produced airflow directed toward the rear exhaust system, and reduced recirculation was observed near the breathing zone. Smoke visualization showed a similar airflow pattern. These findings indicate airflow conditions that may reduce the potential for contaminant movement toward the operator. Before HCW installation, 84.2% of workers (16/19) reported process odor perception, while worker-rated odor and dust control scores improved following HCW implementation. The results indicate that local airflow should be considered together with contaminant concentrations when evaluating worker exposure and local exhaust ventilation in semiconductor failure-analysis laboratories.

title: Real-time hydrogen gas explosion prediction from fuel cell vehicles by physics-informed graph neural network
authors: Junjie Li, Zonghao Xie, Jihao Shi, Xinyan Huang, Yuanjiang Chang, Guoming Chen
abstract: Hydrogen fuel cell vehicles (HFCVs) generate electricity from hydrogen via electrochemical reactions and offer an efficient, environmentally friendly pathway to the dual‑carbon targets. Nevertheless, hydrogen leakage can rapidly mix with air to form large flammable vapor clouds. In congested urban areas, the resulting vapor cloud explosions may cause severe structural damage and significant economic losses. Machine learning techniques have been developed to predict the evolution of gas explosions. Nevertheless, accurately capturing the spatial relationships among obstacles and predicting explosion overpressure evolution remain challenging. This study proposes a physics-informed graph neural network model (Physics_ARGNN) for real-time blast wave prediction of hydrogen gas explosion from HFCV in congested urban environment. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations are conducted to model hydrogen gas explosions within urban blocks and to build a benchmark dataset. Using this dataset, the optimal physics factor λ = 1 × 10 −3 was determined, enabling the proposed Physics_ARGNN to achieve an R 2 of 0.9556 and an MSE of 6.94 × 10 −5 for blast wave prediction, and an R 2 of 0.9806 and an MSE of 1.80 × 10 −4 for peak overpressure prediction, outperforming state-of-the-art models while maintaining real-time capability.

title: Crystallinity development in material extrusion additive manufacturing of semicrystalline polymers: A review
authors: Francesca Aliberti, T. Hashemi, Sara Liparoti, Roberto Pantani
abstract: The use of semicrystalline polymers in Material extrusion additive manufacturing (MEAM) remains challenging due to the complex interplay among thermal history, crystallisation kinetics and flow dynamics. The rapid, non-isothermal conditions inherent to the process govern nucleation, crystal growth, and molecular orientation, ultimately determining the microstructure and the resulting mechanical, thermal, and structural properties of printed parts. This review has provided the current state of the art on the analysis of crystallinity development in MEAM of semicrystalline polymers. Fundamental aspects of quiescent and flow-induced nucleation have been discussed alongside modelling strategies that couple heat transfer with crystallisation kinetics. Modelling studies have been reviewed to understand the current accuracy of simulation tools in the prediction of temperature profile, crystallinity degree and dimensions of spherulitic structures. The role of process parameters in determining the mechanical performance has been critically analysed. Particular attention has been given to the competition between crystallisation and interfacial diffusion, which governs interlayer bonding and mechanical performance. The analysis has revealed that process parameters impact on the cooling rate, the polymer chain orientation, part density and porosity beyond the crystallinity degree. Emerging methods for monitoring crystallisation phenomena during the MEAM process have been reviewed, highlighting that X-ray diffraction remains the most precise. Strategies for controlling crystallinity, including process optimisation and thermal post-treatments, have also been examined in relation to their role in improving mechanical performance. Morphological features typical of MEAM-printed semicrystalline polymers have been collected, such as anisotropic structures due to flow-induced crystallisation on the filament surface and larger spherulites in the inner region under quasi-quiescent conditions. Finally, emerging machine learning methodologies have been discussed as promising tools for capturing the complex, multivariate nature of MEAM and enabling predictive materials design.

title: Physics-informed neural control of heat flow rate in a counter-flow heat exchanger: modeling, identification and experimental validation
authors: Konstantinos Skantzikas, Emmanuel Witrant, Bojan Mavkov
abstract: The advanced operation of heat exchangers plays a critical role in the development of efficient and sustainable multivector energy systems. This paper proposes a hybrid physics-informed and data-driven framework for the analysis, identification, and regulation of transient heat transfer in counter-flow heat exchangers. A parameterized physical model combines classical heat-transfer relations with transport equations to capture convective propagation, transport-induced delays, and nonlinear effects associated with flow-rate variations. The heat-transfer coefficient is identified from experimental data, enabling the characterization of flow-dependent heat-transfer dynamics over a broad operating range. The identified model is then used to develop a hierarchical real-time control strategy. An inner loop regulates the volumetric flow rate using a high-order data-driven linear model, while an outer loop regulates the exchanged heat power using a machine-learning controller initially trained on the physical model and subsequently refined with experimental data. Experimental results demonstrate accurate reproduction of transient heat-transfer dynamics and effective heat-flow-rate regulation under varying thermal boundary conditions (identification fit above 94\% in normalized root-mean-square error and total variation of the flow rate reduced by half compared to a proportional-integral controller). The proposed framework combines physical interpretability with data-driven adaptation for the analysis and real-time operation of dynamic heat-transfer systems.

title: Adjoint-based corrective approach for nodal indoor air quality predictions
authors: Nicolas Carnec, Martin Ferrand, Thierry Duforestel, Bénédicte Wall-Ribot, Marc Abadie, Karim Limam
abstract: Indoor Air Quality (IAQ) modelling in building simulations often relies on the nodal approach to evaluate exposure to airborne pollutants. This approach assumes perfect mixing within each zone, which can lead to significant discrepancies compared to CFD predictions, especially under complex airflow configurations. To address this limitation, this study proposes a correction model that modifies the nodal scalar mass balance using a correction factor derived from CFD results. These factors are designed to recover CFD-based spatial average concentrations at steady state while preserving scalar mass conservation through consistency with steady state CFD outlet scalar mass fluxes. To limit the computational cost, an adjoint scalar transport approach is used, enabling the computation of correction factors for all possible emission positions from a number of CFD simulations only equal to twice the number of outlets, for a given geometry and airflow configuration. The method is evaluated on a multizone residential case under isothermal conditions. The results show that the proposed approach significantly improves the prediction of mean concentrations compared to the classical nodal approach, while maintaining a much lower computational cost than forward CFD simulations. Residual discrepancies are mainly associated with transient behaviour, due to the simplified dynamics of the nodal formulation. These results highlight the potential of the method for improving scalar concentration predictions in practical isothermal applications, while also emphasizing that the correction factors remain dependent on the airflow configuration.

title: Studying oscillation death in two-dimensional cylinder-airfoil interactions with synchronization-theoretic autoencoder
authors: Yuta Ushida, Daiki Beppu, Yuzuru Kato, Kai Fukami
abstract: Body-body interactions have long been investigated to leverage the performance of various fluid-based machines. This study analyzes the flow interaction between a cylinder and a NACA0012 airfoil using direct numerical simulation and machine learning. We consider a two-dimensional incompressible flow at Reynolds number 100, where the airfoil is positioned in the wake of a cylinder. By sweeping the parameter space, composed of the distance between the cylinder and the airfoil $Δx$, the relative height $Δy$, and the angle of attack of the airfoil $α$, four characteristic vortex-shedding regimes are observed. This study particularly focuses on suppressed vortex shedding at a certain arrangement as oscillation death in coupled oscillators, with the theoretical prediction of flow stability on a machine-learned low-order coordinate. Independent flows around each body are regarded as a system that exhibits isolated periodic vortex shedding at infinite distance, and interactions appear at smaller distances. We employ a synchronization-theoretic autoencoder to derive models for two coupled oscillators from an aerodynamic coefficient. The proposed approach, which enables the assessment of system stability and the prediction of vortical interaction behavior, may pave the way for the analysis of unsteady body-body interactions from the data-driven and synchronization perspectives.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Heat Transfer and Fluid Flow in a Channel with Isothermal Staggered Wall-Mounted Squares
authors: Igor Wolf, Ozren Bukovac, Mateo Kirinčić, Paolo Blecich
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have been increasingly used for thermal-fluid problems. This study evaluates the performance of the PINN approach for reconstructing laminar forced flow field inside a rectangular channel with four staggered wall-mounted squares. Air is used as the working fluid, at a Reynolds number of Re = 100 and a Prandtl number of Pr = 0.71. The four squares are isothermal at 80 °C while the inlet fluid temperature is 20 °C. The PINN is used to predict velocity, pressure and temperature fields, as well as local and average Nusselt numbers. The PINN solutions are verified against the reference finite volume solution with 225,000 control volumes. The PINN was trained on 100, 250, 1000 and 4000 velocity and temperature sample points. Without samples the PINN fails, with streamwise velocity and temperature errors equal to 65% and 144%, respectively. With 1000 uniformly placed samples throughout the domain, the streamwise and cross-stream velocity errors are 2.4% and 13.0%, respectively. The error for the recovered pressure field is 18.6% while the error in the temperature field is 7.7%. The Nusselt number is underpredicted by 35% and increasing the sample count to 4000 points yields only a marginal improvement. A significant improvement is obtained by placing sample points inside the thermal boundary layer of the isothermal squares. The relative errors in temperature, streamwise velocity, and pressure are reduced to 5.9%, 1.6%, and 9.9%, respectively, while the error in the average Nusselt number decreases to 17% when 35% of the 1000 sample points are placed in the thermal boundary layer.

title: Computational Fluid Dynamics in Biological Systems
authors: Nasiru Musa Haruna, Abdulhalim Musa Abubakar, Yusufu Luka, Hamadou Mamoudou, Muhammad Tariq, Gaurav Kumar Pandit, Rezkallah Chafika, Zannatul Nayem
abstract: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) plays a crucial role in the analysis and simulation of fluid flow in biological systems. From blood flow in arteries to airflow in lungs, CFD models help in understanding the underlying mechanisms that govern biological processes. This article explores the application of CFD in biological systems, highlighting its potential in healthcare, medical diagnostics, and bioengineering. By incorporating various biological parameters and physiological conditions, CFD can provide insights into the behavior of fluids in complex biological systems, aiding in the development of more effective treatments and medical devices.

title: Applications of Advanced Computational Techniques
authors: Sahin Ahmed, Nava Jyoti Hazarika
abstract: This study presents a novel investigation into the behavior of microbes that move in bio-convective fluid in connection with key fluid variables in a non-Darcy porous medium. The incorporation of nanoparticles into base fluids enhances thermal conductivity, but their tendency to agglomerate often reduces fluid stability. This challenge is addressed by introducing motile microorganisms into nanofluids, which improve both fluid stability and mass transport while further enhancing thermal conductivity. In this study, the behavior of microbes in bio-convective fluid is investigated for the influences of magnetic fluid; Bioconvection Lewis number and Forchheimer drag force in a porous medium which is not Darcy medium. The study focused on a two-dimensional magnetic fluid in a Prandtl-character nanofluid that flows along an angled extended sheet while being influenced by inlet and output flow rates. The relevant mathematical adjustments are used to define and solve the governing equations for heat transfer, fluid flow, and bioconvection. A stability study is performed to verify the stability of the finite difference scheme after the modified ODEs are solved using the built-in bvp4c solver in MATLAB. The results demonstrate the significant influence of fluid parameters, such as bioconvection and magnetic effects, on velocity, temperature, and concentration profiles. The results show that shear stress and thermal diffusion rates increase with higher inclination angle ( δ ) and bioconvection parameter ( β ), while the Sherwood number decreases with increasing ( δ ). The origination of this work lies in analyzing nanofluid stability, microbial motion, and transmission of warm dynamics together in a non-Darcy porous medium, offering valuable perceptions for improving thermal and mass transport processes.

title: Simulation Techniques for Fluid Dynamics Problems
authors: Eny Tayang, Sahin Ahmed
abstract: The novelty of this investigation is to highlight the behavior of hydromagnetic flow of a water-based nanofluid that is chemically reacting across a vertical channel that has porosity and heat production. The vertical channel of porous wall uses water as the base fluid where SWCNT and MWCNT are immersed. The tool of similarity transformations reduces the leading system of PDEs to nonlinear ODEs, which are then analytically solved using the perturbation approach. The visual outputs of better configuration have been derived in connection with the prime fluid variables via MATLAB algorithms. With the fluids of constant viscosity and variable viscosity, the plotted curves of the nanofluid velocity, temperature, and concentration for the relevant material parameters are shown. This work has numerous applications, such as solar collectors and geothermal reservoirs. In aerospace and automotive industries, such research can guide the development of lightweight, high-performance thermal management systems. The inclusion of both constant viscosity and variable viscosity of fluids extends the applicability of the findings to a broader range of practical scenarios, including polymers, biological fluids, and other complex fluids used in advanced engineering systems. The current study is unusual in that it considers a first-order homogeneous chemical reaction in addition to porosity and the generation of heat.

title: Mathematical Techniques for Environmental Fluid Dynamics
authors: Km Shelly Chaudhary, Lalit Mohan
abstract: In this research, we have examined the fractional model of Oil Spill in Caputo sense by an efficient numerical technique. Water pollution due to oil leaks has serious side effects on the marine life. It is critical to predict the area of oil spread earlier in order to take corrective action against the disaster and safeguard the environment and marine life. We can forecast the spillage area by using the model that controls the flow field and mass transport phenomena. The fractional Diffusion equation is used to model the process of Oil Spill. The Laplace Adomian decomposition technique is utilized for finding solution of the given model. The presented technique is an excellent combination of Laplace transform and Adomian polynomial-based technique. The Laplace transform effectively takes care of the nonlinearity and other constraints. The Adomian polynomial decomposes the nonlinear term and reduces the computational difficulties. We have solved two different test examples of the given problem. The solution is analyzed by two-dimensional as well as three-dimensional graphical representations. The solutions of the presented approaches are collated with other numerical techniques and supremacy of the presented technique is established with the help of tabulated data.

title: From solar heat to digital drying: integrating computational fluid dynamics, process optimisation, and digital twins for sustainable tuber-chip drying
authors: Chinyere Nneoma Ugwu
abstract: Root and tuber crops such as cassava, yam, and sweet potato are central to tropical food systems but remain highly vulnerable to postharvest deterioration because of their high moisture content. Solar drying offers a renewable route to stabilisation, yet practical performance is constrained by fluctuating weather, non-uniform airflow, spatial temperature and humidity gradients, product loading, and strong coupling between external convection and internal moisture transport. This structured narrative mini-review, informed by SANRA and PRISMA reporting principles, synthesises evidence on active solar drying, computational fluid dynamics (CFD), experimental validation, response-surface and multi-objective optimisation, artificial intelligence (AI), sensor systems, and digital twins for tuber-chip processing. Six databases were searched, sources were screened against explicit eligibility criteria, and each of the 45 cited sources was classified by its relationship to tuber-chip drying so that tuber-specific evidence is separated from evidence transferred from other foods and dryer types. Only 12 of the 45 sources were tuber-specific; they concentrate on yam drying kinetics, cassava dryer performance, and one integrated machine-learning and 4E study of sweet-potato solar drying. CFD validation, robust optimisation, surrogate modelling, and digital-twin architectures are, in the evidence assembled, largely transferred from other products or from unloaded or non-tuber systems. Reported effective moisture diffusivities for yam span roughly 6.4 × 10 −9 to 1.6 × 10 −7 m 2 s -1 (up to 4.2 × 10 −8 m 2 s -1 for water yam); an indirect solar dryer for sweet potato achieved 15% overall thermal efficiency, 4.5 kWh per kilogram of moisture removed, and a 29-month payback; and a CFD–ANN–genetic-algorithm framework reproduced no-load airflow and temperature fields to within 7.3% error. Because these values arise from different dryers, products, and metric definitions, they are compared critically rather than ranked. The evidence suggests that CFD is most valuable when it resolves spatial transport phenomena that cannot be inferred from inlet and outlet measurements, and that AI is most defensible when it accelerates validated physics rather than replacing it. A prioritised research agenda is proposed, beginning with tuber-specific property data and loaded-dryer CFD validated against product moisture, and progressing conditionally to robust optimisation, validated surrogates, digital shadows, and multidimensional sustainability assessment for cassava, yam, and sweet-potato chips.

title: Numerical Methods in Fluid Dynamics and Disease Modeling
authors: Anil Nangkar, Sahin Ahmed, Bikash Das
abstract: Understanding the influence of arterial stenosis on blood flow behavior is an important step toward improving therapeutic strategies for vascular diseases. Although numerous investigations have addressed stenosis-induced changes in hemodynamics, the combined role of stenosis location, bioconvection, and nanoparticle transport has received limited attention. In this chapter, blood flow characteristics and transport behavior are examined in a bifurcating carotid artery using finite element simulations performed in COMSOL Multiphysics. Two geometrical configurations are considered: stenosis located in the common carotid artery before bifurcation and stenosis positioned in the internal carotid artery after bifurcation. Blood is modelled as an incompressible Newtonian fluid, and the analysis is carried out under varying non-dimensional parameters, including the Bioconvection Rayleigh number, Reynolds number, and Hartmann number, to assess flow dynamics, transport characteristics, and magnetic field effects. The results indicate that prebifurcation stenosis produces higher flow velocities due to upstream constriction, whereas post-bifurcation stenosis leads to enhanced accumulation of nanoparticles and microorganisms in the external carotid artery, particularly at lower Reynolds numbers. The presence of an applied magnetic field introduces a velocity-damping mechanism, demonstrating the capability of magnetohydrodynamic control to regulate arterial flow behavior. Temperature distribution is also influenced by stenosis location and bioconvective effects, with post-bifurcation stenosis exhibiting a greater rise in temperature and wider downstream thermal spread compared to the pre-bifurcation configuration. These observations highlight the significant role of stenosis positioning and magnetic fields in modulating hemodynamics, heat transfer, and targeted transport within bifurcating arteries. The findings provide useful insights for the design of magnetically guided drug delivery systems and improved therapeutic interventions for vascular disorders.

title: Hemodynamic Assessment of Bleb Formation in Patient-Specific Intracranial Aneurysms using Computational Fluid Dynamics
authors: S. Valiallah Mousavi, M. Barzegar Gerdroodbary, Iman Shiryanpoor, Peiman Valipour
abstract: Bleb formation is widely recognized as an important morphological indicator of intracranial aneurysm instability and rupture risk. However, the hemodynamic mechanisms associated with bleb development remain incompletely understood. In this study, patient-specific computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations were performed to investigate the influence of bleb formation on the hemodynamic environment of intracranial aneurysms. Three aneurysm geometries were reconstructed from medical imaging data and analyzed before and after bleb formation. Blood flow was modeled as a pulsatile, incompressible, laminar, and non-Newtonian fluid using the Casson rheological model, while vessel walls were assumed rigid. The transient Navier–Stokes equations were solved using ANSYS Fluent under physiologically realistic boundary conditions. Key hemodynamic parameters, including wall shear stress (WSS), wall pressure, blood velocity, oscillatory shear index (OSI), and flow streamlines, were evaluated and compared between the original and blebbed aneurysm models. The results demonstrated that the hemodynamic impact of bleb formation strongly depends on aneurysm geometry. In Patient A, bleb formation reduced the mean WSS by approximately 4.1% while increasing the mean sac pressure, velocity, and OSI by 1.7%, 5.9%, and 76.2%, respectively, indicating a substantial alteration of the local flow environment. In contrast, Patients B and C exhibited only minor changes in the averaged hemodynamic parameters following bleb formation, despite maintaining extremely low WSS and high OSI values. Flow visualizations revealed the development of localized recirculation zones and low-velocity vortices within the bleb cavity, resulting in increased flow oscillation and prolonged blood residence time. These disturbed flow conditions may contribute to wall degeneration and aneurysm instability. The findings suggest that blebs act as hemodynamically vulnerable regions characterized by complex flow structures and elevated oscillatory behavior. Patient-specific geometry plays a critical role in determining the extent to which bleb formation alters aneurysm hemodynamics and potentially influences rupture risk.

title: Determination and Standardization of Air Conditioning Requirements for Lecture Rooms: A Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) Modeling and Analysis
authors: Adam F. Rombaoa, Shaye Caroline G. Manlupig, Angelica T. Pangilinan
abstract: This study presents the air-conditioning requirements for a typical lecture room at Tarlac State University by integrating cooling load calculations with computational fluid dynamics focused on thermal comfort simulation. Cooling loads for a 9 m × 7 m × 2.8 m classroom accommodating 51 occupants are calculated based on the Carrier E20 method and Department of Energy guidelines, yielding a peak cooling load of 12.12 kW for top-floor classrooms and 10.20 kW for lower floors, corresponding to two 2.5 HP and two 2.0 HP air-conditioning units, respectively. CFD simulations are performed to assess air temperature, velocity distribution, and Predicted Mean Vote at different positions for window-type and wall-mounted split-type ACUs, considering three volume flow rates with a supply air temperature of 14 °C. Results show that increasing airflow improves air mixing and shifts PMV toward the ASHRAE-recommended comfort range of −0.5 to +0.5. Optimal thermal comfort was achieved within the range of 0.25–0.35 m³/s, with 0.25 m³/s providing near-neutral conditions and 0.35 m³/s yielding slightly cool conditions, equivalent to setting the ACU to 23°C and 21 °C, respectively. Also, the results indicate that the upper position is the optimal installation location for the window-type ACU. For a temperature setting of 24 °C, simulation results indicate slightly warm conditions, particularly at lower airflow rates. The findings of this study contribute to practical recommendations for ACU sizing, placement, and operation.

title: Complex Systems and Nonlinear Dynamics
authors: Dahiru Abdurrahman, Maheshwar Pathak, Pratibha Joshi
abstract: In this paper, the application of the Modified Variational Iteration Method (MVIM) for efficiently solving systems of differential equations encountered in many scientific and engineering applications has been discussed mainly. Differential equations are important mathematical tools for modeling dynamic processes in physics, biology, chemical engineering, electric circuits, mechanical systems, etc. However, solving these systems can still be challenging, especially for nonlinear or complex boundary and initial conditions, using standard analytical or numerical techniques. The Modified Variational Iteration Method (MVIM) is a significant improvement with respect to the classical Variational Iteration Method (VIM) by avoiding such repeated and cumbersome operations that are required at each stage of this iterative work. Such an enhancement makes the algorithm more efficient and decreases the computational effort, making the approach more practical for a wider range of applications. The MVIM produces a sequence of approximate solutions that rapidly converges to an exact or a very accurate solution of the original ordinary equation. Several illustrative examples are used to demonstrate the effectiveness, accuracy, and simplicity of the MVIM for solving the linear and nonlinear systems of differential equations. The results confirm that the proposed approach is not only easy to solve but also capable of producing reliable results with a low computational cost. Due to its flexibility, lower computational costs, and simplicity of implementation, the MVIM is recommended as an alternative semi-analytical method in solving complex differential equations problems that often appear in modern scientific and engineering problems. In this study, some specific examples have been taken from the field of fluid dynamics and disease modeling.

title: A physics-guided Fourier neural operator to predict wind-driven water film/rivulet flows pertinent to aircraft icing phenomena
authors: Jincheng Wang, Charlelie Laurent, Suhas S. Jain, Hui Hu
abstract: Aircraft icing poses a critical threat to aviation safety in cold climates, with the dynamic glaze ice accretion process governed by the transient behaviour of wind-driven runback water film and rivulet (WDRWF/R) flows on wing surfaces. Despite its significance, accurately modelling this complex multiphase flow phenomenon remains a fundamental challenge for conventional numerical and theoretical approaches. This study introduces a physics-guided Fourier neural operator (PGFNO) that achieves unprecedented accuracy in predicting the spatiotemporal evolution of WDRWF/R flows relevant to aircraft icing. To establish a high-fidelity training dataset, we conducted an extensive experimental campaign utilising a novel digital image projection (DIP) technique, which enables temporally and spatially resolved measurements of water film thickness distributions over a flat plate under diverse operating conditions. The PGFNO architecture incorporates a composite loss function that enforces physical constraints, ensuring both accurate field reconstruction and mass conservation. The trained model demonstrates robust predictive capability across a wide range of flow conditions, including extrapolation to unseen wind speeds, water flow rates and initial conditions, while accurately capturing both the film thickness field and its spectral characteristics. A comprehensive ablation study systematically evaluates the contributions of key architectural components to model performance, including the physics-guided loss function, embedding-layer configuration and Fourier mode/block selection. Long-term predictions via recurrent forecasting achieve errors approaching the experimental uncertainty of DIP measurements, while robustness tests with spatially distributed random noise confirm exceptional model stability. These results establish PGFNO as a powerful predictive framework for complex multiphase flows, with direct implications for aircraft icing prediction and mitigation strategies.

title: Rheology of dense suspensions of granular spherocylinders by particle-based simulation
authors: Alex Dixon, John H.E. Hone, Gavin Melaugh, Christopher Ness
abstract: Dense suspensions of rod-shaped granular particles are widespread in nature and manufacturing, where their fluid mechanical properties are often paramount. We have developed a particle-based simulation that models such suspensions under simple shear flow, providing predictions of the viscosity and microstructure for a given solids volume fraction and particle aspect ratio. The model tracks the trajectories of spherocylindrical rods under the action of short-range frictional contact and hydrodynamic forces, inspired by similar tools that have generated new insight into suspensions of granular spheres. It incorporates new schemes for the computation of lubrication forces between spherocylinders and the dynamic determination of the time step. For aspect ratios up to 20, the model predicts a viscosity spike at shear startup, giving way to steady-state viscosities that increase systematically with volume fraction and aspect ratio. Likewise, particle alignment increases with volume fraction up to an aspect-ratio-dependent critical point. Our model corroborates the limited experimental rheology data available for suspensions of granular rods, and offers a tool for fundamental exploration of the fluid mechanics, microstructure and rheology of this widespread material.

title: Attachment-line turbulent boundary layer over a swept leading edge at Mach 6: Simulation and flow physics
authors: Youcheng Xi, Song Fu
abstract: Direct numerical simulations (DNS) are performed to investigate the spatial evolution of a three-dimensional (3-D) turbulent boundary layer over a swept blunt leading edge at freestream Mach number upper M Subscript normal infinity Baseline equals 6.0 M ∞ = 6.0 $M_\infty =6.0$ and unit Reynolds number 1.8 times 10 Superscript 7 Baseline m Superscript negative 1 1.8 × 10 7 m − 1 $1.8 \times 10^7\,\text{m}^{-1}$ . Unlike canonical configurations, this flow evolves continuously from a quasi-two-dimensional equilibrium state at the attachment line to a highly 3-D, non-equilibrium state downstream under strong geometry-induced pressure gradients. The near-wall turbulent streaks exhibit a pronounced structural lag, characterised by an ordered angular response of the streak orientation relative to the external streamline and the wall shear direction. This lag is accompanied by a progressive stress depletion: the Townsend structure parameter collapses below its equilibrium value, and the turbulent kinetic energy budget reveals a global production deficit, indicating a progressive chordwise tendency towards relaminarisation. Spectral analysis further shows that this relaminarisation tendency is scale-selective – low-wavenumber motions are strongly suppressed within the resolved DNS domain, whereas highly organised, skewed near-wall streaks survive. The temperature field remains structurally locked to these residual momentum streaks throughout the process, with the strong Reynolds analogy holding robustly, while wall-normal and lateral thermal transport are effectively extinguished. The dataset exposes fundamental limitations of linear eddy-viscosity closures in this regime and provides a benchmark for developing advanced models capable of capturing such strongly non-equilibrium 3-D boundary layers.

title: A Fundamental CFD Study of a Plate-Type Foil Gas Thrust Bearing
authors: Seung Mok Hwang, Jongin Yang
abstract: A CFD-based analysis was conducted to investigate the gas lubrication film behavior of a plate-type foil gas thrust bearing. The gas film thickness was varied to evaluate its effects on thermo-fluid characteristics, pressure distribution, and axial load capacity. In addition, laminar and turbulence models were applied to examine transition effects and the influence of heat transfer coefficients. The results show that decreasing film thickness significantly increases pressure gradients and shear stresses, leading to higher axial load capacity and power loss, particularly in the thin film region. Thermal effects cause substantial temperature rise due to viscous heating, strongly affecting bearing performance. Furthermore, the flow is predominantly laminar under thin film conditions, while turbulence models tend to underestimate axial load in fully laminar regimes. These findings highlight the importance of appropriate flow modeling and thermal boundary conditions for accurate performance prediction.

title: Performance Evaluation of Low-Pressure Axial Turbine using CFD-based Throughflow Method
authors: Minsuk Choi, Dae Hyun Kim, Donghwa Kim
abstract: The CFD-based throughflow (TF) method was applied to assess the accuracy of predicting the performance of a low-pressure axial turbine. In comparison to commercial CFD analyses, the CFD-based TF accurately estimated the performance parameters such as the choking mass flow rate, expansion ratio and total-to-total efficiency for an initial axial turbine design within minutes. Evaluation against the performance test results for the final manufactured axial turbine revealed that the CFD-based TF yielded predictions of the mass flow rate, expansion ratio and efficiency with a maximum error of 1.61%. However, limitations of the CFD-based TF were identified in resolving the passage vortex and the tip clearance flow due to its characteristics using only a singe computational cell in the pitchwise direction, leading to a local numerical error increase near 20% and 80% spans particularly influenced by these two flow features. Despite these constraints, the demonstrated accuracy suggests potential for integrating the CFD-based TF into the axial turbine design process for predicting the performance quickly.

title: Surrogate-Guided Generative Modeling with Physics Verification for Expensive Multiphysics Inverse Problems
authors: Hyungjun Kim, Alessandro Persico, Logan Burnett, Benoit Forget, Majdi I. Radaideh
abstract: High-fidelity multiphysics simulations provide physically rich information for nuclear reactor analysis, but their computational cost often limits the duration and diversity of conditions that can be practically simulated. This work introduces a physics-informed guided generative modeling framework that learns from limited high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) data and expands them into a searchable distribution of candidate states for coupled-physics inverse problems. Tabular generative models learn assembly-level spatial patterns from high-fidelity CFD simulations, while a differentiable surrogate guides candidate generation toward improved responses from a downstream neutronics model. Importantly, the surrogate is used only for sampling-time guidance; every generated candidate is independently evaluated by SIMULATE3 (a neutronics solver), ensuring that optimization decisions remain grounded in verified physics calculations. Two strategies are developed to balance prior fidelity, exploration, and computational cost: a hybrid explorer--generator framework and a more economical rank-weighted generative framework. The methodology is demonstrated for assembly-level DLT field inference for fuel assembly bowing using the BEAVRS benchmark. Starting from a baseline detector root-mean-square (RMS) error mismatch of approximately 5.1%, brute-force evaluation of the CFD-informed dataset alone achieved 4.2%, whereas generative optimization reduced the best verified RMS to 1.86%. The rank-weighted TabDDPM framework reached 2.08% using substantially fewer SIMULATE3 evaluations, while TabDiff reached 3.12\% with greater spatial smoothness. The results further show that improved detector agreement requires controlled exploration beyond direct reproduction of the CFD prior. Overall, the proposed framework establishes a general strategy for combining limited high-fidelity data, generative exploration, surrogate guidance, and continuous physics verification to enable computationally tractable inverse analysis of expensive multiphysics systems.

title: Learning PDE solution operators with variable initial conditions via Latent Dynamics Networks
authors: Stefano Maria Pizzamiglio, Stefano Pagani, Regazzoni, Francesco
abstract: In many-query scenarios, data-driven surrogate models provide an efficient alternative to high-fidelity solvers for simulating physical systems governed by Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). In this context, the Latent Dynamics Network (LDNet) has recently demonstrated remarkable performance in predicting the response of spatio-temporal systems, combining Neural Ordinary Differential Equations with nonlinear dimensionality reduction. However, the original formulation assumes a fixed initial condition, limiting its applicability to many real-world applications where a system evolves from varying starting states. In this work, we overcome this limitation while keeping the end-to-end training procedure of the original LDNet and its encoder-free nature, which preserves its intrinsic independence from spatial resolution and grid topology. We infer the initial latent state directly from a small set of early-time observations, treating latent-state initialization as an adaptation problem, and investigate two strategies: an auto-decoding formulation and a meta-learning approach in which the initial latent state acts as a task-specific context variable. We demonstrate the accuracy of the proposed methods across diverse physical phenomena, spanning advection-diffusion, fluid dynamics, and solid mechanics. Meta-learning markedly accelerates latent-state inference and induces smoother, better-conditioned optimization landscapes, and spontaneously organizes the latent space into a structured representation that reflects physically meaningful features of the underlying dynamics. The coordinate-based decoder enables training from spatially subsampled data while recovering high-resolution solution fields at inference. The resulting approach provides an efficient and resolution-independent surrogate modeling framework for many-query simulations of time-dependent PDEs with varying initial conditions.

title: Physically Organized Latent Spaces in Unsupervised Autoencoders: Evidence from Aerodynamic Databases
authors: Renato Tognaccini, Ettore Saetta, Gianluca Iaccarino
abstract: Using aerodynamic databases of progressively increasing complexity - from linear analytical theory to nonlinear separated RANS flows - we demonstrate that an autoencoder, trained solely by reconstruction, can spontaneously organize the latent representation according to physically meaningful variables and aerodynamic laws. Although the latent coordinates themselves vary under random initialization, the underlying physical organization is reproducible, even quantitatively. In addition, we present a three-dimensional latent space representation of the airfoil flow obtained by an unsupervised autoencoder with sequential training in which the inviscid field is decoupled from the boundary layer effects with the third latent variable strongly correlated with the Reynolds number and aerodynamic drag. Cross-validated regression and affine-alignment measures show that physical parameters and responses are strongly and linearly encoded in the learned coordinates, consistently across independent trainings.

title: Shaping the Wind: Nested Potentials for Kinematically Admissible Urban Wind Prediction
authors: Yidi Wang, Zhang, Yunhe, Jiawei Gu, Ziyue Qiao, Pengyang Wang
abstract: Predicting transient urban winds is fundamental to understanding urban microclimates and designing climate-resilient cities. Building-resolving large-eddy simulation produces detailed incompressible urban wind fields at substantial computational cost for each layout. Neural surrogates offer a faster alternative by learning to predict the evolution of velocity fields. However, minimizing velocity prediction error does not guarantee local mass conservation and wall impermeability, which together define kinematic admissibility. This limitation stems from an unconstrained output representation: geometry conditioning guides predictions but does not restrict them to admissible velocity fields. Correcting boundary violations in these outputs changes the flux balance in adjacent fluid cells and may consequently compromise local mass conservation. To address the challenge, we propose Sculpt, a nested potential framework that builds the coupled, geometry-dependent constraints directly into its parameterization. This nested parameterization generates divergence-free velocity updates through the discrete curl of a volume vector potential on the native three-dimensional staggered grid. A shared scalar potential constrains the vector potential's boundary values so that the same operator also enforces impermeability, without a per-step pressure projection. Because backpropagation through this curl attenuates large-scale gradient signals, we parameterize the volume potential at multiple resolutions to better capture large-scale flow structures. We introduce UrbanWindFlow, an LES dataset spanning urban morphologies and inflow conditions, to evaluate accuracy and kinematic admissibility together.

title: The interplay of coronary serial stenoses and their deceptive impact on hemodynamic and surgical planning
authors: Luca Mariani, Guido Nannini, Marta Pillitteri, Simone Saitta, Riccardo Maragna, Gianluca Pontone, Alberto Cesare Luigi Redaelli
abstract: BACKGROUND: Assessing serial stenoses in coronary artery disease (CAD) remains a difficult task, as hemodynamic interactions between lesions can mask individual severity. In this work, we present an automated and non-invasive decision tree-based framework that integrates computational fluid dynamics (CFD)-derived indices with CAD-RADS classification to guide revascularization strategies in cases of serial stenoses. METHODS: A dataset of 400 virtual coronary artery models was generated from 20 patients' anatomies, augmented with serial stenosis severities (CAD-RADS system) and boundary condition configurations. CFD simulations were performed to compute key hemodynamic parameters, including FFR, ΔFFR, ΔP, and PPG. Simulations also evaluated the impact of different angioplasty strategies, including proximal, distal, and combined revascularization. A decision tree was developed to classify cases based on lesion severity and hemodynamic interaction and was validated through a clinical survey answered by experienced cardiologists. RESULTS: CFD simulations revealed notable hemodynamic interactions between lesions. In over 20% of cases, distal angioplasty revealed proximal FFR changes from a non-significant to a significant value (<0.8). Conversely, proximal angioplasty improved distal FFR beyond 0.8. The proposed decision tree outperformed FFR- and stenosis grade-based approaches, achieving an AUC of 0.98 and an accuracy of 0.97 when validated against CFD-based angioplasty simulations. Furthermore, it showed 81.2% agreement with clinicians' final decisions when informed by CFD and reduced iterative invasive procedures by 20%. CONCLUSIONS: This study showed that the proposed CFD-based decision framework enhances accuracy in managing serial CAD by capturing lesion interactions, improving surgical planning precision, reducing patient risk, and supporting more consistent, efficient clinical decision-making.
