title: Dynamic Quadtree Tokenization and Transformer for Adaptive Mesh PDE Forecasting
authors: Yilin Zhuang, Noah Zambrano, Karthik Duraisamy
abstract: The quadratic attention cost of Vision Transformers (ViTs) forces a trade-off between spatial resolution and rollout horizon, particularly for fine-scale PDEs where shocks, reaction fronts, and material interfaces occupy small, evolving regions of the domain. Conventional neural surrogates also lack mechanisms to adapt resolution dynamically. We propose WAMRViT, a ViT that tokenizes inputs as balanced quadtrees using a wavelet-inspired refinement criterion, jointly encodes position and refinement level with 3D rotary positional embeddings, and regrids in cell space during inference for stable long-horizon rollouts. A multi-scale variant retains each leaf at its native source resolution and lets the model learn across resolution levels. Unlike fixed-budget adaptive-tokenization methods, WAMRViT imposes no predetermined token count and supports fully adaptive topology throughout autoregressive rollout. To our knowledge, it is the first machine-learning surrogate to natively tokenize multi-level Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data. On uniform-grid benchmarks, uniform-patch WAMRViT improves finest-level region-of-interest VRMSE over a finest-patch uniform ViT while using substantially fewer tokens. The multi-scale variant achieves the lowest first-step full-field RMSE and VRMSE on both benchmarks and improves rollout-averaged full-field and refined-region accuracy at long horizons. With parallelized regridding, its end-to-end rollout cost lies between finest-patch and approximately token-matched coarser-patch ViTs. On a complex AMR combustion problem whose finest features cannot be represented natively by the evaluated uniform-grid baselines, WAMRViT operates directly on adaptive cells and substantially reduces finest-level error at matched transformer capacity. title: GPU-accelerated wind farm layout search with a distilled endogenous wake model (EndoWake)
authors: Martina Fischetti, Matteo Fischetti
abstract: Wind farm layout optimization decides where to place turbines to maximize annual energy production, and wake effects decide how much of that energy is produced. Accurate wake models are too slow for a search. We build on EndoWake, an endogenous wake model in which the wind speed at every grid cell is a variable linked to its upwind neighbors by linear constraints, so that wake field, siting decisions and project constraints share one mixed-integer model. Its four parameters are calibrated once against the single-wake field of a Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) simulation, and a GPU scores over a million layouts per second per wind direction. Comparing EndoWake-guided searches with a PyWake-based pipeline at Lillgrund, under a RANS judge that no search calls, revealed that the fidelity of a wake model is not the quality of the layouts optimized under it. A search is drawn to the gaps between sampled wind directions, the sirens; a diagnostic of the field finds a second artifact, an optimistic band off each wake edge, the mermaid cells, not reported before to our knowledge. Judged at random directions, the two pipelines are statistically indistinguishable. Our main result puts this speed to use: EndoWake screens the candidate moves of a local search on the GPU, and PyWake confirms every accepted move. On twenty unseen starts, with one GPU and thirty CPU processes, this screen-and-confirm search matches the PyWake value of a search on PyWake alone 7.9 times faster, and 14.9 times faster on the annual energy.

title: Sampling-based integrated design optimization of floating wind turbine substructures with Pywind
authors: Peng Chen, Li Dong, Ruming Feng, Zhongyao Fan, Liyun Zhu, Yirou Kang, Zhengshun Cheng
abstract: Abstract Design optimization of floating wind turbine (FWT) substructures remains computationally demanding due to the extensive time-domain simulations required to explore high-dimensional design spaces. This study builds upon the previously developed Pywind-based integrated design optimization (IDO) framework, extending it by comparing two sampling strategies: Latin Hypercube Sampling (LHS) and Maximin LHS. A 15 MW semi-submersible FWT is employed to assess the performance of these methods in capturing design variability and coupled hydrodynamic and structural responses under stochastic environmental conditions. The analysis shows that Maximin LHS significantly improves space-filling uniformity, reducing the Voronoi coefficient of variation by 41.5% compared to Standard LHS. Additionally, Maximin LHS shows a 46.8% improvement in the mean Voronoi area, resulting in more even parameter-space coverage. This highlights the capability of the Pywind-based IDO framework to conduct efficient, scalable, and statistically robust time-domain optimization. The findings underscore the IDO framework's potential for probabilistic design exploration, supporting intelligent decision-making for the next generation of FWT systems.

title: Long-term nitrous acid evolution modulates ozone and secondary aerosol variations in global megacities
authors: Xuan Li, Can Ye, Huabin Dong, Xuezhen Xu, Haichao Wang, Xiaorui Chen, Zhaofeng Tan, Xuefei Ma, Shiyi Chen, Keding Lu, Yuanhang Zhang
abstract: Nitrous acid (HONO) is a crucial urban source of HOx radicals, promoting surface ozone (O3) and secondary fine particle (PM2.5) formation, yet its long-term evolution and air-quality impacts remain poorly constrained. Here, using a deep neural network established on worldwide field campaigns, we reconstruct global surface HONO distributions. Typical megacities exhibited contrasting trends in 2005–2021, marked by a sharp decline in Beijing (−47.4% in 2013–2021), an increase in Delhi (+10.0% in 2005–2018), and slight decreases in London, New York and Los Angeles. These HONO changes are identified as major driver of O3 and particulate nitrate variations, outweighing contributions of conventional NOx and volatile organic compounds abatement in Beijing and Delhi, while showing comparable impacts in the remaining cities. A fused data-driven framework further uncovers regime-dependent HONO reduction strategies, prioritizing NOx control in summer and co-reduction of NOx, PM2.5 and direct combustion emissions in winter, to accelerate O3 and PM2.5 joint mitigation. Deep learning reveals a sharp decline of HONO in China, modest drops in EU and US but an increase in India. HONO changes drive O3 and PM2.5 variations, outweighing traditional NOx and VOC control, calling for HONO-targeted air quality management.

title: Aerodynamic Analysis and Optimization of a Go-Kart Body Using Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD)
authors: Pranav bagale,Anjali awatikar,Rehan pappuwale,Prathmesh kokate,Harshal Dalu,Rudra tale,Vedant pingale,Siddhesh tarhekar
abstract: A go-kart is a small, lightweight four-wheeled vehicle designed for recreational, educational and competitive driving. This project deals with the design and fabrication of a go-kart powered by an internal combustion (IC) engine. The main objective is to develop a simple, strong, economical and serviceable vehicle using commonly available mechanical components and workshop processes. The project covers the selection of the IC engine, chassis design, steering system, braking system, power transmission, wheels and tyres, accelerator and control mechanism. The frame is designed to support the engine, driver and other components while maintaining adequate rigidity and stability. The engine converts the chemical energy of fuel into mechanical power, which is transmitted to the driving axle through a suitable transmission arrangement. The methodology includes requirement identification, conceptual design, component selection, basic engineering calculations, CAD/drawing preparation, material procurement, fabrication, assembly and testing. The report also discusses important safety aspects such as braking performance, steering response, chain guarding, fastener tightening and driver protection. The project provides practical understanding of automobile engineering, IC engines, manufacturing processes, machine design, welding, power transmission and vehicle testing. The final design can be further improved by reducing weight, improving ergonomics, optimizing power transmission and introducing additional safety and instrumentation.

title: Physics-Informed Transient Modeling of Methane Hydrate Transport Restrictions Using Petrobras 3W Offshore Well-Event Data
authors: CHINEDU  CHARLES ALAMEZIE
abstract: Abstract Methane-dominant gas hydrate formation can restrict offshore production lines, alter pressure response, and interrupt natural-gas transport. Laboratory studies have established that hydrate growth depends on kinetic driving force, mass transfer, heat transfer, and hydrodynamic conditions, whereas field-data sets usually contain pressure, temperature, and flow signatures without direct hydrate-inventory measurements. This study presents a physics-informed framework for evaluating hydrate restriction signatures in offshore well data by combining robust field signal scoring with a one-dimensional transient transport-restriction model. Petrobras 3W class 0 data were used to define normal-operation baselines, while all 13 usable real-well class 8 and class 9 hydrate cases were used for validation. The Hydrate Anomaly Index achieved median event-window F1 = 0.889, median recall = 1.000, and median false-alarm rate = 0.051. In prospective replay, using only preceding normal-operation data to set thresholds, the framework achieved a median F1 = 0.974 and median false-alarm rate = 0.011, with sustained alarms occurring before the final hydrate-event label in 11 of 13 cases. Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis showed that the pressure-drop response was controlled mainly by flow velocity and geometry, while the outlet hydrate-fraction response was controlled mainly by apparent kinetic and deposition parameters. The framework does not estimate the exact hydrate mass or deposit morphology. Its value is a reproducible, field-evaluated pathway for connecting hydrate-growth concepts with operational restriction signatures in offshore natural-gas production systems.

title: AI-Assisted CFD Design of Al2O3–Water Nanofluid Cooling for Perovskite Tandem Solar Modules
authors: Iman MohammadKhani, Amir Javadpour
abstract: Compact flat-tube cooling and nanofluid heat transfer are investigated as a rear-side thermal-management route for perovskite tandem photovoltaic modules. A three-dimensional laminar-flow model of Al 2 O 3 –water nanofluid in a flat tube is retained as the high-fidelity thermal–hydraulic basis, including the effects of nanoparticle volume concentration, particle size, inlet temperature, and inlet velocity. The original CFD results show that nanoparticle addition increases the convective heat-transfer coefficient while also increasing hydraulic loss, with stronger relative heat-transfer enhancement at higher concentration, smaller particle diameter, lower Reynolds number, and higher temperature. To convert the previously conceptual AI layer into a quantitative design tool, an independent reproducible physics-informed Python benchmark was added using 520 Latin-hypercube samples within the validated thermophysical-property and laminar-flow envelopes. Random forest, XGBoost, Gaussian-process regression, and multilayer perceptron (MLP) surrogates were compared using hold-out and cross-validation metrics. The MLP gave the highest mean hold-out R 2 (0.980), with R 2 = 0.997 for T max , 0.994 for h avg , 0.993 for pressure drop, and 0.996 for net electrical power. Surrogate-assisted Pareto screening then quantified the trade-off between maximum temperature, temperature non-uniformity, pumping power, and net power, with selected candidates re-evaluated by the physics model. Additional audits address realistic photovoltaic heat-load levels, multilayer thermal resistance, mixed-convection screening, thermal entrance length, and isolated-particle transport time scales.

title: A CFD-GIS-QMRA framework for post‑release urban bioaerosol risk and healthcare demand assessment
authors: Xin Liu, Zhoupeng Ren, Chao Song, 绪强 邵, Xiaorong Zhang, Bei Liu, Ning Zhang, Haidong Wang, Chunfu Yang, Jianjian Wei, Yongzhong Zhang, Xiaomin Zhang, Hao Lei, Bin Zhu
abstract: Urban bioaerosol releases pose increasing challenges to urban biosecurity resilience, yet their public health impacts remain insufficiently assessed. Here, we developed an integrated CFD–GIS–QMRA framework to simulate bioaerosol dispersion, quantify infection risk, and estimate associated health outcomes and healthcare demand. Using hypothetical releases from a biosafety level 3 laboratory as a case study, we constructed multiple release scenarios involving four representative pathogens (SARS-CoV-2, H5N1, Anthracis, and Brucella) and three release sources (laboratory outlet vent, window, and ground). The results demonstrate that prevailing wind conditions and surrounding building geometry near the laboratory strongly shaped bioaerosol dispersion and deposition patterns. Substantial pathogen-specific differences were observed in infection risk, health outcomes, and healthcare demand. Specifically, SARS-CoV-2 resulted in the largest number of infections, Brucella generated the greatest hospitalization burden in terms of hospitalizations and total hospital days, while H5N1 resulted in the highest number of deaths and ICU admissions, as well as the greatest ICU-related healthcare resource demands, including ICU beds, nurses, and physicians. Quantitative assessment of health outcomes and healthcare demand provides practical support for healthcare-oriented emergency preparedness and medical resource allocation. The proposed end-to-end framework can support systematic urban bioaerosol risk assessment and also provide a scalable approach for diverse airborne hazards (e.g., chemical leaks and traffic-related air pollution) and urban exposure contexts (e.g., landfill sites and wastewater treatment plants).

title: Feasibility analysis of evacuation routes under metro flooding based on 3D modeling of flood inundation dynamics
authors: Zhiwei Dai, Guoru Huang
abstract: Metro stations, characterized by enclosed spatial configurations, are highly vulnerable to extreme flooding, posing severe threats to human life and property. Understanding the hydrodynamic processes of flood intrusion and their implications for evacuation routes is therefore essential for urban flood risk reduction. However, the effects of flood intrusion mechanisms and metro drainage capacity on inundation evolution within metro stations remain poorly understood, and evacuation responses following metro flooding have received relatively limited attention. This study employs a three-dimensional numerical model to investigate flood inundation processes under different inflow and drainage conditions. The simulated inundation characteristics are subsequently incorporated as constraints into empirical evacuation formulas to calculate the feasibility of evacuation routes at different locations for different population groups. Taking Shenzhou Road Station of Guangzhou Metro Line 21 as a case study, the effects of station platform door operation, the number and spatial distribution of inflow entrances, and varying inflow depths on flood evolution and internal flow patterns are systematically examined. Based on the simulated hydrodynamic conditions and the derived evacuation pathways, improved evacuation strategies are proposed. Results indicate that the evacuation time for different population groups varies from 516 s to 782 s, with considerable differences, and elderly females require greater assistance. Staircases located farthest from a single inflow entrance or situated between multiple inflow points exhibit the most rapid increase in water depth and should therefore be avoided during evacuation guidance. When metro tunnels facilitate drainage, the station hall floor may temporarily serve as a refuge space, with priority given to transferring pedestrians from the station platform floor to the station hall floor, alongside the implementation of flood barriers at surface entrances. These findings enhance understanding of evacuation planning under metro flooding scenarios and contribute to risk-informed emergency management strategies for flood-prone underground spaces.

title: Normal-inverse-Gaussian description of the velocity-increment cascade in homogeneous isotropic turbulence: Dissipative-boundary closure and the Reynolds dependence of the asymmetry
authors: Y. Sungtaek Ju
abstract: Intermittency in turbulence causes some scaling exponents of the longitudinal velocity increment to deviate from Kolmogorov's prediction. Multifractal closures reproduce that deviation accurately, but each fits its parameters to the exponents themselves and leaves the underlying increment distribution unspecified. Using direct numerical simulations of homogeneous isotropic turbulence at Taylor-microscale Reynolds numbers of 433, 611, and 1257, we identify the distribution first. Throughout the inertial range, the increment density is normal-inverse-Gaussian; at the highest Reynolds number, it is preferred over Gaussian, Student-t, and skew-t alternatives at every scale tested. Its parameters are fixed at the dissipative boundary by the kinematic viscosity, the mean dissipation rate, and the universal velocity-gradient skewness and are carried through the inertial range by the measured second and third moments. The exponents then follow without being fitted, the fourth-order exponent falling 0.10 below the measured value and the higher even orders falling short in the same direction. This is expected of a single-shape density whose tails are too thin for the rare increments that dominate high moments. The density asymmetry weakens as the Reynolds number rises. Compared at matched large-scale sampling volume, the change is carried by the increment flatness and not by the skewness, whose contribution is unresolved in every matched pair over a factor of 2.9 in the Reynolds number, while the scale dependence of the flatness gives an intermittency exponent μ=0.314±0.020. The increment distribution is thus set by measurable small-scale physics, and its asymmetry inherits the Reynolds-number dependence of intermittency.

title: An AI-assisted Framework for Image-Based Multiphase Flow Simulations
authors: Sidian Chen, Hamdi Tchelepi
abstract: Abstract. Image-based pore-scale models are critical for studying pore-scale multiphase displacement physics and connecting pore-scale processes to Darcy-scale constitutive relationships. However, systematic image-based modeling studies remain challenging due to the fragmentation of image acquisition and processing approaches, pore-scale simulators, and post-processing tools. To address this challenge, we develop a human-in-the-loop, AI-assisted workflow that integrates complex image-based modeling tasks into a state-aware framework for multiphase flow simulations. External or local AI tools (i.e., large language models) are used to translate natural-language instructions into validated model actions and parameter updates, while deterministic codes are implemented to execute image generation/import and processing, quasi-static and dynamic two-phase displacement simulations, postprocessing. We demonstrate the framework through deterministic two-phase displacement simulations, direct comparison with reported primary-drainage measurements, and ensemble analyses across porous-medium realizations. Our simulations show that: (1) Sample-scale constitutive relationships (e.g., capillary-pressure–saturation and fluid–fluid-interfacial-area–saturation curves) from dynamic simulations deviate from their quasi-static counterparts and do not collapse onto universal curves, revealing flow-regime-dependent nonequilibrium behavior. (2) Comparison with reported primary-drainage measurements further shows that model–experiment agreement is strongly affected by pore-body and pore-throat geometric representations. (3) Quasi-static capillary-pressure and interfacial-area relationships are relatively insensitive to microstructural variability, whereas relative permeability is substantially more variable because of its dependence on connected flow pathways. (4) For dynamic displacements, constitutive relationships remain comparatively consistent within each flow regime but distinctly separated among regimes across overlapping saturation ranges. These results highlight the importance of developing regime-aware Darcy-scale constitutive relationships and demonstrate a reproducible framework for model benchmarking, model–data evaluation, and uncertainty-aware pore-scale analysis.

title: Analytic Poisson and planar Poiseuille benchmark data for vascular-flow surrogate evaluation
authors: Brenald Dzonzi, Amit Kumar Mishra, Malebogo Ngoepe
abstract: Benchmark data, trained models and code for two flow problems with exact analytic solutions: a two-dimensional Poisson problem (Level I) and planar Poiseuille flow in a straight two-dimensional channel (Level II). The data compare supervised deep neural networks (DNNs), physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and hybrid data-physics networks on field accuracy, physical consistency and computational cost. These are Levels I and II of the benchmark reported in "When Accuracy, Conservation, and Cost Disagree: A Single-Geometry Benchmark of Vascular-Flow Surrogates" (Dzonzi, Mishra and Ngoepe).LEVEL I: POISSON PROBLEMResults table (CSV) for DNN and PINN models trained with 10, 50, 100, 200 and 500 labelled points, three random seeds each. Variables: relative L2 error and mean squared error on the training domain and on an enlarged domain, and training time.Provenance record (JSON): training protocol, hardware and software versions.Source code and batch scripts that reproduce the table.LEVEL II: PLANAR POISEUILLE FLOWNine runs (DNN, PINN and hybrid; three seeds each) under the scaled training setup. Each run contains its training history (CSV), metrics and configuration (JSON) and trained model checkpoint (PyTorch .pt).Per-seed and summary tables (CSV) for the scaled and unscaled training setups.Variables: velocity RMSE and relative L2 error, pressure RMSE and relative L2 error (raw and gauge-aligned), continuity and momentum residuals, inlet and outlet flux, flux imbalance, cross-section flux variation, wall-velocity error, pressure drop and pressure-drop error, inference latency and training time.Training, Slurm sweep and aggregation scripts, with a regression test. SUPPORTING FILESShared neural-network library code (pinn_library, pipe_flow_2d).Software environment record (Python, PyTorch and pip package versions).README.md with instructions for rerunning both levels.MANIFEST.json listing the size and SHA-256 checksum of every file.USAGEUnzip the archive and run the scripts from its top-level folder; no paths need editing. Re-aggregating the Level II runs reproduces the per-seed table and every summary mean. Standard deviations may differ in the final digit between machines because floating-point sums are accumulated in a different order. Training times depend on hardware; the reported times were measured on an NVIDIA L40S GPU.EXCLUSIONSThe dataset contains no patient data. The patient-specific aortic geometry, its computational fluid dynamics reference simulation and all results derived from it (Level III of the benchmark) are excluded; that reference was used with permission and is not redistributed.

title: From Biological Activity to Flow Assurance: An Evidence-Qualification Framework for Biocatalytic and Bio-Derived Wax Control in Waxy Crude Oils
authors: Inuaeyen Nyaudo Inuaeyen, Ubong U. Isang, Kufre J. Esenowo, Ephriam E. Afia
abstract: Wax accumulation and gel formation remain critical flow assurance obstacles in the extraction and conveyance of waxy crude oils, whereby precipitation, crystal development, aggregation, ageing, rheological behavior, and wall deposition are interrelated yet distinct processes. Traditional mitigation relies on temperature regulation, physical extraction, and chemical supplements. There is an increasing fascination with sustainable oilfield chemistry that has incorporated microorganisms, enzymes, biosurfactants, and renewable formulations as substitutes or enhancements. In many instances of this material, there is a paucity of demonstration about the intermediary causal processes, with signs of hydrocarbon biodegradation, paraffin utilization, or reductions in pour point and viscosity being regarded as proof of wax-deposition control. This comprehensive critique integrates literature from petroleum engineering, wax rheology, and microbiology with a systematic evidence-evaluation methodology, revealing four progressively robust assertions: biological activity, alteration of wax-related characteristics, diminished dynamic deposition, and engineering validation. The assessment delineates five realms of evidence, specifically biological functionality, compatibility with crude oil, change of the wax phase, response to flow assurance, and sustainable implementation. A six-tier qualifying framework is suggested, constraining the validity of a technological assertion to the evidence that has been substantiated. A novel seven-phase experimental approach is introduced, advancing from candidate identification and functional description, through crude oil compatibility, fundamental performance, and mechanistic validation, to dynamic deposition assessment and translation. A five-arm baseline control framework—untreated crude, formulation matrix, inactivated preparation, commercial standard, and active treatment—is suggested to differentiate catalytic, interfacial, carrier, and formulation influences. The synthesis indicates that biological systems present exciting research opportunities; nonetheless, the evidence for direct wax-control mechanisms is far less advanced compared to hydrocarbon degradation or biosurfactant activity. The essential research requirement is not merely further screening but rather reliable, crude-specific, dynamically evaluated data that connects biological activity to wax-phase behavior and pipeline-scale flow assurance.

title: Dopant effects on thermodynamic stability and oxygen vacancy formation in CaMnO3 perovskites for chemical-looping combustion
authors: Jonatan Gastaldi, Alfred Juhlin Onbeck, Joakim Brorsson, Anders Hellman, Tobias Mattisson
abstract: The thermodynamic properties and phase stability of doped CaMnO 3-δ perovskites have been investigated over a range of oxygen non-stoichiometry (δ), from 1/16 to 6/16, to assess their suitability as oxygen carriers for chemical-looping combustion. The computational framework combines machine-learning interatomic potentials for structural relaxation, cluster expansions for configurational energetics, phonon calculations for vibrational contributions, and Monte Carlo simulations for configurational entropy. Doping was explored at the A-site (Ce, Sr, La, Bi) and B-site (Ti, Fe, Si, Cr, Cu, Mo, Mg) at substitution levels ranging from 1/16 to 6/16. Phase stability was evaluated using multi-component equilibrium calculations based on thermodynamic data derived from the calculated enthalpy, entropy, and heat capacity. Ce and Sr (A-site), Fe and Ti (B-site), were identified as promising dopants. Ce and Ti enhanced the overall thermodynamic stability of CaMnO 3 , whereas Fe and Sr promoted oxygen vacancy formation, reflecting a trade-off between reducibility and thermodynamic stability. Where experimental data is available, these trends show good agreement with previously reported studies. These results demonstrate that targeted doping enables systematic tuning of thermodynamic behavior in CaMnO 3 -based perovskites, providing guidance for balancing thermodynamic stability and oxygen release in chemical-looping applications.

title: Conditional Flow Matching for Generation of 3D Multi-variable Instantaneous Urban Microclimate Fields
authors: Peng Liu, Shaoxiang Qin, Theodore Potsis, Lili Ji, Dingyang Geng, Liangzhu Leon Wang
abstract: Rapid and accurate prediction of urban wind and temperature fields is important for urban microclimate design and climate adaptation. Large-eddy simulation (LES) effectively resolves these instantaneous fields, but its application is limited in iterative design of urban microclimate applications due to high computational cost. Existing regressive data-driven models offers quick outputs, but they produce only deterministic point predictions that inherently fail to represent turbulent stochasticity. This paper adopts a novel generative framework of Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) that uses building geometry and mean flow as guidance to generate plausible three-dimensional instantaneous velocity and temperature fields for urban microclimate in seconds. To overcome the GPU memory bottleneck of pixel space 3D generation, the model operates in parallel on overlapping pixel space through a shared-noise initialization that preserves high spatial continuity of flow structure across the entire domain. Against reference LES data, the CFM surrogate can rapidly and accurately restore the first-order statistics with Normalized Root Mean Square Error (NRMSE) of 2.99% for wind and 1.77% for temperature, second-order turbulence metrics with NRMSE of 7.17% for wind and 8.84% for temperature, turbulent kinetic energy with NRMSE of 7%, probability density function and vertical profiles in representative locations. Wind engineering application of local gust prediction demonstrate that the speed and accuracy of CFM, supporting the use of generative AI for making turbulence-aware resilient urban design and climate adaptation more computationally feasible.

title: Evaluating metre-scale methane plume simulations with MicroHH against AVIRIS-4 remote sensing observations
authors: Sandro Meier, Dominik Brunner, Gerrit Kuhlmann
abstract: Abstract. High-resolution imaging spectrometers resolve anthropogenic plumes at metre to sub-metre scales, creating opportunities for emission quantification but requiring models that reproduce turbulent plume morphology at comparable resolution. We evaluate the large-eddy simulation model MicroHH against Airborne Visible/Infrared Imaging Spectrometer (AVIRIS-4) observations from 2024 controlled releases in France. Using site-specific wind, surface, and source parameters, we simulated the four releases with the longest plumes at 1 m horizontal resolution. Synthetic CH4 column enhancements were evaluated using plume structure, turbulence spectra, Gaussian cross-section statistics, along-plume flux variability, and plume power spectral density. For one release with a pronounced double plume, we integrated the three-dimensional model field along the slant illumination and viewing paths to investigate parallax effects. MicroHH reproduced the expected inertial-subrange behaviour of turbulent kinetic energy spectra and observed plume width, intermittency, and spatial power spectra for most releases. However, modelled vertical columns were more Gaussian than the observations and did not reproduce the double plumes. The exploratory slant-path calculation generated a comparable double structure, indicating that observational geometry can explain part of this discrepancy. Other differences likely reflect rapid near-source dilution at finite grid resolution, the absence of online plume-rise and buoyancy treatments, and omitted obstacle effects on near-surface flow. Overall, MicroHH can generate realistic high-resolution synthetic plume imagery for retrieval evaluation and machine-learning applications when inputs are well constrained and observational geometry is considered. This first systematic multi-metric comparison of LES plume morphology with metre-scale imaging-spectrometer observations provides a validation framework for other high-resolution dispersion models.

title: Optimal driving assignment strategies for plug-in hybrid electric heavy duty trucks
authors: Javier Jareño, Bernabè Dorronsoro, P. Ruiz
abstract: The transportation sector faces critical challenges in reducing CO 2 emissions, particularly from heavy-duty trucks (HDTs), which account for 25% of transportation-related emissions. Plug-in hybrid electric (PHE) HDTs offer a sustainable solution for long-distance freight, yet optimizing their battery management under variable route conditions such as topography, load, and speed constraints remains a complex problem. This study addresses this challenge through an integrated route-aware optimization framework for PHE HDTs. The framework combines route and elevation data, a power-constrained speed–acceleration estimator, regenerative braking, charging opportunities, and a Cellular Genetic Algorithm for Multiobjective Optimization (MOCell) to determine the driving-mode assignment between the electric motor and the internal combustion engine. A deterministic constructive heuristic, GreenRoute, is also included as a baseline for assessing the benefits of multi-objective optimization. Validation across three long-haul routes (Cádiz-Madrid, Madrid-Donostia, Paris-Berlin) demonstrates significant improvements: MOCell achieves up to 9% greater electric range and 17.5% lower emissions compared to the heuristic GreenRoute. For instance, on the Cádiz-Madrid route, MOCell reduces emissions by 5.7% and increases electric range by 4.6% when en-route charging is not considered, with further gains (6.6% and 4.1%, respectively) when charging is included. The study also reveals that heavier trucks benefit from enhanced regenerative braking, extending electric range despite higher total CO 2 emissions. These results underscore the efficacy of metaheuristic approaches in balancing emissions reduction and operational efficiency, advancing sustainable freight transportation aligned with global climate goals.

title: Investigation of the effect of albatross bill impact on CFRP and GFRP wind turbine blades using Diomedea exulans collision scenarios
authors: Ariyana Dwiputra Nugraha, Ahmad Mamba’udin, Benny Susanto, Ardi Jati Nugroho Putro, Yustinus Erwin Nugroho, Nugroho Karya Yudha, Abdul Syukur Alfauzi, Masaaki NISHIKAWA, Muhammad Akhsin Muflikhun
abstract: Wind turbine blades are highly vulnerable to damage from transverse loads such as bird collisions, which can compromise structural integrity, reduce aerodynamic efficiency, and raise ecological concerns. This study employed finite element simulations in Abaqus Explicit to examine the collision of a Diomedea exulans (wandering albatross) bill with Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer (CFRP) and Glass Fiber Reinforced Polymer (GFRP) blades. The albatross bill was modelled in two configurations: a shell model representing the realistic hollow, lightweight anatomy based on β-keratin properties, and a solid model serving as an extreme/conservative case to assess upper-bound impact severity. Impacts were simulated at three blade positions—tip ( IP #1 ), mid-span ( IP #2 ), and root ( IP #3 )—with velocities of 57.59, 47.04, and 36.60 m/s, respectively. This study contributes to the existing literature by introducing an anatomically representative albatross bill impactor model based on β-keratin properties and by systematically evaluating damage progression under repeated impacts. Results indicate that CFRP blades provide superior impact resistance, showing peak von-Mises stress of 1654 MPa (CFRP-B1), maximum contact force of 46.98 kN (CFRP-B2), and energy absorption of 242.33 J. GFRP-B1 exhibited the maximum displacement among all scenarios, with a value of 148.79 mm. While no major failure was observed, fiber damage was detected at IP #2 in CFRP under repeated impacts, emphasizing the role of local stiffness. albatross bird models, especially the solid bill, experienced severe deformation and fracture, underscoring ecological risks. These findings provide a quantitative basis for improving blade design, including bioinspired coatings and bird deterrent strategies to enhance both durability and wildlife safety.

title: Machine-learning-assisted phase-amplitude reduction for fast synchronization of airfoil wakes with constrained fluctuations
authors: Daiki Beppu, Vedasri Godavarthi, Koichiro Yawata, Hiroya Nakao, Kai Fukami
abstract: This study considers rapidly modifying the wake shedding frequency of the flow around an airfoil using sparse sensor information, subject to constraints on the lift coefficient fluctuations. This is achieved by combining phase-amplitude reduction with nonlinear machine-learning-based sparse sensor reconstruction. We derive time-varying phase and amplitude sensitivity fields that identify the optimal spatial locations and timing for actuation from merely three sensors. Through the sensitivity fields, we analytically obtain the optimal waveform for fast synchronization of wake shedding frequency while minimizing amplitude deviation of aerodynamic responses. The proposed approach is evaluated using flows over various NACA airfoils at several post-stall angles of attack, all of which exhibit unsteady periodic vortex shedding. With the identified optimal forcing, the wake frequency is altered much faster than with a standard sinusoidal actuation. Furthermore, the amplitude-penalized forcing achieves $20\%$ suppression of the lift coefficient fluctuation compared to the optimal forcing without amplitude penalty. The current amplitude-penalized technique may offer an efficient path for fast flow modification without causing detrimental fluctuations in periodic aerodynamic and aeroelastic systems with fluid-structure interactions.

title: Design and characterization of passive managed aquifer recharge desalination: Multilayer material optimization and techno-economic modelling
authors: Abdulrasheed Ibrahim Yerima, Abdulrasheed Ibrahim Yerima, Haylay Tsegab, AKM Eahsanul Haque, Auwal Yerima, Auwal Yerima, Jameel Shehu Yalli, Muhammad Kyari Muhammad, Md Yeasin Arafath
abstract: Advancing managed aquifer recharge (MAR) is critical towards tackling global freshwater shortages. In this study, layered geological horizons and engineered sorbent sinks were upscaled into a multilayer model to optimize passive underground desalination, using saline groundwater ( C 0 = 35000 mg/L) extracted from depleted hydrocarbon reservoirs. Skipping computationally heavy, microscale partial differential grids, this study involved a reduced-order modelling (ROM) combining volumetric asset inventory and algebraic block-centred transport solver to evaluate a 20-year operation period. Baseline infiltration routing loops ( q = 100.0 mm/day) show an empirically parametrized drop in total dissolved solids (TDS) to 1945.13 mg/L in the unamended layers. Passive desalination is largely transport-controlled, dictated by halophytes and low-permeability clay-silt hydraulic bottleneck that increases fluid residence time and amplifies pore-scale advective-dispersive attenuation. Vectorized integration of a hybrid reactive amendment matrix composed of mass fractions of biochar, clinoptilolite zeolite, and granular activated carbon (GAC) modified with trimethylammonium (R–N(CH 3 ) 3 + ) enables engineered salinity attenuation to an illustrative upper-bound quality of 334.0 mg/L under verified mass-balance constraints. Active chemisorption and ion exchange permanently remove highly mobile ions from the bulk fluid without significant mineral precipitation or crystalline salts clogging pore networks. An explicit parametric sensitivity analysis highlights the clay-silt and fine sandstone layers as key optimization zones. Multi-criteria lifecycle assessments confirm solid project viability under parameter uncertainty, yielding an extended net present value ( NPV EXT ) of up to USD 1361.9 million. This upscaled approach is an evaluation tool for mapping subsurface resource potential before implementing in-depth, site-specific techno-economic models and comprehensive field validation workflows.

title: A physics-assisted deep neural network-based closure framework for velocity gradient dynamics in compressible flows with vibrational non-equilibrium
authors: Deep Shikha, Sawan S. Sinha
abstract: In this study, we propose a dynamical model for the evolution of velocity gradients in compressible turbulent flows with vibrational non-equilibrium effects, using physics-assisted deep neural networks. Such models provide a powerful framework for understanding the nonlinear physics associated with small-scale structures. In compressible flows, the influence of thermodynamic fields on velocity-gradient dynamics is represented through the thermodynamic gradient field (TGF) tensor. The TGF tensor is one of the primary unclosed terms in the velocity-gradient evolution equations. The TGF tensor comprises contributions from the pressure-Hessian tensor, rho bold italic upper H ρ H $\rho \boldsymbol{H}$ , and the baroclinic tensor, bold italic upper B B $\boldsymbol{B}$ . Accordingly, the proposed framework incorporates closures for both bold italic upper H H $\boldsymbol{H}$ and bold italic upper B B $\boldsymbol{B}$ tensor dynamics. Building upon existing phenomenological closures for the bold italic upper H H $\boldsymbol{H}$ tensor governing mechanisms, we develop a neural-network-based closure for the inviscid mechanism responsible for generating the bold italic upper B B $\boldsymbol{B}$ tensor. Unlike the other recently used tensor bases, the presented work employs a novel tensor basis allowing for the inclusion of non-symmetric features in the model. The framework also incorporates a data-driven closure for vibrational non-equilibrium effects. The resulting framework combines phenomenological and data-driven representations of various bold italic upper H H $\boldsymbol{H}$ and bold italic upper B B $\boldsymbol{B}$ tensors governing mechanisms, termed as the hybrid enhanced homogenised Euler equation (H-EHEE) model. Model predictions are evaluated across a range of turbulent Mach numbers and compared against direct numerical simulation (DNS) data and existing compressible velocity-gradient models. The H-EHEE model exhibits close agreement with DNS statistics and provides significant improvements over existing models, particularly in highly compressible flow regimes.

title: Full Turbulence Simulation of Channel Flow at Re_{\tau} \approx 1000
authors: Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Yoshiyuki Tsuji
abstract: Abstract A Full Turbulence Simulation (FTS) of turbulent channel flow at friction Reynolds number ($Re_{\tau}$) $\approx 1000$ was performed by resolving the Kolmogorov wavenumber in all spatial directions. At this Reynolds number, the intermediate layer attains a physically meaningful width. Analysis of the FTS demonstrates that the most restrictive conditions for the proposed resolution criteria occur within this region, highlighting its important role in determining DNS resolution requirements.&#xD;The wall‑normal grid spacing of the FTS also confirms that, when the Kolmogorov length scale is sufficiently resolved, the second‑order central‑difference scheme introduces no adverse numerical effects in the wall‑normal direction. In the wall‑parallel directions, two resolution criteria were identified based on the present FTS: a first‑approximation DNS resolution that resolves approximately 99\% of the turbulent kinetic energy and accurately reproduces the dissipation rate ($\Delta x^{+} \approx 19$, $\Delta y^{+} \approx 8$, where $\Delta x^{+}$ and $\Delta y^{+}$ denote the stream and spanwise spatial resolutions in wall units), while a stricter full-dissipation criterion ($\Delta x^{+} \approx 7.5$, $\Delta y^{+} \approx 5.0$) is required to resolve all dissipation-spectrum contributions.&#xD;&#xD;The first‑approximation resolution by means of spectral method reproduces the essential turbulence statistics within approximately 1\% accuracy while requiring only one‑eighth of the grid points used in the FTS, demonstrating its practical efficiency. In contrast, even the highest‑resolution second‑order central‑difference case ($\Delta x^{+} \approx 5.0$, $\Delta y^{+} \approx 4.5$) fails to match the accuracy of the first‑approximation spectral resolution.&#xD;&#xD;Comparison of the dissipation spectra between $Re_{\tau}\approx1000$ and $Re_{\tau}\approx16000$ further supports the applicability of the proposed resolution criteria at substantially higher Reynolds numbers. These findings provide important resolution guidelines for high-Reynolds-number DNS, particularly for simulations at $Re_{\tau}=\mathcal{O}(10^{4})$.

title: Brief communication: A fast parabolic RANS numerical model with analytical pressure closure for continuous induction-to-far-wake prediction in wind farm flows
authors: Frédéric Blondel, Majid Bastankhah
abstract: Abstract. Parabolic Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) approaches offer an attractive compromise between the accuracy of RANS and the efficiency of analytical methods. However, due to neglecting pressure gradients, these models often require near-wake corrections. Moreover, they are typically based on over-simplistic turbulence closures. To address these limitations, this brief proof of concept couples a recently developed analytical pressure-gradient formulation (Bastankhah et al., 2026) with a parabolic RANS framework. It also uses the k − ε − fp turbulence closure, well suited to strong near-wake velocity gradients (van der Laan et al., 2015). The model closely reproduces RANS results, while reducing per-core computational costs by more than three orders of magnitude.

title: Aerodynamic Optimization of a Multi-Rotor UAV for Power-Line Inspection Using a Coupled CFD-BEMT Framework
authors: Balram Panjwani, Przemysław Dominik Gacia
abstract: Predicting the aerodynamic performance of multirotor unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) remains challenging because of complex rotor–rotor and rotor–body interactions. Experimental characterisation of these interactions is often costly and time-consuming, making computational methods valuable for aerodynamic design and optimisation. This study presents a coupled computational ﬂuid dynamics and blade element momentum theory (CFD-BEMT) framework for evaluating a multirotor UAV developed for power-line inspection. The airﬂow was simulated using OpenFOAM, while the propellers were represented as virtual rotors through distributed momentum-source terms calculated using BEMT. The CFD methodology was assessed by comparing predicted Ahmed-body drag coeﬃcients at diﬀerent yaw angles with experimental measurements. Steady-state Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations provided satisfactory predictions at low yaw angles, while unsteady simulations generally improved the predictions at higher yaw angles, where large-scale ﬂow separation and wake unsteadiness became signiﬁcant. Standalone static-thrust measurements were also used as reference data to examine changes in rotor loading after integration with the UAV. The computational framework was subsequently applied to a baseline bluﬀ-body conﬁguration, V01, and a redesigned conﬁguration, V02, incorporating smoother fuselage contours, improved payload integration, and modiﬁed rotor placement. A comprehensive simulation matrix was used to investigate the eﬀects of forward velocity, propeller rotational speed, and nose-down angle of attack. The results show that propeller operation substantially modifies the aerodynamic response through nonuniform rotor-induced flow and rotor–body interactions. Compared with V01, the redesigned V02 configuration generally exhibits smaller variations in lift, drag, and lift-to-drag ratio across the investigated angles of attack. However, V02 does not provide uniformly lower drag or a consistently higher lift-to-drag ratio under all operating conditions. Its principal advantage is a more consistent aerodynamic response and reduced sensitivity to changes in nose-down angle of attack. The results demonstrate the capability of the coupled CFD-BEMT framework to assess installation effects, quantify rotor–body interactions, and support the aerodynamic development of multirotor inspection UAVs.

title: A data-driven framework to identify restenosis-prone regions in femoral arteries from geometric and inflow waveform parameters
authors: Chotirawee Chatpattanasiri, Federica Ninno, Vanessa Díaz‐Zuccarini, Stavroula Balabani
abstract: Haemodynamic indices derived from computational fluid dynamics (CFD), such as time-averaged wall shear stress (TAWSS) and oscillatory shear index (OSI), are closely associated with restenosis risk in peripheral arterial disease (PAD). We present a machine learning-reduced order modelling (ML-ROM) framework to predict critical, restenosis-prone, haemodynamic regions accounting for both vessel geometries and inlet flow waveforms. We generated 500 parameterized virtual femoral-artery geometries, each paired with a synthetic physiologically realistic inflow waveform. CFD was used to obtain the wall shear stress (WSS) distribution, from which TAWSS and OSI were computed. Critical regions were then defined by applying different thresholding criteria based on TAWSS and OSI, as found in the literature. These were then used to construct ROMs using Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD), and to train ML models from which the critical regions could be reconstructed. Four ML architectures were explored: a geometric-parameter-only model and three alternatives that also incorporate inflow waveform information via Fourier coefficients, long short-term memory (LSTM), and convolutional neural networks (CNN). The Fourier models achieved the highest predictive performance, with the median values of balanced accuracy (BA) exceeding 0.92 across all critical-region definitions. The model also offered a substantial speed-up ratio of the order of 109 compared with traditional CFD.

title: Physics-Encoded Learning for DAS-Based Flow Allocation: A Comparative Study
authors: P. Moradi, N. Kalia
abstract: Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) has become an important surveillance technology for injection and production wells because it enables dense acoustic measurements along the wellbore using fiber-optic sensing channels. Each DAS channel behaves as a distributed strain-sensitive acoustic measurement over a finite gauge length, recording broadband acoustic disturbances generated by flow-induced vibrations. The resulting high-resolution spatial and temporal measurements provide a rich dataset that can support a wide range of applications, including flow allocation, event detection, completion-integrity monitoring, flow-assurance diagnostics, production surveillance, and well testing. Despite these capabilities, quantitative interpretation of DAS data, particularly for flow allocation, remains challenging. Conventional workflows often depend on high signal-to-noise ratios, long spatial apertures, transient low-frequency events, or calibration against controlled measurements. Such requirements can limit applicability in field operations because calibration conditions may change with time, drift from actual downhole conditions, or fail to capture the complexities of multiphase flow and completion heterogeneity. Here, we present a physics-encoded neural network (PeNN) framework for estimating downhole flow parameters from acoustic measurements. The proposed method combines physics-informed preprocessing, multi-domain feature extraction, and a neural network architecture in which prior physical knowledge is embedded directly into the model structure. The preprocessing workflow includes de-drifting, denoising, sound-transmission-loss compensation, attenuation-informed frequency-wavenumber filtering, noise matching, phase-based stacking, and data standardization. Extracted features include time-domain, spectral, higher-order spectral, cepstral, frequency-wavenumber, and spatial-wavelet descriptors. The proposed PeNN model encodes physical relationships, such as turbulent-flow behavior, noise-logging relationships, and mechanistic constraints, directly into the model layers. This structure is designed to improve generalization, reduce dependence on large, labeled datasets, and support the transition from instance-based learning to continuous learning. The workflow is further extended through federated learning, enabling local assets to train models on site while sharing only model updates with a central server. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, a synthetic injection-well case study was developed using computational fluid dynamics simulations of a 2.5 m water-injection section with two injection zones. The proposed PeNN model was compared with a conventional neural network of identical architecture but without embedded physical constraints. Results showed that the physics-encoded model required approximately 2.5 times fewer labeled training samples to achieve comparable prediction performance under sparse-label conditions.

title: Operator learning for efficient quantum computation
authors: Paul Lauterbur Over, Sergio Bengoechea, Leonardo Borello Busilacchi, Martin Kiffner, Thomas Rung, Alexios A. Michailidis
abstract: Abstract An efficient implementation of quantum algorithms is often hindered by the lack of efficient primitives for operators and state preparation. This limits both the ability of near-term quantum hardware to simulate complex problems and the potential of fault-tolerant algorithms to achieve practical quantum advantage. To address this, we propose a framework that maps discrete operators onto compact, structured quantum circuits. The resulting variational circuits can be tailored to the connectivity and long-range interaction of the target hardware. The learning process employs backpropagation together with a cost function that efficiently optimizes unitary operators and non-unitary --dense or sparse-- operators using only a single ancilla qubit for block encoding. Additionally, we introduce a regularization term that reduces the approximation error. The approach is validated for both quantum mechanical and engineering applications. In the former case, we learn propagators that arise in native quantum problems --such as quantum simulation and quantum chemistry-- and achieve improved resource scaling in comparison to standard Suzuki--Trotter expansions. In the latter case, we demonstrate the approach's ability to implement the second-order central finite difference approximation of the Laplace operator --relevant for solving partial differential equations-- while improving upon current error metrics. The final example deals with learning a dense, non-unitary operator that arises in the analysis of inviscid potential flow around an airfoil. These results motivate the extension of the framework to a broader class of operator-synthesis problems beyond the prototypical engineering and quantum applications considered here.

title: Data-driven fault detection in wind turbine systems using support vector machines and artificial neural networks
authors: Ahlame Bentata, Farah Echiheb, Mohammed Bennani Taj, Mihai Oproescu, Shimaa Aly Hussien, Mohamed I. Mosaad, Badre Bossoufi
abstract: Efficiency and reliability of wind turbine systems are very important in the production of clean sustainable energy sources. Malfunctioning of sensors, actuators, or other system components may affect system functionality and increase maintenance costs. This study presents a data-driven approach to fault detection in wind turbine systems using Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques, including Support Vector Machines (SVMs) and Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), with Random Forest (RF) included as an additional baseline for comparison. A comprehensive benchmark model of a variable-speed wind turbine system is implemented using the FAST/Simulink environment under realistic turbulent wind conditions. The key system variables, namely generator speed, generated power, and blade pitch angles, were monitored. Multiple fault scenarios are introduced to evaluate system performance. A five-fold blocked temporal cross-validation strategy was used to evaluate the generalization performance of the models while preserving the temporal ordering of the simulated data. Simulation results show that fault-detection performance depends strongly on the fault type, with SVM and ANN generally providing stronger performance than RF, while ANN shows advantages for some nonlinear and challenging fault patterns, particularly in terms of recall and robustness under noisy conditions. This research highlights the effectiveness of AI-based, data-driven approaches in enhancing fault detection capabilities and improving the reliability of wind turbine systems.

title: A novel simulation-based framework for predicting the basic performance data of structured packing
authors: Halina Murasiewicz, Jerzy Maćkowiak, Jan F. Maćkowiak
abstract: Generally, establishing design guidelines for structured packings has required prolonged empirical testing inside pilot-scale columns. While vital for mapping multi-phase fluid dynamics and mass transfer, these physical trials drain financial resources, take excessive time, and create major bottlenecks. Specifically, determining foundational Basic Performance Data (BPD) - such as pressure drop in packed bed and capacity range of the packing - remains shackled to physical experiments. Crucially, the flooding line, which defines the ultimate hydrodynamic operating limit and maximum gas throughput capacity of the column before operational failure, is traditionally not estimated by standard Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations. Without the ability to predict this vital parameter, utilizing predictive mathematical tools for column design and scale-up remains deeply restricted. This paper presents a virtual engineering strategy to leapfrog traditional trial-and-error workflows. By embedding a mechanistic "Suspended Bed of Droplets" (SBD) model directly within a high-resolution CFD domain, this cohesive tool permits the standalone determination of the complete BPD profile, including direct flooding line prediction. Consequently, counter-current pressure gradients and hydrodynamic capacity boundaries are computed directly from first principles, stripping away the need for preliminary laboratory measurements. To verify accuracy, these digital predictions are rigorously cross-examined with archival field data from commercial-grade structured packing installations. This methodology represents a profound shift toward a nimble, software-centric discovery model in thermal separation engineering, radically shortening performance profiling timelines, mitigating infrastructure expenses, and providing a powerful digital platform to optimize future packing geometries.

title: PINNeAPPle: A Python platform for physics-informed machine learning with physics-based trust checks
authors: Yan Barros, Enrico Schiassi
abstract: PINNeAPPle: Physics-Informed Machine Learning and Scientific Computing PINNeAPPle is an open-source framework for physics-informed machine learning (Physics AI) and scientific computing, designed to facilitate the development, integration, and evaluation of machine learning methods for physical systems governed by ordinary and partial differential equations (ODEs and PDEs). The framework aims to bridge scientific computing, numerical simulation, physical modeling, and machine learning through a composable and extensible software architecture. Rather than replacing established numerical solvers or promoting a single model family, PINNeAPPle provides a foundation for combining physics-based knowledge, computational methods, and learning-based models within reproducible scientific workflows. Key capabilities Physics-informed learning: Tools and abstractions for incorporating governing equations, physical constraints, and differential operators into machine learning workflows. Multiple model paradigms: A framework designed to accommodate physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), neural operators, and other learning architectures for scientific problems. Composable scientific workflows: Reusable components for connecting data, physical representations, models, transformations, and training procedures. Scientific computing integration: An extensible foundation for connecting machine learning methods with numerical simulation and domain-specific computational tools. Reproducible experimentation: A software-oriented approach to organizing computational experiments, evaluating methods, and supporting systematic comparisons. Open-source extensibility: Modular design intended to support research, collaborative development, and application-specific extensions. Motivation Scientific machine learning increasingly requires more than isolated neural network architectures. Practical applications must account for governing equations, boundary and initial conditions, data representations, numerical methods, computational constraints, and evaluation protocols. PINNeAPPle addresses this integration challenge by providing reusable software components and a common framework for developing physics-aware learning systems. Its broader objective is to make scientific machine learning more accessible, composable, and reusable across scientific and engineering domains. Applications Potential application areas include computational fluid dynamics (CFD), heat transfer, solid mechanics, inverse problems, parameter estimation, surrogate modeling, reduced-order modeling, uncertainty quantification, and engineering design optimization. Intended audience PINNeAPPle is intended for researchers, scientific software developers, computational scientists, and engineers working at the intersection of machine learning, applied mathematics, physics, and numerical simulation. Availability and citation Source code, installation instructions, documentation, and development resources are available through the project's GitHub repository. This record identifies the PINNeAPPle software release archived in Zenodo. For reproducibility, cite the specific version used in your research and consult the corresponding release documentation for implementation details and supported functionality.

title: Periodic–Kink, Lump, and Rogue Waves with Parameter Discovery in an Integrable Model: Bilinear and Physics-Informed Neural-Network Approaches
authors: Ghulam Hussain Tipu, AllahBakhsh Yazdani Cherati, Hamid Momeni, 姚锋平, Elham Hafezieh
abstract: This research investigates nonlinear wave dynamics of the integrable (3+1)-dimensional extended Bogoyavlensky- Konopelchenko equation, which models the interaction of a Riemann wave and a long wave in fluid dynamics. The equation has important applications in the modeling of shallow water waves, ion acoustic waves, and the propagation of fluids. Initially, we employ Hirota’s bilinear framework with symbolic single-hidden-layer neural-network architectures, referred to as bilinear neural networks (BNNs), and prescribed analytical activation functions to construct complex wave structures, including periodic–kink waves, M-lumps, lump–kink interactions, and modulated lump solutions. A Jacobielliptic activation function is employed within the symbolic BNN ansatz to construct and investigate rogue-wave solutions. In the second phase, an enhanced Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN), equipped with a global adaptive activation function and residual-based attention, is introduced for physics-informed solution approximation and inverse parameter identification. The proposed PINN accurately reproduces the periodic–kink, M-lump, and lump–kink dynamics, showing good agreement with the analytical solutions and low error metrics, while the comparative analysis highlights the complementary strengths and limitations of the analytical and physics-informed numerical approaches. The framework also exhibits good stability in recovering nonlinear coefficients from noisy data, demonstrating its potential for parameter discovery. The results demonstrate that combining BNN-based exact solution construction with enhanced PINN-based numerical forward and inverse modeling provides a versatile framework for nonlinear wave analysis and the investigation of complex wave phenomena in applied mathematics and nonlinear physics.

title: Learnable coarsening for two-phase flow in porous media
authors: Viacheslav Naumov, Nikolay B. Yavich, Alexander A. Ryabov, Sayan Ranu, N. M. Anoop Krishnan, Evgeny Vladimirovich Burnaev, Vladimir Vanovskiy
abstract: Abstract Hydrodynamic simulations of multi-phase flow in porous media are essential for oil production forecasting but require significant computational resources. Traditional approaches lead to high memory and time demands, restricting multi- scenario analysis. We propose a learnable coarsening algorithm based on graph neural networks (GNNs) with node aggregation for 2D two-phase flow modelling. The coarsened grid adapts to the reservoir geometry, its properties, and production data. Our algorithm is integrated with a graph-based finite volume method (FVM) solver, differentiable Voronoi tessellation, and a fully implicit upwind scheme. The unstructured computational grid is modeled as a graph with cell centers, adjacency edges, and rich a set of node features: coordinates, permeability, masks, distances to wells, permeability gradients, and wells influence potential. GNN produces soft assignments for probabilistic clustering, preserving wells and sensors. Training employs an FVM solver with physics-informed loss matching saturation and production rate time series at wells, promoting grid uniformity. Extending our prior works, our method enables coarsening by 10 times with relative error below 1%, accurately reproducing saturation fields, oil production, and water breakthrough on synthetic and realistic permeability fields

title: Aero‐breakup of droplets: Recent progress and outlook
authors: Ben Guan, Weijie Zhang, Jian Wang, Chih‐Yung Wen, Yu Liang
abstract: Abstract Aero‐breakup of droplets is a classic academic topic in fluid mechanics that describes the process of droplets breaking into multiple smaller ones or fine mists in an air flow. An in‐depth understanding of the aero‐breakup of liquid droplets is essential for the applications of spraying, atomization, ink printing, liquid fuel combustion, and other natural phenomenon explorations and industrial technology developments. Extensive studies have been conducted on this topic from different perspectives for decades. This review systematically summarizes the recent progress of droplet aero‐breakup studies. Starting from a brief introduction of research history, the intrinsic correlation between breakup modes and the governing parameters is sketched. The theoretical works on droplet breakup are first described from the views of interface instability theory and internal flow theory. These theories jointly construct the theoretical framework of droplet aero‐breakup. Second, several newly discovered breakup modes are demonstrated. Third, the influences of specific fluid properties, including viscosity, non‐Newtonian rheology, metallic natures, and volatility, on the mechanisms of droplet breakup are presented. The scenarios of multi‐droplet and droplet cloud are then discussed, which are believed to prevail in industrial applications. Last, an outlook for future explorations of droplet aero‐breakup is presented by providing several possible research directions.

title: The Navier–Stokes Equations: A Critical Review of Theory, Computation, Turbulence, and Data-Driven Frontiers
authors: Wei-Guang Huang
abstract:
The Navier–Stokes equations describe the motion of viscous fluids and stand at the center of modern fluid mechanics. They also define one of the hardest open problems in mathematics, for the question of whether smooth three-dimensional solutions can develop singularities in finite time remains unresolved. This review provides a critical, evidence-based synthesis of the subject from its foundations in the work of Leray and Hopf through the mathematical, computational, and data-driven landscape of 2026. We first examine the equations and their physical content, then trace the theory of well-posedness: weak and strong solutions, regularity criteria, partial regularity, uniqueness, and nonuniqueness. We appraise what is known about possible singularities and the energy and attractor theory that governs long-time behavior. The statistical description of turbulence, from Kolmogorov scaling to anomalous dissipation, is then reviewed alongside its unresolved tensions. We evaluate the numerical toolbox — finite difference, projection, finite element, spectral, discontinuous Galerkin, lattice Boltzmann, and finite volume methods — with attention to stability, accuracy, and the pressure-velocity coupling that complicates incompressible computation. Modeling hierarchies from direct numerical simulation through large-eddy and Reynolds-averaged closures are assessed, as are physics-informed neural networks and machine-learning-accelerated solvers that have reshaped the field since 2019. Applications in cardiovascular hemodynamics, geophysical flows, multiphase systems, combustion, and viscoelastic fluids illustrate both achievement and persistent gap. We close with a concrete research agenda, emphasizing the convergence of mathematical proof, high-resolution computation, and physical measurement.

Keywords: Navier–Stokes equations; weak solutions; regularity; turbulence; direct numerical simulation; large-eddy simulation; physics-informed neural networks; hemodynamics; Reynolds number.

title: A Review of Numerical Modeling of Internal Flow, Cavitation, Erosion, and Flow-induced Vibration in Hydropower Valves
authors: S. Wu, J. Zhou, X. Chen, X. Yu, J. Liu, C. Gu, H. Du
abstract: Hydropower valves operate under transient, high-pressure conditions in which local throttling, pressure recovery, vortex evolution, and pressure pulsation govern hydraulic performance, cavitation, erosion, and flow-induced vibration. This review synthesizes recent advances in numerical modeling of these coupled phenomena and links internal-flow evolution with hydraulic response, damage initiation, and structural behavior. The evidence base comprised 90 primary studies and five contextual reviews. Twelve primary studies (13.3%) directly addressed hydropower valves or hydropower valve–system interactions, whereas 78 studies (86.7%) provided transferable mechanistic or methodological evidence from related valve and hydraulic systems, highlighting the limited availability of hydropower-specific validation. Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS)-based computational fluid dynamics (CFD) remains the principal engineering method for global hydraulic quantities, whereas large-eddy simulation (LES), multiphase erosion models, and fluid–structure interaction (FSI) methods are more appropriate for unsteady cavitation, particle-induced damage, and structural response. Quantitatively, one direct hydropower butterfly-valve study reported an approximately 10% mean absolute error between CFD predictions and experimental flow-field data. In a transferable three-way globe-valve study, geometric optimization reduced the simulated percentage of cavitation by 49.5%, from 34.90% to 17.62%, while the response-surface model predicted 19.06%. The former supports case-specific confidence in hydropower-valve FSI modeling, whereas the latter demonstrates transferable optimization potential rather than direct hydropower performance. Major limitations include incomplete uncertainty reporting, uneven numerical verification and model calibration, scarce prototype-scale evidence, and limited long-term multiphysics validation. Standardized benchmarks, prototype measurements, and physics-informed monitoring are required to support transferable design and life-cycle decisions.

title: In silico proof of concept for reconstruction of blood flow velocity with 4D phase contrast MRI and variational autoencoders
authors: Bruno Sixou, Monica Sigovan
abstract: In this work, we investigate a new deep learning method for the reconstruction of blood velocity from 4D phase contrast MRI measurements based on variational autoencoders. The principle of this approach is to leverage lower resolution velocity measurements to train a variational autoencoder. The approach identifies optimal latent variables within the latent space and uses the generative process of the variational autoencoder to enhance reconstruction accuracy. Realistic simulations demonstrate that the proposed deep learning approach outperforms classical regularisation methods under undersampled and noisy conditions. The nonlinear encoding of the velocity field achieves better reconstruction results and compensates for missing information.

title: Non intrusive parametric Reduced Order Models based on physics for incompressible flow
authors: Cyrille Allery, Claudine Béghein
abstract: Reduced order modeling provides an efficient alternative to high fidelity simulations for the rapid prediction of fluid flows in many query settings. Among non intrusive approaches, Operator Inference (OpInf) enables the identification of reduced dynamical operators directly from data while preserving a prescribed mathematical structure. The present work extends physics structured OpInf to the construction of parametric Reduced Order Models for transient incompressible flows governed by the Navier-Stokes equations. The velocity and pressure fields are represented using separate global reduced bases, and their reduced operators are identified directly from temporal and parametric POD coefficients. The identification procedure is formulated as a sequence of uncoupled least squares problems, leading to an efficient offline stage while avoiding the explicit projection of the governing equations. The approach is first evaluated on a lid driven cavity flow in a periodic regime to assess temporal extrapolation and prediction at previously unseen parameter values. Its applicability is then demonstrated for transient flow through a porous medium with a square obstacle, for which the nonlinear terms are not directly amenable to a standard Galerkin projection. The results demonstrate that the approach can accurately reproduce both velocity and pressure fields while providing computationally efficient predictions for unseen parameter values.

title: Thermal characteristic analysis and optimization research of new energy vehicle battery thermal management system based on numerical simulation
authors: Jingyuan Qu, Ziqiang Yu
abstract: Abstract To address the issues of excessive temperature rise, uneven temperature distribution, and increased cooling energy consumption in new energy vehicle power batteries under high-rate charging and discharging and complex operating conditions, this paper proposes a multi-physics coupled modeling and optimization method for battery thermal management systems based on numerical simulation. First, an electro-thermal-fluid coupling framework is established, including SOC estimation, an electrical model, a Bernardi heating model, an equivalent thermal network, and a fluid-structure interaction heat transfer model, to describe the battery’s heat generation, solid-state heat conduction, and convective heat transfer processes of the cooling medium. Second, temperature, velocity, and pressure field analyses are conducted for both air-cooled and liquid-cooled structures to reveal the influence mechanisms of flow channel structure, flow distribution, and local heat transfer capacity on battery thermal uniformity. Based on this, nonlinear model predictive control and the NSGA-II multi-objective optimization method are introduced, with the highest temperature, maximum temperature difference, and cooling energy consumption as optimization objectives, to obtain a Pareto compromise solution between thermal safety and energy consumption. Finally, the effectiveness of the model is verified by comparing experimental temperature data with the model prediction results. The results show that the proposed method can effectively capture the battery’s thermal response characteristics and provides a theoretical basis for the structural design and operational optimization of power battery thermal management systems. The numerical results demonstrate a 6.7% reduction in maximum battery temperature and a 15.3% reduction in cooling energy consumption after optimization. The reduced-order model achieves an R2 of 0.987 with an RMSE of 0.38 K and provides an 18.0× computational speed-up compared with the full-order model, while experimental validation achieves an R2 of 0.986 with an RMSE of 0.41 K. The NSGA-II optimization converges at approximately 150 generations with a final hypervolume of 0.965, confirming the effectiveness and computational efficiency of the proposed framework.

title: Differences in Predicting Hollow Structures of Water‐Assisted Injection‐Molded Rectangular Tubes Between Laminar and SST k – ω Turbulence Models Under Various Water‐Injection Pressures
authors: Wei Lu, Hesheng Liu, Wenfeng Lai, Ke Gong, 张飞宇, Qingsong Jiang
abstract: ABSTRACT To investigate the influence of flow models on hollow structure prediction in water‐assisted injection molding (WAIM), three‐dimensional numerical simulations were performed using the finite volume method with the laminar model and the shear stress transport (SST) k – ω turbulence model. The hollow profile evolution, the hollow ratio distribution, and the coefficient of variation ( CV ) predicted at water‐injection pressures of 6, 8, and 10 MPa were validated against experimental measurements. The results indicate that both flow models successfully captured the trends of increasing hollow ratio and decreasing CV with increasing water‐injection pressure. Nevertheless, the SST k – ω turbulence model yielded hollow profile evolution and hollow ratio distribution that agreed more closely with the experimental measurements, owing to its ability to capture local turbulent and interfacial fluctuations associated with high‐Reynolds‐number water penetration. In contrast, by neglecting turbulent effects, the laminar model produced pronounced conical distortion in the hollow profiles at the rear cross‐sections and unrealistically smooth hollow ratio distributions at high water‐injection pressures. Although the laminar model yielded CV values that were numerically closer to the experimental results, this agreement was largely an artifact of its smoother hollow ratio distributions combined with the inability of CV to capture local distortions in hollow profile. Overall, the SST k – ω turbulence model provided a more realistic representation of the flow field and superior capability in predicting hollow structure evolution during WAIM.
