title: Extending convolutional neural networks to finite-volume meshes for fine-scale reconstruction of wall-bounded turbulence
authors: Hesam Tofighian, Jordan A. Denev, Kornev Nikolai
abstract: Standard convolutional neural networks for turbulence super-resolution are restricted to uniform structured grids, preventing their direct application to the non-uniform and non-orthogonal meshes commonly used in wall-bounded flows and complex geometries. We introduce a finite-volume convolution unit (FVCU) that removes this restriction. The key idea is to construct convolutional layers using finite-volume operators that are applicable to non-uniform and unstructured meshes. To this end, we use an exact representation of a 3D convolution as a linear combination of successive axis-wise convolutions. We adopt axis-wise gradient, averaging, and identity operators, as they can be evaluated on arbitrary polyhedral cells using finite-volume discretization. The resulting FVCU is well-defined on general meshes, serving as a drop-in replacement for conventional convolution layers. The FVCU is embedded in a super-resolution neural network and trained to reconstruct 3D velocity fields from $4\times$ coarsened low-resolution fields in turbulent channel flow on a non-uniform mesh, and in circular-pipe flow on a non-orthogonal O-grid mesh. Inspired by the role of the Van Driest damping function in near-wall subgrid-scale modelling in large-eddy simulations, this function is supplied as a conditional input to encode wall proximity. An ablation study confirms that the network interprets this input in a physically consistent manner. In both configurations, the model accurately reconstructs instantaneous velocity fields, Reynolds-stresses and their anisotropy, and energy spectra beyond the Nyquist limit of the low-resolution mesh. On an elliptic pipe unseen during training, the model reproduces the main flow features and local statistics, with a modest overprediction of small-scale energy. These results demonstrate a framework for extending CNN-based super-resolution to general finite-volume grids.

title: Machine-learning-enhanced discretize-then-project reduced-order modeling of turbulent flows on collocated grids
authors: Nadim Rooholamin, Kabir Bakhshaei, Giovanni Stabile
abstract: This study presents a hybrid reduced-order modeling (ROM) framework for incompressible flows on collocated finite-volume grids, combining a discretize-then-project consistent-flux formulation for velocity and pressure with a non-intrusive neural-network closure for turbulent viscosity. The intrusive formulation preserves discrete mass conservation and pressure-velocity coupling, while a reduced pressure reference-cell constraint fixes pressure gauge ambiguity. We evaluate Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Transformer, and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) closures. For a three-dimensional lid-driven cavity at $Re=100$, the LSTM-based ROM achieves relative errors of 0.7% in velocity and 4% in turbulent viscosity. At $Re=3200$, a mode-sensitivity study identifies $N=15$ POD modes as the best overall configuration, balancing accuracy, dimension, robustness, and cost. It yields a final relative velocity error of approximately 12.3% and an online wall-clock speedup of approximately $50\times$ over the full-order model; energy and enstrophy errors remain below 11% for all three architectures. This regime requires case-specific neural-network retraining and pressure reference-cell parameter retuning. In a time-extrapolation test trained on $t\in[0,3]$,s and rolled out to $t=6$,s, the ROM remains bounded, although velocity and pressure errors increase beyond the training window. The LSTM turbulent-viscosity closure remains robust, identifying long-horizon pressure accuracy as the main limitation. These results demonstrate the potential of consistent projection-based modeling combined with data-driven turbulence closure for efficient reduced-order simulation.

title: On the relationships between pressure geometrization and vortex identification
authors: Han Tu, Hang Zhao, Qi Gao
abstract: The profound mathematical and conceptual analogy between pressure in fluid mechanics and gravity in general relativity motivates a novel geometric reinterpretation of flows. This article proposes a theoretical framework for geometrizing pressure by establishing a Newton-Cartan geometry and applying a conformal transformation to the spatial metric. The pressure field is reinterpreted as a geometric potential that induces an effective spatial curvature, encoded in the Ricci tensor Rij and the associated Einstein-like tensor Gij. Within this curved effective space, fluid particles under the exclusive influence of pressure follow geodesics, and the classical Euler equation is recovered in the weak-field limit. The pressure Poisson equation emerges naturally as a consequence of the geodesic equation and the Bianchi identity, revealing pressure as an instantaneous geometric constraint rather than an external force. This framework provides a unified geometric interpretation of widely used vortex identification criteria, demonstrating that the prevailing Eulerian and Lagrangian schemes correspond to different geometric invariants or projections of the effective curvature. In the degenerate two-dimensional (2D) limit, the effective spatial tensor vanishes identically, and the global integral of the total curvature vanishes as well. This topological constraint offers a novel interpretation of the dual-cascade scenario in 2D turbulence: the inverse energy cascade arises from geometric condensation of positive-curvature structures toward larger scales, while the forward enstrophy cascade results from geometric dispersion of negative-curvature structures toward smaller scales.

title: Turbulent atmospheric particle fluxes in the High Arctic: surface type dependence and variability
authors: Theresa Mathes, Ian M. Brooks, Sonja Murto, Michael Tjernström, Julia Kojoj, Paul Zieger, John Prytherch, Birgit Wehner, Andreas Held
abstract: Abstract. The Arctic is warming at a significantly faster rate than the global average, which is affecting local climate processes. Aerosol particles play a central role by influencing the energy balance directly through the scattering and absorption of solar radiation and indirectly by acting as cloud condensation nuclei. However, the processes that control aerosol concentrations, such as the mechanisms governing vertical particle exchange, are not well understood, particularly over sea ice. During the ARTofMELT campaign in spring 2023, five weeks of continuous eddy covariance measurements of turbulent particle fluxes were conducted in the High Arctic to investigate the spatial and temporal variability of particle sources and sinks over three surface types. Overall, net particle deposition dominated, with median deposition fluxes of −0.02 × 106m-2 s-1 over closed ice. This confirms the role of ice surfaces as a particle sink under low to moderate turbulence. Under strong winds, net particle emission fluxes of up to 0.98 × 106m-2 s-1 were observed over closed ice surfaces, which are likely linked to processes involving blowing snow. A mixture of emission and deposition was observed over leads and open water surfaces. These observations highlight how surface heterogeneity and turbulence intensity can influence particle exchange in the High Arctic. As sea ice retreats and the extent of open water increases, local particle sources are expected to become more relevant to Arctic aerosol budgets and cloud processes. The results provide observational constraints on particle fluxes, helping to reduce related uncertainties in Arctic model simulations.

title: Deep learning-based high-resolution downscaling of terrain-driven near-surface winds
authors: Nora Helbig, Florian Hammer, Gert‐Jan Duine, Leila M. V. Carvalho, Charles Jones, Hugo Merzisen, Isabelle Gouttevin, Sarah Barber
abstract: Abstract. Spatio-temporal wind fields in mountainous terrain are complex due to strong flow modifications when wind interacts with topography. Machine-learning (ML)-based wind downscaling models offer a computationally efficient alternative to high-resolution atmospheric model simulations and to dynamical downscaling, but their transferability beyond the training regions and conditions in which they were developed remains largely untested. We present an enhanced version of DEVINE, a deep-learning-based downscaling model for near-surface terrain-forced wind flow, being trained on atmospheric model ARPS simulations over Gaussian Random Field synthetic topographies with a wide range of slopes and feature shapes. Incorporating wind direction-dependent input features enables rotational data augmentation and facilitates preprocessing. Using enhanced DEVINE, we systematically assess its performance across previously unseen terrain (synthetic, alpine, coastal mountain environments), wind regimes (terrain-forced flow, sea-breeze circulation, downslope windstorm), and driving model data, using both high-resolution atmospheric wind and ground station data as reference. We find that DEVINE generalizes well to unseen mountain regions when flow is primarily terrain-forced. Its spatial wind speed mean absolute error (MAE) and correlation in the alpine and non-storm coastal environments are lower and higher, respectively, than the station-based results reported by previous ML wind downscaling studies. DEVINE’s own station-based performance remains broadly comparable to, or slightly improves on, these studies’ station-based results (e.g., MAE of 1.13 m s−1), despite simultaneously transferring across new topography, wind regime, and driving data. Performance degrades under complex atmosphere-terrain interactions such as a downslope windstorm (e.g., MAE of 5.6 m s−1); under non-storm conditions, however, DEVINE outperforms the dynamical model WRF-LES at stations for MAE (1.13 m s−1 versus 1.23 m s−1) and matches it for normalized root mean square error (13 %). We further show that station-based and spatial-pattern evaluations can diverge substantially, including in the sign of bias, indicating that the evaluation basis itself shapes apparent performance, and that spatial evaluation may better separate genuine model limitations from local representativity effects. Our findings clarify strengths and limitations of the enhanced DEVINE wind downscaling model under out-of-sample conditions, and more broadly underscore the value of systematically evaluating ML wind downscaling methods across scale and under unseen conditions.

title: Effects of Multi-objective Optimization of the First-stage Impeller on the Energy Loss Characteristics of a Multistage Molten Salt Pump
authors: Q. Chen, X. Yongkang, L. Shilin, Qi Zhipeng, W. Xiaohui
abstract: To mitigate the prohibitive cost of simultaneously modifying all stages in multistage molten salt pumps used in concentrating solar power plants, address the substantial degradation of hydraulic performance under off-design operating conditions, and resolve the difficulty of tracing cross-stage flow-loss coupling mechanisms, this paper presents a cost-effective retrofit strategy that limits geometric modifications to the first-stage impeller and harnesses the interstage flow-matching effect to improve system-wide performance. The methodology proceeds in four sequential phases. First, a comprehensive sample database is constructed using Latin hypercube sampling combined with high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics simulations. Second, the Adam optimization algorithm is used to train a backpropagation neural network, establishing a computationally efficient surrogate model to replace time-intensive numerical simulations. Third, the surrogate model is coupled with the NSGA-II multi-objective evolutionary algorithm to perform Pareto-front optimization, simultaneously maximizing hydraulic head and efficiency at the design operating point. Finally, based on entropy production theory, the evolution of energy loss before and after optimization is systematically characterized at four hierarchical levels: total entropy production, component-level entropy production, wall entropy production, and vortex structure evolution, through the joint analysis of local entropy production rate distributions and vortex identification using the Q-criterion. The optimization yields notable improvements: the hydraulic efficiency of the first-stage impeller increases from 78.42% to 81.83%; total entropy production under design conditions decreases by 8.63%; and entropy production within the first-stage guide vanes decreases by 45.23% at 1.2 times the design flow rate. Crucially, the second-stage impeller geometry remains unchanged, confirming that first-stage optimization propagates performance gains to all downstream stages through the interstage flow-matching mechanism. By limiting the scope of hydraulic modification from the full pump assembly to a single stage, the proposed framework establishes a practical pathway for low-cost hydraulic optimization of multistage molten salt pumps.

title: AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Complex Systems Perspective
authors: Sharath S. Girimaji
abstract: Despite widespread enthusiasm, applying artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) to turbulence modeling has yielded only modest progress, primarily due to a lack of situation-aware deployment. Data-driven Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (ML-RANS) closures frequently fail to generalize across diverse flow regimes, while scale-resolving simulations (SRS) remain computationally prohibitive. As a result, ML-RANS is often misapplied outside its domain of validity, and ML-SRS is unnecessarily deployed on flows fully amenable to RANS. To guide optimal AI/ML deployment, we propose a turbulence taxonomy map parameterized by degrees of freedom ($Re$) and the degree of non-equilibrium ($SK/ε$). By applying Weaver's well-recognized complexity framework, we classify turbulence into distinct physical regimes. This categorization identifies where local ML-RANS surrogates can generalize, clarifies where explicit scale resolution is physically mandatory, and highlights where physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are most effective. Ultimately, this perspective establishes a physics-grounded framework for the flow-aware, successful deployment of AI/ML in turbulence.

title: Data-driven surrogate models for forecasting experimentally measured fluid flows
authors: Peter I. Renn, Emily H. Palmer, Cong Wang, Morteza Gharib
abstract: Data-driven modeling shows significant promise for faster-than-real-time forecasting of fluid flows. For real-world engineering applications (e.g., flow control), models must contend with limited, imperfect, and incomplete experimental measurements. However, most data-driven surrogates have been developed and demonstrated entirely within the computational domain. In this work, we present an analysis of data-driven surrogate models trained to forecast the time evolution of experimentally measured cylinder wakes. Using a dataset of two-dimensional, two-component particle image velocimetry measurements, we train fully convolutional neural networks, U-Nets, Fourier neural operators, and dynamic mode decomposition-based models to forecast the development of experimentally measured velocity fields. To characterize data-driven approaches contending with transient flow features and limited, imperfect observations, the development of predictions over extended forecast horizons is examined at a fixed Reynolds number (Re=590). Next, models are trained at a range of Reynolds numbers (Re=230–2920) to investigate the impact of increasingly turbulent and three-dimensional flow phenomena on forecast quality. Through a triple decomposition of measured and forecast velocity fields, we find that error is dominated by the fluctuating velocity component, with all surrogates exhibiting a decay in estimated planar turbulent kinetic energy. The characteristics of this decay are architecture-dependent. Regardless, we find that the experimentally trained surrogate models can provide meaningful predictions over short time horizons, propagate low-frequency dynamics over longer forecast periods, and achieve faster-than-real-time evaluation in the considered contexts. These results highlight the opportunities and challenges that remain for data-driven fluid dynamics in real-world, real-time engineering applications.

title: Diffusion Model Driven Airfoil Design: From Geometry Encoding to Practical Applications
authors: Yingfan Geng, Jinhong Wang, Teng Cao
abstract: The diffusion model, the state-of-the-art generative machine-learning architecture, has shown promising results in airfoil inverse designs. In this study, we implement and trained a series of diffusion models on three different airfoil geometry data encoding formats [principal component weights, ordered [Formula: see text] coordinates, and 2D signed distance functions (SDF)] to generate 2D airfoils. By systematically comparing the performance of diffusion models trained on different data structures, it is found that for 2D airfoil design problems the diffusion model performs the best when directly trained with coordinates. Training with latent space (principal component analysis weights in this study) limits the model’s design freedom and decreases the training effectiveness. Although the 2D SDF data appear to result in the least performing model, it proves its feasibility in aerodynamic shape generation, paving the way toward 3D problems where SDF is more favored. This study also investigated deploying the diffusion model in practical engineering applications. A multitarget optimization procedure is proposed based on the stochastic nature of the diffusion process, which drastically simplifies the procedure compared to conventional methods. The extrapolation performance of the model is also investigated by tasking the model with both aerodynamic and flow condition labels that are extrapolated beyond the training set boundaries.

title: Characterisation and Extension of a Rigid Body Dynamics Solver Coupled with OpenFOAM® for Flight Performance Analysis of Flapping-wing Drones
authors: Romain Poletti, Emanuele Bombardi, Lilla K. Koloszar, Miguel Alfonso Mendez, Joris Degroote
abstract: The extraordinary aerial agility of hummingbirds and insects continues to inspire the design of flapping-wing drones. To replicate them, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations must be coupled with rigid body dynamics solvers. While OpenFOAM® provides a general articulated-body algorithm (ABA) for these multiphysics simulations, its current implementation is restricted to passive joints and lacks thorough verification for free-flight applications. This work addresses these limitations by introducing an extension of the ABA to support active joints with prescribed kinematics, allowing the body dynamics and the imposed motions to be solved simultaneously. The imposed motion is implemented in a new imposedMotion library that directly prescribes joint positions, velocities, and accelerations. The proposed approach is verified using a hierarchical strategy, including analytical benchmarks, comparison with quasi-steady aerodynamic models, and grid- and time-integration sensitivity analyses. Results demonstrate the robustness of the proposed framework and its ability to capture body–wing inertial coupling effects, contributing to the OpenFOAM® community with an extensible open-source platform for simulating partially actuated multibody systems in unsteady flows.

title: Flow Characteristics and Air-distribution Uniformity in Passenger-coach Air-conditioning Ducts
authors: Y. Y. Li, Y. X. Zhao, Y. C. Wei, T. Sun, H. L. Dai
abstract: Nonuniform air distribution in passenger-coach air-conditioning ducts commonly causes insufficient distal airflow and reduces cabin thermal comfort. In ducts with uniform cross-sections, continuous air discharge through distributed outlets induces streamwise static-pressure attenuation, resulting in a typical front-dominant, rear-deficient airflow pattern. This study combines theoretical analysis, computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and multiobjective optimization to investigate the flow characteristics and uniform air-supply strategy of a passenger-coach air-conditioning duct. The results demonstrate that static-pressure decay is the primary mechanism responsible for outlet-flow maldistribution and that global outlet-radius reduction provides only limited improvement. In contrast, a streamwise graded-radius scheme, in which the outlet radii generally increase from the upstream to the downstream region with local corrections at selected outlets, effectively compensates for pressure attenuation and enhances distal airflow. Based on CFD data, cubic polynomial correlations between the preliminarily optimized outlet radius and the distance from the fan-side reference position are established for both ducts, with coefficients of determination exceeding 0.90. Guide-vane optimization using Gaussian process regression, support vector regression, and a genetic algorithm further indicates that guide vanes mainly provide local flow regulation, whereas radius gradation governs the global redistribution of airflow. The optimized radius scheme reduces the left-duct flow nonuniformity coefficient by 8.2%. Because the radius fitting and guide-vane optimization are based on limited simulation samples, the resulting correlations should be regarded as preliminary design references that require further validation.

title: Example-driven Parametrisations for Bayesian Shape Optimisation
authors: Gabriel Diaz-Aylwin, Joseph Neighbor, Abiel Malkani Talwar, Rui-Yang Zhang, Henry B. Moss
abstract: Bayesian optimisation is the natural tool for shape design when objectives are expensive and non-differentiable, but it needs a compact yet expressive parameterisation of the search space. Hand-crafting one is a complex endeavour requiring domain expertise, and often yields implicit infeasible regions, artificial bounds, and coupled, unordered coordinates. We instead learn the parameterisation from a collection of existing designs, applying principal component analysis to the deformations between shapes. The result is a linear, interpretable search space in which the number of components explicitly trades expressivity against dimensionality. Across aerofoils, wings, and radio-frequency cavities, spanning 2D geometry to 3D aerodynamics and electromagnetics, we show improved sample efficiency and the ability to explore beyond the confines of hand-crafted baselines.

title: Sim-to-Real RL for ASVs using SysID
authors: Cody Sheltraw, Tsimafei Lazouski, Maani Ghaffari, Alan Papalia
abstract: Autonomous Surface Vehicles (ASVs) operating in dynamic marine environments require robust control policies for tasks such as path following and station keeping, making reinforcement learning (RL) a promising alternative to classical controllers. However, existing ASV simulators rarely support parallel environments for RL training. Such existing simulators require accurate hydrodynamic modeling from computational fluid dynamics solvers or towing tank tests for setting hydrodynamic parameters to address the sim-to-real gap. To address these challenges, we present an ASV simulator and accompanying pipeline that enables training policies starting from unknown vehicle dynamics. Our framework uses only a CAD model and brief set of open-water field trajectories for approximating and refining both hydrodynamic and thruster parameters. Real-world deployments on a BlueBoat ASV demonstrate successful zero-shot sim-to-real transfer in path following and station-keeping tasks without prior hydrodynamic and propeller information.

title: Dynamics of Advanced Launch Vehicles Thrust Chambers: Theoretical Foundations and Technical Optimization
authors: Роман Марчан, Samir Vekilov, O.D. Nikolayev, Inna Bashlii
abstract: Modern space launch vehicles require cost-effective, safe, and reliable propulsion systems with reduced environmental impact. To meet these criteria, contemporary space-launch thrust chamber designs leverage advanced components, innovative materials, and additive manufacturing technologies. Dynamic instability in a liquid rocket engine (LRE) thrust chamber can be driven by acoustic oscillations of the combustion products, accompanied by surface vortex shedding. Numerical modeling was performed to simulate the unsteady gas flow within the thrust chamber of an advanced LRE produced via additive manufacturing. A computational analysis of the combustion product flow parameters was conducted using the ANSYS Fluent finite-element analysis suite. Based on the numerical investigation of the chamber dynamics, it was determined that the turbulent flow of gaseous combustion products along the cylindrical walls is characterized by the formation of vortices. These vortices periodically break down as the gas flow progresses from the injector head to the nozzle throat. A self-excited (limit-cycle) dynamic process develops within the chamber, where low-frequency pressure oscillation amplitudes can reach 3 bar–5 bar. The numerical results show satisfactory agreement with hot-fire test data. The root cause of the dynamic instability was identified by analyzing the influence of the increased surface roughness inherent in chambers fabricated through additive manufacturing. Theoretical analysis of the unsteady flow demonstrated that reducing surface roughness significantly diminishes the intensity of turbulent vortex shedding and substantially lowers pressure oscillation levels – a finding subsequently validated by experimental fire tests.

title: Localized Generative Design of Ship Hulls with Diffusion Models and High-Fidelity Assessment
authors: Hadi Keramati, Mohammed A. Hannan, Patrick Kirchen, Sina Tousi, Joonas Riekkinen, Jim Pyra, Rajeev K. Jaiman
abstract: Practical ship design requires localized refinement and performance evaluation. This paper presents a reward-directed diffusion framework for localized hull optimization. Parametric masking during dataset generation restricts geometric changes to selected variables, including the bulbous bow and forebody, while preserving full-hull continuity. Surrogate-assisted sequential Monte Carlo sampling targets reduced predicted calm-water resistance, with stability retained through training data and displacement matched during screening. An automated viscous free-surface CFD pipeline, validated against measurements for two benchmark container ships, evaluates a generated variant and GenHull E, a hull refined by a naval architect within the same representation. At matched KRISO Container Ship (KCS) displacement, the generated variant has comparable total resistance at $F_n=0.195$ but 45-50% higher resistance at $F_n=0.250$ and $0.260$, missed by empirical screening. GenHull E achieves 6-8% lower total resistance up to $F_n=0.240$ but higher resistance above $F_n=0.250$ as opposing friction and pressure trends reverse the gains. Aggregating resistance across this crossover can conceal tradeoffs that emerge when friction and pressure components are evaluated separately. The assessment reveals an inability to represent a faired bulbous bow and a reward lacking viscous pressure and stability terms. These findings show how high-fidelity assessment informs improved representations and objectives for physically realizable generative designs.

title: High-fidelity Three-Dimensional Flow Field Reconstruction Driven by Turbulent Fluid Dynamics
authors: Han-Lin Kong, Jia-Nan Wei, Yun-Tian Chen, Yu-Jia Wang, Wen-Guan Wang
abstract: High-fidelity three-dimensional turbulent flow fields are essential for scientific and engineering analyses, yet obtaining them through direct numerical simulation or high-resolution measurements remains expensive. Super-resolution reconstruction from coarse-grained data therefore offers a promising alternative, but remains fundamentally challenging because fine-scale structures are intrinsically three-dimensional and dynamically coupled across scales. Existing data-driven approaches still struggle to recover multiscale volumetric structures and their coherent temporal evolution. To address these limitations, we propose a turbulence-aware framework for time-resolved three-dimensional flow reconstruction. The framework couples a multiscale neural operator, designed to recover volumetric structures, with a state space model to promote temporal consistency in the reconstructed dynamics. In addition, Navier-Stokes residuals are incorporated as soft constraints to regularize the reconstruction toward physically plausible dynamics. A mixture-of-experts mechanism is also introduced to support unsupervised adaptation to unknown coarse-graining. Across evaluations on canonical turbulent systems and atmospheric reanalysis data, the proposed framework reduces reconstruction errors relative to learning-based and classical baselines, while better preserving multiscale spatial structure and coherent temporal evolution. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in reconstructing high-fidelity three-dimensional flow fields from coarse-grained data.

title: Comparison between field experiment and CFD modeling of the surface stabilization of fine-grained bulk materials with biopolymer reagent
authors: V. Nikolova, K. Dedelyanova
abstract: Tailings storage facilities are a significant source of fugitive dust emissions, and the susceptibility of their surface layer to wind erosion is directly related to both the environmental safety and the geomechanical stability of the facility. This report presents results of a field test with a biodegradable polymer reagent for surface sealing. A 0.5% aqueous solution of the reagent was used to conduct the test, applied by a water carrier onto a dry section of the field. The formation of a surface crust of varying thickness was observed due to the uneven application caused by strong winds during the test. In order to better understand the observed unevenness, a simplified three-dimensional CFD model was developed in ANSYS Fluent, reproducing the wind flow over a stepped slope – a geometrically simplified analogue of the tailings slope. The simulation results show a clearly pronounced recirculation zone in the leeward part of the slope, which is in qualitative agreement with the observed uneven application of the reagent in the field.

title: Learning to reconstruct Germano Differential Filtered Fields with Convolutional Neural Networks for Large Eddy Simulation of Plasma Turbulence
authors: Jony Castagna, Josh Williams
abstract: We present a novel method which combines the invertibility of the differential filter of Germano, with convolutional networks to accelerate plasma turbulence simulations. Rather than learning the mapping from coarse-grid LES fields to fine-grid DNS, the proposed method learns the mapping from coarse LES fields to the differential-filtered DNS fields. We then use the inverse of Germano's filter to reconstruct the fine-scale details and hence calculate exactly the nonlinear terms in the governing equations and subgrid-scale terms in the LES equations. The method is tested on the 2D Hasegawa-Wakatani (HW) and modified Hasegawa-Wakatani (mHW) plasma turbulence models at $256^2$ and $512^2$ DNS resolutions using 2, 4 and 8 times smaller LES grids in each direction. We compare the model with DNS results on energy, enstrophy, spectra, probability distributions, poloidal and radial fluxes and computational cost. Validation extends to 1000 simulation time units for HW and 100 for mHW, whose faster dynamics lead toward laminarization. For the $256^2$ cases, the finer LES meshes preserve several integral and spectral features, whereas the coarsest mesh yields unphysical behavior. In contrast, for the $512^2$ cases, even the coarsest LES mesh preserves the turbulent character of the flow and maintains acceptable statistics for both the HW and mHW models. Moreover, we show how our methodology is superior to traditional algebraic numerical LES models, which traditionally fail to capture important design features. Finally, benchmarks show an MPI task-time reductions of 4.82--49.45, with a maximum wall-clock speedup of $1.55\times$ when compared to full CPU socket.

title: Airfoil pitch control in the wake of a backward-facing step via spatiotemporal deep reinforcement learning
authors: Cheng Hu, Wei-Yuan Sun, Shun-Xiang Cao, Jing-Ying Wang
abstract: Closed-loop lift control for an airfoil in a strongly nonuniform inflow is challenging, especially when only partial surface-pressure observations are available. This study investigates pitch control of a NACA (National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics) 0012 airfoil descending through the wake of a backward-facing step. A spatiotemporal deep-reinforcement-learning-based control framework is developed, in which the controller adopts sparse surface pressure and airfoil kinematics as feedback. The proposed MSALSTM policy, trained with proximal policy optimization, combines multi-head self-attention for spatial pressure encoding with long short-term memory for temporal inference of hidden flow states. Among the learned architectures, MSALSTM provides the most stable lift tracking and the smallest pitch oscillation. It also outperforms the fixed-angle and gain-scheduled proportional–integral–derivative baselines under the same descent condition. When a drag penalty is added to the reward function, the learned policy further increases the mean lift-to-drag ratio by 46%. Further analysis reveals that the attention module adaptively redistributes sensor emphasis according to the evolving flow state, while the recurrent memory organizes pressure-history information into structured hidden-state trajectories. These results demonstrate that spatiotemporal learning can reconstruct effective flow-state information from sparse wall-pressure data for high-Reynolds-number aerodynamic control.

title: Phase-Change Transpiration Cooling for Hypersonic Vehicles: A Comprehensive Review of Mechanisms, Modeling, Experiments, and Future Direction
authors: Xing-Yu Chen, Ming-Yun Lv
abstract: Phase-change transpiration cooling, in which a liquid coolant flows through a porous medium, absorbs heat, and undergoes phase change while forming a protective gas film, is widely regarded as one of the most efficient active thermal protection concepts for next-generation hypersonic vehicles. This paper presents a comprehensive and critical review of the technology, tracing its evolution from early feasibility studies to recent flight demonstrations and systematically synthesizing advances in numerical modeling, experimental investigation, and engineering application. In modeling, existing approaches are classified into three categories: macroscopic two-phase mixture models, pore-scale interface-capturing methods, and mesoscopic direct numerical simulation and lattice Boltzmann methods. The mutual isolation of these three classes and the absence of a cross-scale coupling framework are identified as core methodological gaps. In experimentation, the review surveys mechanistic studies, ground-based qualification tests on complex structures, and the only two publicly reported flight validations, revealing a critical shortage of full-scale, long-duration, and multi-physics qualification data. Key physical phenomena, including vapor blockage, temperature oscillations, cooling hysteresis, and low-pressure freezing, are critically discussed. Beyond summarizing the state of the art, the review argues that the dominant research of small-scale, short-duration, single-physics studies fundamentally limits the generalizability of existing findings to real flight conditions. Six future research directions are proposed, emphasizing the need for a transition toward integrated, multi-physics, system-level demonstrations. This review is intended to serve as a reference for researchers and engineers working on hypersonic thermal protection, porous media heat transfer, and multiphase flow.

title: Coupled phase-field and lattice Boltzmann modeling of dendritic growth and bubble entrapment during solidification of an Al–4.5 wt.% Cu alloy
authors: Zhi-Ming Gao, Chuang-Xin Zhang, Zhong-Tang Gao, Sai-Nan Liu, Yan Liu, Chuan-Wei Zhang
abstract: A coupled phase-field/lattice Boltzmann (PF-LBM) framework was employed to investigate the migration, deformation, and entrapment of initially prescribed bubbles during dendritic solidification of an Al–4.5 wt.% Cu alloy. Solidification experiments combined with scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray computed tomography (XCT) were performed to characterize the pore morphologies and provide experimental comparison with the numerical predictions. The interactions between dendritic growth and the migration and entrapment of pre-existing bubbles under convective conditions were examined. The interactions between bubble dynamics and dendritic growth in multiphase flow were simulated using a coupled Shan–Chen multiphase flow model and a phase-field lattice Boltzmann (PF-LBM) model. The buoyancy-driven behaviors of bubbles, including rising, deformation, breakup, and coalescence, were found to be strongly influenced by the melt Reynolds number(Re) and Eötvös number(Eo). A reduction in surface tension significantly intensified bubble deformation. During the interaction between bubbles and dendrites, the migration velocity of bubbles gradually decreased and eventually approached zero due to the blocking effect of the growing dendrites, accompanied by pronounced changes in bubble morphology. Furthermore, the coupled evolution behavior of bubbles and dendrites in multiphase flow was strongly dependent on the solidification mode. Under equiaxed solidification conditions, bubbles were confined within interdendritic spaces and exhibited isolated, nearly spherical morphologies as a result of the spatial constriction imposed by multidirectional dendritic growth. In contrast, under columnar solidification conditions, bubbles migrated along the direction of heat flow, where they were pushed and eventually captured by dendrite tips, leading to the formation of elongated pore morphologies aligned with the dendritic growth direction. SEM and XCT observations further revealed isolated and randomly distributed pores within the equiaxed dendritic structure, whereas elongated and directionally distributed pores were observed within the columnar dendritic structure. Quantitative XCT analysis further revealed estimated mean pore sphericities of 0.76 and 0.66 within the equiaxed and columnar dendritic structures, respectively. These experimental findings support the distinct morphological trends predicted by the numerical simulations.

title: Interface Dynamics and Heat Transfer in Droplet-Laden Rayleigh–Bénard Convection: A Triple-Distribution-Function Lattice Boltzmann Simulation
authors: Xiang Li, Xiao-Ru Zhuang, Hiroshi Yamaguchi, Zhi-Qiang Dong
abstract: For the present study, a triple-distribution-function lattice Boltzmann model was developed to simulate immiscible multiphase thermal flows with coupled interfacial dynamics and heat transfer in droplet-laden Rayleigh–Bénard convection. Within the single-relaxation-time lattice Boltzmann framework, three sets of mesoscopic lattice Boltzmann equations for density, order parameter, and temperature distribution functions were systematically coupled to recover the macroscopic governing equations including the Navier–Stokes equations, the Cahn–Hilliard equation, and the energy equation. The macroscopic equations could be accurately recovered through Chapman–Enskog expansion analysis. Compared with existing multiphase lattice Boltzmann approaches, the present scheme suppresses mass dissipation at phase interfaces and enables concurrent computation of flow field evolution, complex interface deformation, and thermal transport for immiscible multiphase thermal systems with high-fidelity. Owing to these favorable numerical properties, we first validated the model against the benchmark of single-phase Rayleigh–Bénard convection, and the predicted temperature contours and volume-averaged Nusselt numbers (Nuave) showed good consistency with the theoretical and published numerical benchmarks. Furthermore, systematic numerical investigations were performed for droplet-laden Rayleigh–Bénard convection to reveal the effects of the droplet diameter and the thermal conductivity ratio. The present numerical simulations demonstrate that larger droplets settling on the hot bottom wall produce a blocking effect that suppresses hot plume ejection and monotonically decreases Nuave. In addition, the thermal conductivity ratio induces non-monotonic variation of the heat transfer performance. The relatively smaller ratios enhance heat transfer as the droplet acts as a local thermal fin, while a critical threshold around 30–40 triggers local instability and a sharp drop in Nuave. On further increasing the ratio, reorganization is driven of the small vortices back into large convection cells for the numerical cases of D = 0.3. These results confirm the accuracy and robustness of the triple-distribution-function lattice Boltzmann model for immiscible two-phase thermal convection and offer theoretical guidance for engineering applications such as thermal management and phase-change heat transfer.

title:
Computational Fluid
Dynamics Modeling of Bubble Column
Reactors: Review
authors: Sarang G. Tamhankar, Channamallikarjun S. Mathpati, Jyeshtharaj B. Joshi
abstract: Abstract Bubble column reactors are essential equipment in the process industries, with a wide range of applications, but their hydrodynamics and design are very complex. For the past five decades, researchers and industry have relied on Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) to predict the local hydrodynamics of multiphase reactors, developing predictive tools capable of capturing the complex gas–liquid interactions occurring within them. Conventional design practices are primarily based on empirical and semi-empirical correlations that provide global quantities of design parameters, including gas holdup, interfacial area, mass and heat transfer coefficients, etc. These correlations depend on the operating parameters and gas–liquid systems for which they were developed, limiting their general applicability and making CFD an increasingly important tool for understanding the behavior in bubble columns. A large body of literature has been analyzed in this review to cover state-of-the-art modeling approaches. Following an introduction to the history of bubble columns, scale-up challenges, and operating flow regimes, the discussion then transitions to modeling methodologies, including the algebraic slip mixture model, the Eulerian–Lagrangian and Eulerian–Eulerian frameworks. Particular attention is given to interphase momentum transfer, including the drag force (with swarm correction), lift force, virtual mass force, turbulent dispersion force, and wall lubrication force. The significance of turbulence modeling is also considered through Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS), Large Eddy Simulation (LES), Reynolds Stress Model (RSM), and formulation methodologies of bubble-induced turbulence. Population Balance Modeling (PBM) is examined as a significant tool for the prediction of bubble size distribution and integrating it with CFD through bubble breakup and coalescence kernels. Numerical factors affecting the simulation’s predictive capabilities, including dimensionality, grid resolution, discretization methodologies, and transient solution strategies, are also taken into account. Numerical investigations reported in the literature over the past 25 years have been examined, including various model configurations, their predictive capabilities, and their limitations. A clear agreement between simulated results and the operation of real bubble columns, particularly through comparisons of gas holdup, velocity profiles, bubble size distribution, mixing, heat transfer, and mass transfer, has been established. The review shows that CFD has become a powerful tool for bubble column analysis but is still limited by closure-model uncertainty, scale dependence, and the need for systematic validation under industrially relevant conditions.

title: Machine Learning Modeling of Drill Cuttings Transport Based on Computational Fluid Dynamics Simulation Data
authors: Kathrin Skinder, Mostafa M. Abdelhafiz, Khizar Shahid, G. Brenner
abstract: Drill cuttings transport is a critical operation in drilling deep wells. Inefficient removal of cuttings can lead to both hydraulic and mechanical problems during drilling operations. High‐fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations provide detailed insight but are computationally expensive. Alternative models often oversimplify the relationships between operational parameters and particle transport, thereby failing to predict critical quantities. These quantities include transport efficiency or cuttings concentrations. In this study, surrogate models are developed using a common data set generated by validated multiphase CFD simulations. The data set consists of 269 CFD simulations varying the Reynolds number, Taylor number, particle concentration, and particle size. Five surrogate models, namely, Decision Trees (DTs), Random Forest (RF), Extra Trees (XTRs), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Gaussian process regression (GPR), were trained to predict the domain‐averaged particle velocity. The models are evaluated in terms of prediction accuracy, learning behavior with respect to training data size, robustness through bootstrap resampling, and physical consistency of the response trends. All trained models achieved very high predictive accuracy (), confirming that CFD‐based particle transport can be reliably emulated using data‐driven surrogates. The learning‐curve analysis showed that performance improves rapidly with increasing data, saturating beyond approximately 60% of the data set. Despite the statistical accuracy, tree‐based ensembles produced piecewise‐constant, nonsmooth response surfaces. However, GPR generated smoother and more physically consistent trends. Sensitivity analysis revealed that the Reynolds number dominates the system behavior, explaining more than 95% of the output variance. The high predictive accuracy observed across all surrogate models (), with most predictions within of CFD reference values, reflects the low‐dimensional character of the system, where the output is dominated by the Reynolds number. The trained models enable global sensitivity analysis through Monte Carlo simulation and real‐time prediction of cuttings velocity, supporting continuous monitoring, control, and optimization of borehole cleaning in deep drilling operations, while demonstrating how information from expensive high‐fidelity CFD simulations can be retained in fast, computationally cheap surrogates.

title: Development of A Lightweight Neural Network for Predicting Reaction Rates in RANS Simulations of Flame-Wall Interactions
authors: Maximilian Bambauer, Vipin Michael, Markus Klein, Nilanjan Chakraborty
abstract: Abstract Accurate prediction of Flame-Wall Interactions (FWI) is crucial for the design of compact, high-efficiency combustors but remains a significant challenge for Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) simulations. This study presents the development and validation of a lightweight data-driven closure for the mean reaction rate, trained on high-fidelity Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) data of a V-shaped turbulent premixed flame. To ensure numerical stability and physical consistency, the training methodology incorporates a logarithmic transformation of the reaction rate target and a novel error-function transformation of the wall distance, effectively localizing the model’s sensitivity to the near-wall quenching zone. A-priori validation demonstrates that the neural network accurately captures the mean reaction rate statistics and extrapolates successfully to unseen spatial regions. However, a-posteriori assessment in coupled RANS simulations reveals a critical sensitivity to input feature consistency. The full-feature model (7 input parameters), which includes turbulent kinetic energy and dissipation rate as inputs, fails to predict the correct quenching behavior due to significant discrepancies between the DNS-extracted turbulence quantities used for training and the corresponding quantities obtained from RANS. In contrast, a reduced-feature model (3 input parameters), relying exclusively on the mean progress variable, its gradient, and the transformed wall distance, demonstrates remarkable robustness. By decoupling the prediction from uncertain turbulence quantities, the model with 3 input parameters accurately reproduces the V-flame structure, achieving performance comparable to a manually tuned algebraic closure. Furthermore, the reduced model exhibits strong generalization capabilities, successfully predicting the transient physics of a Head-On Quenching (HOQ) configuration that was not present in the training dataset. These findings highlight that for data-driven RANS closures, selecting input features that remain consistent across fidelity levels, is paramount for achieving predictive stability and generalization.

title: Machine Learning-Driven Optimization of Multiphase Chemical Processes for Energy-Efficient and Sustainable Manufacturing
authors: Mustafa Soniwala, Taha Mandviwala
abstract: There are many industrial chemical manufacturing processes that involve multi-phase chemistry, such as gas–liquid, liquid–liquid, gas–solid, solid–liquid and three-phase systems, and these are among the most energy-intensive and complex unit processes to optimise, due to the complex, nonlinear and often unmeasurable interfacial phenomena. The hydrodynamic, thermal and mass transfer coupling involved in these systems are difficult to model with traditional first-principles or empirical optimization approaches and make it challenging to progress towards industrially relevant scales and energy efficient, sustainable manufacturing targets. This narrative review aims to collect and condense the surge of literature on the application of machine learning (ML) algorithms for optimizing multiphase chemical processes, which spans from classic statistical process control (SPC) to advanced data-driven, hybrid and physics-informed learning algorithms. We study the use of supervised learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, Bayesian optimization and evolutionary algorithms in important multiphase unit operations for surrogate modelling, soft sensing, real-time control and multi-objective optimization. The literature reviewed indicates that the combined results of the different strategies with ML can produce energy efficiency gains ranging from 8% - 28%, improvements in yield and product quality and predictive accuracy can be identified, and computational costs can be reduced when compared to other conventional approaches such as computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and first-principles (FP). The challenges highlighted include issues such as limited data, interpretability of models, scalability, and real-time deployment. The future scope for this research is physics-informed and hybrid models, digital twins, transfer and federated learning, and benchmarking.

title: Fractional-Order Advection–Diffusion Equations: A Critical Review of Physical Origins, Analytical and Numerical Methods, and Applications
authors: Weiguang Huang
abstract: The advection–diffusion equation is the canonical continuum description of transport, yet it fails for a broad class of systems in which particle motion is non-Fickian. Fractional-order advection–diffusion equations replace integer derivatives with operators of non-integer order and, in doing so, encode long-range spatial jumps and long-memory waiting times that classical models discard. This review provides a critical, evidence-based synthesis of the field from its foundations in continuous-time random walks and Lévy motion through the mathematical and numerical landscape. We first examine the family of fractional operators and the physical meaning of their kernels. We then trace the micro–macro derivations that connect fractional advection–diffusion equations to anomalous transport, mobile–immobile systems, tempered and variable-order processes. Analytical methods and the now-mature toolbox of finite difference, finite element, spectral, meshless and lattice-Boltzmann discretizations are appraised for accuracy, stability and computational cost. Inverse problems and parameter estimation, which decide whether such models earn their extra complexity, are reviewed next. Applications in hydrology, porous media, plasmas, space physics, heat and mass transfer, biology and finance illustrate both success and unresolved tension. Throughout, we identify trends—rising use of non-singular-kernel operators, machine-learning solvers and realistic benchmarking—and we flag persistent gaps: inconsistent operator conventions, sparse validation against real data, and scarce higher-dimensional and multiscale results. We close with a concrete research agenda for making fractional advection–diffusion models predictive rather than descriptive. Keywords: fractional calculus; anomalous diffusion; advection–diffusion equation; Lévy motion; Caputo derivative; mobile–immobile transport; finite difference methods; inverse problems.

title: Plug-and-play predictive energy management for fuel-efficient platooning of gasoline-powered autonomous vehicles
authors: Behrouz Samieiyan, Anjali Awasthi
abstract: In this paper, we present a plug-and-play predictive energy management framework for fuel-efficient platooning of gasoline-powered autonomous vehicles. Unlike existing approaches that target electric or hybrid drivetrains, the proposed architecture addresses the nonlinear thermodynamic and aerodynamic challenges inherent to internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles. The framework integrates an Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System optimized via Teaching-Learning-Based Optimization (ANFIS-TLBO) with Model Predictive Control (MPC) and a Quantum-inspired Long Short-Term Memory (QLSTM) network that broadcasts a 10-second leader state prediction horizon to all follower vehicles simultaneously. A cooperative power-sharing mechanism and a predictive gap policy are superimposed as a lightweight supervisory layer that leaves the internal structure and parameters of each local controller entirely unchanged, modifying only its reference inputs (predicted leader trajectory, desired gap, and coordinated fuel-cut activation). The framework is validated across four standardized driving cycles, HWFET, US06, Artemis HW130, and Artemis HW150, in both 4-vehicle and 6-vehicle homogeneous platoon configurations, each subjected to 20 statistically independent runs incorporating stochastic wind (Weibull) and road grade (Rayleigh) disturbances. Under the HWFET cycle, the proposed method achieves an average per-vehicle fuel consumption of 6.64 L/100 km (4-vehicle platoon) and 6.61 L/100 km (6-vehicle platoon), outperforming all benchmarks including Adaptive MAB, Pure ANFIS, Pure MPC, and Pure TLBO. NOx emission reduction rates from leader to last follower reach 5.74% and 6.23% in the respective configurations, the highest recorded across all methods, reflecting a trade-off in which the leader operates at a higher absolute NOx level to sustain tighter velocity tracking, while followers benefit disproportionately from predictive power management. The plug-and-play architecture is validated on a 6-vehicle platoon with zero controller retuning, confirming scalability across platoon sizes without local-controller modification.

title: Levenberg–marquardt based ANN solution for MHD nanofluid flow and heat transportation over a thin needle with thermophoresis effects
authors: Haider Ali, Aaqib Majeed, Taoufik S. Saidani, Parvez Ali
abstract: Artificial neural network (ANN) techniques have emerged as powerful data-driven tools for their effectiveness in analysis, modeling, and simulation. These supervised learning approaches are designed to reduce the error between predicted and observed data, providing accurate approximations of complex physical systems. To improve training performance, the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm (LMA) is widely adopted due to its fast convergence and suitability for nonlinear problems. The objective of this study is to develop an ANN-based computational framework using the LMA to accurately predict the flow and heat transfer characteristics of an MHD nanofluid over a thin needle based on Buongiorno’s model. The novelty of the present work lies in applying an ANN-based predictive framework to the Buongiorno nanofluid model over a moving thin needle, which has received limited attention in the existing literature. The impacts of transverse magnetic field, Brownian motion, and thermophoresis are contained in the mathematical model. The governing equations for fluid flow are converted to ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and numerically solved. The results are also predicted by using Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) techniques. The effect of physical parameters like magnetic parameter ( $$M$$ ), Prandtl number ( $$\Pr $$ ), thermophoresis parameter ( $${Nt}$$ ), Brownian motion parameter ( $${Nb}$$ ), and Schmidt number ( $${Sc}$$ ) on velocity, temperature and concentration profiles are explored. The outcomes indicate that the velocity of the fluid decreases with the upsurge of the magnetic parameter while the temperature increases. Higher values of $$\Pr $$ and $${Sc}$$ reduce the temperature and concentration profiles, correspondingly. The Brownian motion parameter boosts the temperature but lowers the concentration, while the thermophoresis parameter rises both temperature and concentration. It is also observed that the magnetic field increases the skin friction coefficient but decreases the heat and mass transfer rates. The ANN results are very close to the numerical results, showing that ANN is an accurate and reliable method for predicting complex nanofluid flow problems.

title: Tipping point forecasting in nonstationary dynamics on function spaces
authors: Miguel Liu-Schiaffini, Clare E. Singer, Nikola Kovachki, Sze Chai Leung, H. Jane Bae, Kamyar Azizzadenesheli, Anima Anandkumar
abstract: Tipping points are abrupt, drastic, and often irreversible changes in the evolution of nonstationary and chaotic dynamical systems. For instance, increased greenhouse gas concentrations are predicted to lead to drastic decreases in low cloud cover, referred to as a climatological tipping point. In this paper, we learn the evolution of such nonstationary dynamical systems using a recurrent neural operator (RNO), which learns mappings between function spaces. After training RNO on only the pre-tipping dynamics, we employ it to detect future tipping points using an uncertainty-based approach. In particular, we propose a conformal prediction framework to forecast tipping points by monitoring deviations from physics constraints (such as conserved quantities and partial differential equations), enabling forecasting of these abrupt changes along with a rigorous measure of uncertainty. We illustrate our proposed methodology on nonstationary ordinary and partial differential equations, such as the Lorenz-63 and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equations. We also apply our methods to forecast a climate tipping point in stratocumulus cloud cover and airfoil wake and stall transitions using only limited knowledge of the governing equations. For the latter, we show that our proposed method zero-shot generalizes to forecasting multiple future tipping points under varying Reynolds numbers. In our experiments, we demonstrate that even partial or approximate physics constraints can be used to accurately forecast future tipping points.

title: Genetic programming control of quasiperiodic and chaotic oscillations in a thermoacoustic system
authors: Bo Yin, Zhijian Yang, Yu Guan, Stéphane Redonnet, Vikrant Gupta, Larry K.B. Li
abstract: Self-excited thermoacoustic oscillations remain a key obstacle to low-emission combustion, especially in time-aperiodic regimes where quasiperiodic and chaotic dynamics hinder conventional controller design. We experimentally demonstrate data-driven suppression of such aperiodic thermoacoustic oscillations in a flame-driven Rijke tube using genetic programming (GP). In closed-loop form, the GP-discovered control laws are static nonlinear feedback maps that generate, in real time, actuation commands from a sensor signal. Performance is evaluated by a cost function that penalises both the thermoacoustic amplitude (state cost) and the actuation effort (input cost), enabling efficiency comparisons. We benchmark GP closed-loop control (GCC) against GP open-loop control and conventional open-loop harmonic forcing. In the quasiperiodic regime, all three strategies achieve nearly 90 percent sign 90 % $90\,\%$ amplitude reduction, but the closed-loop strategy is the most efficient. The low-amplitude controlled state is dominated by a preferred (high-gain) mode of the open-flame describing function, and can persist even after control deactivation, indicating basin-of-attraction switching. In the chaotic regime, GCC again outperforms both open-loop strategies, achieving the largest thermoacoustic amplitude reduction with minimal actuation effort. Synchronisation analysis reveals phase trapping, drifting and locking between pressure and heat-release-rate fluctuations, while the 0–1 test and complexity–entropy diagnostics reveal that the GP-suppressed state retains measurable signatures of deterministic chaos. Overall, this study shows that GP control can provide an efficient model-free tool for suppressing aperiodic thermoacoustic oscillations by autonomously exploiting high-receptivity flame pathways with state-dependent actuation.

title: Seasonal lags and legacy effects on vegetation cover and carbon uptake in Kuwait from 2014 to 2024: A MODIS GPP–ET–NDVI analysis
authors: Shereen Nadoum
abstract: Abstract Remote sensing provides a consistent framework for quantifying vegetation dynamics in hyper-arid environments where field observations are sparse. This study integrated MODIS-derived gross primary productivity (GPP), evapotranspiration (ET), and normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) with GPM IMERG precipitation to evaluate seasonal variability, carbon–water coupling, rainfall-response lags, and cumulative hydroclimatic controls across Kuwait during 2014–2024. Vegetation activity peaked in spring, when mean GPP reached 2.25 ± 0.41 g C m⁻² d⁻¹ and NDVI 0.26 ± 0.05, compared with 0.92 ± 0.21 g C m⁻² d⁻¹ and 0.12 ± 0.03 in summer. ET was strongly associated with GPP (R² = 0.680, p < 0.001) and NDVI (R² = 0.533, p < 0.001), whereas same-month precipitation explained substantially less variation in GPP (R² = 0.189, p = 0.003) and NDVI (R² = 0.081, p = 0.061). Cross-correlation analysis showed that both vegetation indicators responded strongly when rainfall preceded vegetation activity by one month (GPP: r = 0.711; NDVI: r = 0.678; both p < 0.001), with the NDVI response persisting longer than GPP. At the cumulative interannual scale, ET remained significantly associated with GPP (R² = 0.524, p = 0.012) and NDVI (R² = 0.630, p = 0.004), whereas cumulative precipitation was not significant. These findings demonstrate that vegetation dynamics in Kuwait are better characterized by ecosystem water use and antecedent rainfall than by contemporaneous or cumulative precipitation alone, highlighting the importance of rainfall timing and short-term hydroclimatic legacy effects in hyper-arid ecosystems.

title: Dipteran wing damage discriminates between flight motor inertial-elastic distributions
authors: Najmeh Asadimoghaddam, Jiaqi Shi, Dorian Decout, Arion Pons
abstract: Abstract Insects frequently experience irreversible wing damage, yet many maintain flight by adjusting their wingbeat. In Diptera, wingbeat frequency generally increases as wing inertia is lost, but considerably less than predicted by classical models of the flight motor. In this work, we use an inverse-problem approach to identify passive mechanical features of the dipteran flight motor that explain this discrepancy and reproduce experimentally-observed frequency scaling. Combining spatially resolved reconstruction of wing inertia and motor elasticity, finite-element analysis of thoracic deformation, and data-driven viscoelastic models of asynchronous flight muscle, we identify that a compounding interaction between wing root flexion, wing aerodynamics, and muscular viscoelasticity explain the depressed scaling of wingbeat frequency with loss of inertia. Wing inertia is strongly non-uniform and dominated by the vein structure, leading to further depression with respect to loss of area. But, by contrast, thoracic effective inertia is negligible across a wide array of Dipterans and does not contribute to damage-related scaling. Together these results indicate that much of the dipteran flight motor’s responses to wing damage can emerge passively from interactions between the wing, thorax, and muscles; and suggest that a hybrid-elastic architecture with a compliant wing root may be widespread across Diptera. More broadly, we identify wing damage as a tool that can quantitatively discriminate between different candidate models of the insect flight motor, and suggest that altered motor operating conditions can identify mechanical properties difficult to infer from intact flight alone.

title: A partitioned state-exchange physics-informed neural network for bidirectionally coupled particle–fluid systems
authors: Nai-Jie Ye, Jing-Kuan Huang, Yuxuan Jin, Li-Jie Yin, Ke-Zhen Qian, De-Zhen Chen
abstract: Unresolved particle–fluid systems require coupled prediction of fluid motion, particle dynamics, and interphase momentum exchange. We develop bidirectionally coupled physics-informed neural networks (Bi-PINNs) based on partitioned state exchange. F-PINN reconstructs velocity and pressure fields governed by the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations with particle feedback, whereas P-PINN predicts particle velocity and recovers trajectories through differentiable time integration. The subnetworks form a closed loop by exchanging the local background-velocity proxy, particle state, and interphase force. Multiscale temporal Fourier encoding and refined collocation sampling in particle near-field and near-wall regions improve the representation of transient and localized disturbances. Faxén parallel-wall drag correction, annular background-velocity sampling, and discretely normalized Gaussian momentum feedback define the force closure for confined low-Reynolds-number transport. Architecture and sampling analyses show that lower physics losses do not necessarily imply greater predictive accuracy and that balanced regional sampling improves multivariable reconstruction. Verification against computational fluid dynamics solutions based on the same governing equations and closure model shows close agreement for the bulk flow, particle-induced disturbance, particle Reynolds number, and trajectory over 0–1 s. Across six independently trained cases, with the inlet centerline-to-initial-particle velocity ratio α ranging from 0.85 to 1.15, the mean terminal-trajectory relative error is 1.34%, with a maximum of 2.79%. The case-wise L2 relative errors in streamwise velocity and pressure range from 3.52 × 10−4 to 4.64 × 10−2 and from 3.42 × 10−3 to 1.18 × 10−2, respectively. These results demonstrate that the Bi-PINNs framework accurately reconstructs coupled particle–fluid dynamics without labeled data during optimization.

title: Reduced-Order Modeling for Efficient Simulation of Enhanced Geothermal Systems
authors: Ming Gao, Wen-Yue Sun, Yu-Yang Jia
abstract: Simulation of enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) requires reliable models of coupled fluid flow and heat transport in stimulated fracture networks, but repeated full-order model (FOM) simulations are computationally expensive. This study develops a reduced-order modeling framework based on proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and trajectory piecewise linearization (TPWL) for fluid flow and heat transfer simulation in EGS. Separate POD bases are constructed from pressure and temperature snapshots to define a low-dimensional representation of the reservoir state. The reduced-order model (ROM) provides substantial simulation speedup by locally linearizing the nonlinear governing equations at training states and projecting the resulting high-dimensional linear systems onto the low-dimensional representation, avoiding repeated full nonlinear solves during online prediction. A three-dimensional EGS model was developed using the embedded discrete fracture model (EDFM) to evaluate the proposed ROM under variable well controls. A primary training simulation with constant well controls was first conducted to generate the initial snapshots and derivative matrices. 81 combinations of pressure and temperature POD energy-loss thresholds were first evaluated using the snapshots from the primary training simulation. A second training simulation with variable well controls was then conducted, and the resulting pressure and temperature snapshots were added to the training dataset to improve the ROM's predictive capability. Both Galerkin and least-squares Petrov-Galerkin projections provided accurate predictions, while the Galerkin ROM produced lower overall errors and was therefore selected as the final model. The ROM was evaluated over 30 years under quarterly well-control perturbations of 0%, 5%, 10%, 15%, and 20%. Although the prediction errors increased with the perturbation amplitude, they remained low throughout the tested range. For the 20% case, the pressure-field, temperature-field, and producer-temperature root-mean-square errors were 2.0 × 10−5 MPa, 0.04 °C, and 0.09 °C, respectively. The ROM required 0.1 s online, compared with approximately 520 s for the FOM, giving a speedup of approximately 5000×.

title: Hydrographic response to winter shamal winds in the Northwestern Arabian Gulf
authors: T. Alrushaid, F. Al Senafi, A. Anis
abstract:
This study investigates the effect of air–sea heat fluxes associated with cold, dry Shamal wind events on the physical dynamics and vertical mixing of the shallow, semi-enclosed northwestern Arabian Gulf.
 In situ
 observations were combined with one-dimensional numerical simulations that used two two-equation turbulence closures, the
 k
 –
 ϵ
 and
 k
 –
 kl
 formulations. Field measurements were collected from mid-January to mid-April 2013 at two coastal stations near Qarooh Island, Kuwait, during the initial phase of an extended monitoring program. Continuous records of water temperature, dissolved oxygen, light penetration, and current profiles were obtained, together with meteorological observations used to force the models. Reynolds stresses, vertical eddy diffusivity, turbulent kinetic energy (TKE), and its dissipation rate were estimated from a pulse-coherent Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler (ADCP) and used to evaluate the simulations. Two winter Shamal events, with winds of up to 15 m s
 -1
 , increased surface heat loss through latent heat and drove convective mixing that reached the seabed. Turbulence in the bottom boundary layer was controlled by two processes. Shear instability generated by the semidiurnal tidal currents dominated under low wind conditions, whereas convective overturning during the Shamal peaks homogenized the water column vertically, which reduced the tidal shear and weakened the shear-driven mixing. Model–observation comparisons were evaluated using the mean bias error, root mean square error, Pearson correlation coefficient, and Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency. Under observationally constrained temperature and velocity conditions, both closures represented the general temporal variability of the turbulence quantities, with correlation coefficients ranging from 0.63 to 0.86. Agreement was strongest for the broader tidal modulation, whereas some short-duration turbulence peaks were substantially underestimated. During SE1, for example, the peak dissipation rate and Reynolds stress were underestimated by factors of approximately five and three, respectively, and the TKE Nash–Sutcliffe efficiencies were only 0.37 and 0.08. Because the temperature and velocity fields were relaxed toward observations, these comparisons evaluate the behavior of the closures under measured hydrographic and current conditions rather than provide fully independent model validation.

title: Development and validation of predictive models for the hemodialysis adequacy index (Kt/V) using multiple linear regression and machine learning algorithms
authors: Le-Le Li, Rui-Feng Xu, Liang-Liang Huang, Bing-Rui Lu, Shu-Ting Zhang, Ya Tuo, Hui-Qing Liu, Rui Ren, Shu-Fang Wang, Ming-Xia Sun, Xiao-Tong Zhang, Jian-Rong Zhao, Lei Yu, Yan Meng
abstract:
Kt/V is a widely used indicator for assessing hemodialysis (HD) adequacy, but conventional measurement methods require blood sampling and are impractical for large-scale or real-time use. This study aimed to develop and validate predictive models for Kt/V using multiple linear regression (MLR) and machine learning algorithms, enabling clinicians to estimate dialysis adequacy before a session begins using simple, non-invasive parameters.
 
 
 
 
 A total of 1,017 eligible patients were enrolled from seven HD centers in Hohhot City, China, and divided into training (
 n
  = 677), internal (
 n
  = 220), and external validation (
 n
  = 120) sets. From 26 candidate variables, eight clinically meaningful derived features were constructed, and a multi-algorithm fusion strategy integrating
 F
 test, Mutual Information, Random Forest importance, XGBoost importance, LASSO coefficients, Permutation Importance, Recursive Feature Elimination, and Boruta was employed for feature selection. Five final features (body surface area, pre-dialysis weight, standardized blood flow, sex, and circulating blood volume) were selected. Eight point-prediction models (MLR, XGBoost, LightGBM, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, KNN, SVM, and BPNN), a simple average ensemble of the three top-performing models, and two probabilistic prediction methods (LightGBM Quantile Regression and NGBoost) were developed. Hyperparameter tuning was performed using GridSearchCV with 5-fold cross-validation. Model performance was evaluated using R
 2
 , RMSE, and MAE on internal and external validation sets.
 
 
 
 
 
 On external validation, the SVM model achieved the highest R
 2
 (0.5931) and lowest RMSE (0.1633) and MAE (0.1214) among individual models, followed by Gradient Boosting (R
 2
  = 0.5748, RMSE = 0.1670, MAE = 0.1276) and XGBoost (R
 2
  = 0.5681, RMSE = 0.1683, MAE = 0.1288). The ensemble model achieved the best overall performance (R
 2
  = 0.5911, RMSE = 0.1637, MAE = 0.1240). Calibration assessment revealed all models were well-calibrated without requiring post-hoc adjustment. For probabilistic prediction, NGBoost provided well-calibrated 80% prediction intervals (PICP = 82.27%) with narrower intervals than LightGBM Quantile Regression. SHAP analysis identified BSA, standardized blood flow, and gender as the most influential predictors.
 
 
 
 
 Machine learning models, particularly SVM, the ensemble model, and NGBoost, can provide accurate, interpretable, and uncertainty-aware predictions of Kt/V using non-invasive, readily available parameters. The development of a local standalone executable application further facilitates clinical translation, enabling pre-dialysis prediction and real-time prescription adjustment. Prospective validation in diverse populations is warranted to confirm generalizability.
