title: Development of a Visual Digital Twin Dashboard for Two-Phase and Three-Phase Flow Regime Classification in Industrial Systems
authors: M. Hamilton, Issah N. Suleiman, Sormeh Serpoosh, Nadine Elkholy, A. Sleiti, H. Ferroudji, M. A. Rahmann
abstract:
Accurate classification of multiphase flow regimes is critical for efficient operation in energy and process industries. While significant progress has been made in two-phase flow classification, extending these techniques to three-phase systems introduces additional complexity due to interactions among phases and variations in flow geometry.
 In this study, we develop a visual digital-twin-based dashboard for real-time classification and visualization of flow regimes in both two-phase and three-phase flows. Experimental data were generated using the multiphase-flow facility at Hamad Bin Khalifa University, whose principal horizontal test section is approximately 6 m long with a 50.8-mm (2-in.) internal diameter and transparent acrylic sections for video observation. The two-phase water-air dataset contains 65 no-leak experiments spanning liquid superficial velocity from 1.0711 to 3.2134 m/s and gas superficial velocity from 0.6252 to 3.4041 m/s. The three-phase oil-water-air dataset contains 36 experiments spanning water superficial velocity from 1.4059 to 3.1427 m/s and air superficial velocity from 0.063 to 0.320 m/s, including 12 no-leak, 12 single-leak, and 12 dual-leak experiments.
 Flow dynamics were characterized using high-response dynamic pressure sensors to capture time-series pressure signals representative of multiphase flow behavior. In addition, high-speed imaging (up to 2000 frames per second) was employed to capture the visual characteristics of the flow regimes. Supporting measurements included thermocouples, differential pressure sensors, and electrical process tomography to enhance flow characterization.
 Visual inspection of the three-phase records reveals bubbly and dispersed structures that are more heterogeneous than those in the two-phase water-air reference data, motivating an analysis workflow that preserves the relationship among sensor signals, video, and operating conditions. These synchronized experimental records are organized as digital threads and streamed to the cloud-hosted digital twin software-as-a-service (SaaS) system. As pressure data arrive, deployed leak-detection models analyze the signals, and the visual twin dashboard presents the associated time series, pipeline video, operating state, and mapped detection or localization outputs for operator review. The MGSB two-phase model achieved a mean held-out detection F1 score of 0.930 +/- 0.082 and an F1 score of 0.783 +/- 0.110 under the prescribed input-corruption test. The MGSB three-phase model achieved an F1 score of 0.984, ROC AUC of 0.9987, false-alarm rate of 0.09%, and mean detection delay of 0.03 +/- 0.01 s on an eleven-experiment dual-orifice evaluation matrix.
 The novelty of this work lies in integrating experimental multiphase flow measurements with AI-based classification and a visual digital twin interface capable of identifying both two-phase and three-phase flow regimes across multiple geometries in real time.
 This framework provides a practical decision-support tool for industry applications, including pipeline monitoring, flow assurance, separator performance evaluation, and multiphase transport optimization in oil, gas, and broader process industries. By enabling rapid and reliable flow regime identification using minimal sensor inputs, the proposed system has the potential to significantly improve operational efficiency, reduce uncertainty in multiphase transport, and support next-generation digital oilfield applications.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Physics-Based and Machine-Learning Models for CO2–Brine Relative Permeability Prediction
authors: Musa E. M. Ahmed, B. Dindoruk, M. Martin, S. Drylie
abstract:
Relative permeability (kr) is one of the governing parameters of multiphase flow in porous media and directly influences predictions of CO2 plume migration, trapping efficiency, and injectivity in Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) projects. However, measuring CO2–brine relative permeability under reservoir conditions is experimentally challenging and time-intensive. Consequently, several predictive approaches have been proposed. This study evaluates the accuracy of empirical, capillary-pressure-based, and machine-learning models by benchmarking them against experimentally measured CO2–brine relative permeability data obtained under representative reservoir conditions.
 Primary-drainage CO2–brine relative permeability was measured using unsteady-state coreflooding on a Nugget Sandstone core at 150°F and 1,500 psi. Relative permeability values were normalized using permeability to water at full water saturation (kw at Sw = 1 ~ absolute permeability, k). The experimental dataset captures primary-drainage behavior over gas saturations from 0 to approximately 0.66. Mercury Injection Capillary Pressure (MICP) measurements on the same core were used to characterize pore-throat-size distribution. Because MICP is performed in a mercury–air system, the capillary-pressure curve was converted to equivalent CO2–brine conditions using experimentally measured CO2–brine interfacial tension at the same pressure and temperature. The contact angle was estimated using Neumann's equation of state, allowing the MICP data to be scaled to the CO2–brine system before applying capillary-pressure-based models. Seven prediction methods were evaluated individually: Corey and Lomeland, Ebeltoft, and Thomas (LET) correlations, Brooks–Corey and Van Genuchten capillary-pressure models, Purcell and Burdine models derived from capillary-pressure data, and a machine-learning model based on gradient boosting trained on published CO2–brine datasets. Curves from all seven methods were evaluated at 13 experimental saturation points; principal error statistics use the 11 points with both phases measured, with the two terminal-stage points assessed separately as endpoint evidence. Hybrid formulations using different models for the gas and water phases were also tested. In total, 49 combinations (seven gas-phase × seven water-phase models) were evaluated using performance metrics: root mean square error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and coefficient of determination (R2).
 Results show clear differences in predictive performance, and separate calibrated fits from independent predictions: Corey and LET were fit by least squares to 11 of the 13 measured points and evaluated on that same set. Brooks–Corey/Burdine, Van Genuchten/Burdine, Purcell, direct Burdine, and the machine-learning model were not calibrated to this core's measured krg/krw data. Among the independent predictions, Brooks–Corey/Burdine gave the most accurate water-phase result (RMSE = 0.0087, R2 = 0.999), but all four capillary-pressure-derived methods systematically overpredicted gas relative permeability. Corey and LET fit the calibration data closely (LET: krg R2 = 0.995, krw R2 > 0.999), but comparison with the two terminal krg responses—excluded from response fitting—shows that LET fails to extrapolate beyond its calibration range, while Corey extrapolates only partially. The machine-learning model reproduced the water-phase curve reasonably well (R2 = 0.97) but overpredicted gas mobility at intermediate saturations. Purcell showed the largest deviations of any model, reflecting its sensitivity to entry pressure and the absence of a tortuosity correction. Among all 49 gas/water pairings, LET applied to both phases gave the lowest combined error, though this reflects its calibration advantage rather than independent hybrid performance; the best true two-model hybrid was LET (gas) with Corey (water), and the best pairing among only the independently predicted methods was Brooks–Corey/Burdine applied to both phases.
 This study provides a systematic comparison of empirical, capillary-pressure-derived, machine-learning, and phase-paired CO2–brine relative-permeability methods that explicitly distinguishes calibrated fits from independent predictions and evaluates terminal krg responses separately from response fitting. As expected, the calibrated correlations achieved lower in-sample error than the independent predictions; however, this does not establish superior predictive accuracy. The terminal-response comparison further shows that close calibration does not guarantee reliable extrapolation beyond the fitted range. These findings provide practical guidance for selecting and validating relative-permeability models for CO2 storage and CCUS reservoir simulations.

title: Gas Lift Evaluation and Production Forecasting Through a Transfer Learning Dual-Track Machine Learning Framework
authors: A. A. Al Raisi, H. Karami, D. Devegowda
abstract:
As reservoirs deplete and natural flow declines, artificial lift becomes necessary to sustain production, and gas lift is one of the most applied methods in unconventional horizontal wells. Injecting high-pressure gas lowers the density of the flowing column and increases drawdown, but the production response is not proportional to the gas injected. It is governed by nonlinear interactions among injection rate, wellbore pressures, geometry, and fluid properties. Beyond an optimum, additional gas reduces production. Machine learning captures such relationships well and predicts oil rate with high accuracy, yet that accuracy is almost always measured within the same wells a model was trained on. A companion study of 11 Eagle Ford wells (Al Raisi et al., 2026) reported R2 as high as 0.960 under a random split but strongly negative values under leave-one-well-out (LOWO) evaluation, because field measurements cluster in a narrow band of conditions and much of the gas lift domain is never observed.
 This study's framework combines two tracks. Track A applies data-driven models to daily field data from the 11 wells. Track B uses a steady-state multiphase flow simulator to build a physics-consistent synthetic dataset in two complementary designs: a broad dataset of 6,000 nodal-analysis cases sampled by Latin Hypercube Sampling, establishing which operating conditions exist and where gas lift helps, and a controlled sweep of 700 scenarios evaluated at 11 injection rates each, resolving how production responds to injection. Together these required 13,700 simulation cases. A deep learning neural network is then trained through a staged transfer learning procedure that pre-trains on the broad dataset, refines on the sweep dataset, and fine-tunes on field data.
 The simulations reproduce established gas lift behavior, which is what makes them usable as a training signal. Feasibility rises from 90% to 99% with gas lift, 285 of 295 otherwise non-productive cases are enabled, and the resulting performance curves fall into monotonic, plateau, and post-peak decline classes separated by tubing size, wellhead pressure, and fluid properties. Under LOWO evaluation, staged transfer learning raises the average R2 from 0.149 to 0.414, reduces MAE from 70 to 56 STB/D, and lowers MAPE from 56% to 38%. Neither dataset suffices alone: broad-only pre-training yields 0.146 and sweep-only 0.322, so breadth and structure are both required and the order matters. The gains concentrate on wells the baseline fails, most notably Well 4, which moves from a strongly negative to a positive R2.
 Applied to a well-level injection scenario, the model ranks lift responsiveness across operating states in the physically expected order, supporting open-loop screening and gas allocation. The study also reports a useful negative result: despite 135 post-peak-decline scenarios in training, predicted curves rise monotonically and do not reproduce over-injection. Expanded coverage and explicit physical constraints are therefore complementary rather than interchangeable.

title: Melting Heat Transfer in Ferromagnetic Carreau Fluid Flow Under a Magnetic Dipole: Critical Eckert Number and Entropy Generation
authors: M. S. Alqarni
abstract: This study investigates melting heat transfer in the unsteady two-dimensional boundary-layer flow of a ferromagnetic Carreau fluid over a linearly stretching sheet under the influence of a magnetic dipole, with emphasis on thermodynamic consistency and interfacial stability. The thermal model incorporates a Stefan condition, the full magnetocaloric work term, and the exact Carreau differential viscosity. A relaxing stretching law is employed to obtain a well-posed far-field formulation, while entropy-generation and Bejan numbers quantify local irreversibility. The resulting nonlinear system is solved using adaptive collocation with an asymptotic far-field condition that removes the algebraic truncation error of the temperature tail. It is also independently validated through a mesh-free physics-informed extreme learning machine, which is in agreement with up to nine significant figures on a common truncated domain and with the recovery of the classical Crane and Grubka–Bobba limits. The similarity reduction is further tested against a marching solution of the parent equations in exact non-similar variables. For a static dipole with negligible induced currents, Joule heating vanishes, and the magnetic field influences irreversibility indirectly through changes in velocity and temperature gradients. A multi-start search reveals a second solution branch with near-wall flow reversal; a spectral solution of the linear temporal-stability problem shows that this branch is unstable, while the first branch is stable over all parameter ranges examined. A critical Eckert number is identified, above which magnetocaloric cooling reverses the interfacial temperature gradient and prevents sustained melting, thereby defining the physically admissible regime for a sustained melting interface. The locally similar model predicts this threshold at Ec = 0.352 in the reference state, whereas the parent-equation solution places it at 0.498, so the critical value is reported as a prediction of the locally similar model with an explicitly quantified non-similar correction. For a self-consistent phase-change ferrofluid (Mn–Zn ferrite in n-octadecane), the threshold corresponds to draw speeds of about 2 m s−1 per kelvin of Curie-point margin.

title: Impact of CO2 Storage Time on CO2-Brine Relative Permeability in Berea Sandstone
authors: Musa E. M. Ahmed, B. Dindoruk
abstract:
Prolonged exposure of reservoir sandstone to injected CO2 may alter rock–fluid interactions and potentially affect multiphase flow behavior. While geochemical effects of CO2 storage have been widely studied, the time-dependent impact on CO2–brine relative permeability remains insufficiently quantified. This study evaluates whether extended CO2–brine–rock interaction modifies relative-permeability behavior in quartz-rich Berea sandstone under representative reservoir conditions.
 Core samples were aged in CO2-saturated brine for one and three months at 1500 psi and 150 °F, alongside a brine-only control to isolate CO2-specific effects. Pre- and post-aging characterization included mineralogical analysis using X-ray diffraction (XRD), pore-structure evaluation via mercury intrusion capillary pressure (MICP) and NMR, and routine core analysis for porosity and permeability. Wettability behavior was evaluated by estimating contact angle from CO2–brine interfacial tension (IFT) measurements using Neumann's equation of state, while brine chemistry was quantified using inductively coupled plasma–optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) and titration techniques. Relative-permeability behavior was estimated by deriving Brooks–Corey parameters from capillary-pressure data in combination with machine-learning predictions trained on published CO2–brine datasets. Together, the two approaches provide complementary indirect estimates for assessing aging sensitivity.
 Results indicate minimal geochemical and petrophysical alteration following CO2 exposure within the time frame considered. Minor mineralogical changes were detected, including the disappearance of trace siderite cement and slight reduction in chlorite clay content; however, overall mineral composition remained within experimental uncertainty, suggesting geochemical stability of the quartz-rich matrix. For the CO2-exposed samples, porosity increased by only 0.17–0.59 percentage points, while permeability declined modestly (~6–12%), with no evidence of severe pore clogging or structural compaction. Brine chemistry analysis confirmed limited dissolution consistent with the low abundance of reactive mineral phases.
 Critically, the pre- and post-aging CO2–brine relative-permeability estimates remained closely overlapped. Brooks–Corey/Burdine parameterization and machine-learning predictions showed no resolved systematic shift beyond the resolution and uncertainty of the two indirect methods. These findings support use of a time-invariant relative-permeability description as a practical first-order assumption during early-stage CO2 injection in comparable quartz-rich sandstone systems, when advective multiphase flow is active, while longer-term reactive-transport effects should be evaluated separately.
 This work provides an integrated experimental assessment of time-dependent CO2 exposure on relative permeability, combining mineralogical, petrophysical, capillary-pressure, wettability, and fluid-chemistry analyses within a unified framework. The study provides an experimentally constrained assessment of a modeling assumption frequently used in CO2-storage simulation and quantitative evidence that no systematic aging-related relative-permeability change was resolved in quartz-dominated Berea sandstone over the tested 1–3 month period.

title: Application of Composite Materials in the Lightweight Design of Wind Turbine Blades
authors: Haowen Wang
abstract: In the process of global transition towards sustainable energy infrastructures, continuous optimization of mechanical design parameters of wind energy harvesting is required. The blades of wind turbines are aerodynamic parts that are related to efficiency, structural stability and mass of the material. This is a narrative review to examine the development of composite materials in lightweight blade architectures. Standard Glass Fiber Reinforced Polymers (GFRP), advanced Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymers (CFRP) and emerging Carbon Glass Hybrid configurations are evaluated by engineers. Structural optimization is done based on multi objective criteria. The objectives of this study are fatigue resistance, tensile strength and weight reduction. This paper summarizes the present research needs in weight reduction strategies, including material evolution, advanced manufacturing paradigms like Vacuum Assisted Resin Transfer Molding (VARTM) and end of life recycling challenges. The review identifies emerging wind energy trends including full digital simulation, and the shift to recyclable thermoplastic resins as part of a circular economy.

title: Temperature-Field Reconstruction and Heat-Source Inversion Estimation Method for High-Voltage Switchgear Based Reduced-Order PINN Surrogate Model
authors: Sheng-Xue Tang, Xiang-Chao Zheng, Er-Peng Wang, Song-Yang Han, Yi-Ze Cheng
abstract: Localized overheating induced by poor electrical contact, loosened busbar connections, and insulation degradation is a major precursor to failures in high-voltage switchgear. To address the difficulty in directly measuring internal heat sources, a fast three-dimensional temperature-field reconstruction, candidate heat-source identification, and heat-source power inversion method for high-voltage switchgear is proposed based on a reduced-order surrogate model integrating Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) and physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). First, a coupled three-dimensional thermal–flow coupled computational fluid dynamics(CFD) model is established to generate temperature fields under different heat-source conditions. POD is then applied to extract the dominant thermal modes and their corresponding low-dimensional modal coefficients from the high-dimensional temperature fields. A PINN-based reduced-order surrogate model is subsequently trained to establish the nonlinear mapping from heat-source parameters to POD modal coefficients, while residuals of the steady-state heat conduction equation and boundary-condition constraints are incorporated into the loss function to enforce physical consistency and enhance prediction accuracy. Based on external temperature measurements, an Improved Grey Wolf Optimizer (I-GWO) is further adopted to identify the active fault heat source from a predefined set of candidate locations and inversely estimate its corresponding heat-source power. Numerical simulations and temperature-rise experiments show that the proposed method accurately reconstructs the three-dimensional temperature distribution and identifies local high-temperature regions. In the temperature-rise experiment, the relative error of heat-source power inversion is only 2.27%, demonstrating that the proposed framework enables rapid and accurate temperature-field reconstruction and heat-source inversion.

title: Machine-learning surrogates enable rapid prediction of 3-D substrate gradients in industrial bioreactors
authors: Víctor Puig-I-Laborda, Jorge Carrasco Muriel, Andrea Castañeda Tena, Teddy Groves, Johan le Nepvou de Carfort, Ulrich Krühne, Krist V. Gernaey, Cees Haringa, Ignasi Puig‐de‐Dou, Lars Keld Nielsen
abstract: Abstract High-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) provide detailed substrate gradient predictions in industrial stirred-tank bioreactors but are computationally intensive, limiting their routine application. We developed surrogate models trained on $$760$$ 760 CFD simulations to rapidly predict fully 3-D substrate concentration fields from global operating conditions (e.g., stirring speed, feeding strategy, feeding point location, fluid density and viscosity, liquid height, bio-kinetic parameters, biomass concentration), and local spatial descriptors (e.g., distance to the feeding point). Among various methods, attention-based neural networks achieved the highest accuracy (test $${{{\rm{R}}}}^{2}\approx 0.91$$ R 2 ≈ 0.91 ), capturing essential mixing features and enabling millisecond-scale inference—up to a million-fold speed-up compared to CFD. These surrogates facilitate rapid exploration of operating spaces, supporting real-time optimization and digital-twin frameworks in bioprocessing. Our results demonstrate that data-driven models can effectively couple hydrodynamics and biokinetics to provide fast, accurate spatial predictions, advancing capabilities for industrial bioreactor design and control.

title: Intelligence-enabled smart inhalable biomaterials for chronic inflammatory airway diseases: integrating responsive carrier engineering, lung-on-chip validation, and patient-specific pulmonary modeling
authors: Qi Fan, Zhongxu Li, Yongliang Sun, Yu Liu, Hangyu Chen
abstract: Chronic inflammatory airway diseases, particularly asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), are commonly treated by inhalation, yet the nominal dose placed in an inhaler often differs substantially from the dose that reaches diseased airway regions, crosses mucus, enters target cells, and remains pharmacologically active. Airway narrowing, heterogeneous ventilation, mucus plugging, impaired mucociliary clearance, oxidative and proteolytic stress, epithelial barrier dysfunction, inflammatory-cell diversity, device characteristics, and patient-specific inhalation maneuvers jointly shape therapeutic exposure. Smart inhalable biomaterials can be designed to address some of these barriers by controlling transport, retention, activation, or release, but many systems are still optimized primarily at the nanoparticle level and evaluated in static models that do not capture realistic aerosol performance or patient-specific deposition. This review develops an intelligence-enabled bioengineering framework linking disease-informed material design with machine-learning-assisted formulation optimization, formulation–device–patient coupling, lung-on-chip validation, and patient-specific pulmonary modeling. Within this framework, airway features such as mucus architecture, redox gradients, protease activity, epithelial permeability, immune-cell state, extracellular-matrix remodeling, and regional airflow are considered measurable variables that can inform material design and evaluation. The material platforms considered include mucus-penetrating and mucoadhesive carriers, responsive materials, transformable nano-in-micro systems, polymeric and lipid nanoparticles, biomimetic carriers, extracellular vesicles, and systems for pulmonary delivery of nucleic acids and biologics. Their development is considered alongside structured experimental design, machine learning, active learning, mechanistic aerosol modeling, physics-informed surrogates, multi-objective optimization, and uncertainty analysis. Lung-on-chip systems provide human-relevant settings in which deposited dose, mucus transport, barrier function, immune responses, and repeated-exposure effects can be examined under air–liquid-interface and breathing-like conditions. Patient-specific computational fluid dynamics and reduced-order models can complement these platforms by predicting regional deposition, whereas the term digital twin should be reserved for longitudinally updated, uncertainty-aware models linked to actionable decisions. Together, these approaches support a closed-loop design–delivery–validation strategy in which material performance, aerosol behavior, biological response, and patient-specific deposition are evaluated as connected rather than separate development problems.

title: CO 2 Capture in MOFs: Connecting Experiments, Multiscale Simulations, and Data‐Driven Approaches
authors: Prakash Govindaraj, Mullapudi V. Jyothirmai, Kathirvel Venugopal, Anand Rajkamal, Hern Kim
abstract: ABSTRACT Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have emerged as promising porous materials for CO 2 capture due to their tunable pore structures and chemically versatile adsorption sites. However, achieving efficient capture at low CO 2 concentrations while balancing adsorption strength, regeneration, and structural stability remains challenging. Existing reviews often treat experimental and computational investigations separately, limiting the development of unified design principles. This review integrates experimental insights with multiscale computational approaches, including density functional theory (DFT), grand canonical Monte Carlo, molecular dynamics, and computational fluid dynamics (CFD). DFT calculations provide molecular‐level understanding of adsorption behavior, highlighting the role of electronic structure at open metal sites and functionalized pores. Classical simulations predict adsorption capacity, selectivity, and diffusion, while CFD extends these insights to macroscopic transport and process‐level performance, enabling direct comparison with experiments. In addition, emerging data‐driven approaches are discussed to uncover structure–property relationships and accelerate performance prediction across large materials spaces. The integration of these methods establishes a closed‐loop framework linking theory, simulation, and experiment, guiding the rational design of efficient and stable porous materials for practical CO 2 capture applications.

title: Tokamak Pedestal Region Profile Prediction in Transport-Limited Regimes
authors: Steven Molesworth
abstract: Accurately predicting temperature and density profiles in the near-edge region—roughly the outer 10% of closed flux surfaces—is critical for modeling tokamak performance because fusion power scales with the square of pedestal-top pressure. Building upon an existing framework for accelerated core transport solutions, this dissertation presents a workflow for self-consistently solving transport-limited pedestals using 1D, steady-state flux matching. Inverse scale lengths are represented using an asymmetric hyperbolic tangent parameterization, anchored at the separatrix. Modular near-edge physics including neutral and impurity penetration are added to account for their effects on source terms in the flux matching solution. Diamagnetic and neoclassical terms in the rotation profile are self-consistently updated, while the toroidal velocity is held constant at this stage. Neoclassical and turbulent transport models developed for core plasmas were chosen to determine their range of validity. Five discharges spanning L-mode, H-mode at contrasting collisionalities, negative triangularity, and I-mode are used to test the workflow. Only the NT result falls within the desired sub-10% error in pedestal-top pressure for reactor predictions, while the remaining cases miss the experimental pedestal-top pressure by 17–84%. That error is attributed to three factors: uncertainties in the separatrix boundary conditions, degeneracy between solver objective and pedestal values, and transport model limitations most severe in the region that most strongly determines pedestal shape. Together, these errors do not exclude flux matching as a solution to the transport-limited pedestal prediction problem, but do suggest limitations of the approach, particularly until an accurate near-edge turbulence model can be made tractable within an iterative framework. This work is thus a step toward a unified, self-consistent treatment of core-edge coupling suitable for integrated tokamak modeling.

title: Probabilistic Simulation of Gas-Liquid Interfaces with Coupled Flow Matching on Spherical Harmonics
authors: Kiet Bennema ten Brinke, Rachna Ramesh, Douwe Orij, Ivo Roghair, Vlado Menkovski
abstract: Bubbly flows involve strongly coupled bubble motion, deformation, and hydrodynamic interactions, making high-fidelity simulation computationally expensive. We propose a neural surrogate that jointly predicts bubble trajectories and interface deformation in a compact, shared representation, replacing costly mesh-resolved simulation with fast generative inference. Because two-phase flow dynamics is nonlinear and chaotic, we treat forecasting as a conditional generative problem rather than deterministic regression, predicting entire future windows in a single pass. We train and evaluate the surrogate on BubbleSH, a Front-Tracking dataset of rising deformable bubble swarms, assessing performance using trajectory, shape, and distributional metrics over kinematic, morphological, and interaction-based properties. The surrogate reproduces key flow statistics while running several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying DNS solver.

title: Comparative Study of Canvas- and Coordinate-Based Geometry-Conditioned Neural Networks for Real-Time Prediction of Indoor Environments with Varying Room Dimensions
authors: Shaofan Wang, Philipp Geyer
abstract: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) is computationally expensive for iterative building design. Deep learning surrogates offer faster predictions, but generalization across varying room dimensions remains challenging. This study compares two geometry-conditioned neural network surrogate models for rapid indoor airflow and temperature field prediction under varying room sizes. During the architectural design stage, this method is relevant for real-time assessment of whether conditioned supply air will effectively provide fresh and cool air throughout rooms with varying heights and lengths. The canvas-based neural network (CaNN) explicitly encodes room size by preserving different occupied regions within a fixed canvas, whereas the coordinate-based neural network (CoNN) uses normalized coordinate channels. Both employ U-Net autoencoders to separately predict airflow and temperature fields. Evaluation uses simplified rooms with varying heights and lengths as a controlled benchmark. The results show that CaNN achieves higher agreement with CFD results than CoNN, demonstrating its potential to support performance-driven building design.

title: SPLICE: Sparse Physics Library Identification and Compositional Expansion
authors: Lucas Thil, Jesse Read, Guillaume Doquet, Rim Kaddah
abstract: Neural operator splitting composes a library of neural operators, one per physical mechanism, into zero-shot simulators of new equations. Existing approaches, however, require these mechanisms and their labels to be specified in advance. We ask whether a pretrained library can instead be adapted and grown from unlabeled trajectories in which multiple mechanisms act simultaneously. We introduce SPLICE, a framework that discovers operators without mechanism labels on mixture data. The contributions of the candidate operators to each trajectory are inferred by solving a convex optimization problem. A calibrated test then assigns each discovered operator the mechanism it implements. Failure cases are also detectable, when the library lacks the required physics or when mechanisms are insufficiently separable. Across one and two dimensional systems, the discovered operators recover mechanisms from unlabeled mixtures and compose into zero-shot simulators of unseen equations; a frozen library can also grow an operator for physics absent from pretraining, without labels and without forgetting. On Navier-Stokes, the discovered operators compose about as accurately as their supervised counterparts.

title: Structure-preserving fidelity diagnostics for partial differential equations
authors: Kyriakos Flouris
abstract: Machine learning surrogates of partial differential equations (PDEs) are commonly trained on data generated by numerical solvers. Therefore, the training data obey not the PDE but the modified equation of the numerical scheme, and the test loss, computed on data from the same solver, cannot distinguish a model that learned the physics from one that learned the discretization error. Here, we show that the difference is nevertheless visible in the trained model. We propose a suite of structure-preserving fidelity diagnostics, simple scores that measure whether a learned model respects one known property of the physics, such as a conserved quantity, a symmetry or a Hamiltonian structure, without access to the training data or the governing equation. Over five systems, the diagnostics track the error with respect to the true dynamics with a rank correlation of up to $0.94$, while the test loss is uncorrelated or anti-correlated with it. For the Burgers, Korteweg-de Vries and Navier-Stokes equations, the diagnostics separate numerical schemes that the test loss ranks as equivalent, including schemes of the same order. order.

title: Learning Incompressible 3D Flows from Sparse Samples: A Set Transformer Approach to Divergence-Free Kernel Fitting
authors: Ramzi Idoughi, Radouan Boukharfane, Peter Wonka
abstract: Recovering divergence-free velocity fields from sparse and corrupted observations requires reconciling physical consistency, expressive representations, and robustness to missing data. We introduce DFK-Former, a set-to-field transformer that reconstructs divergence-free velocity fields from sparse, noisy, and irregularly sampled 3D observations. The model is inherently invariant to the number and ordering of input samples and predicts the parameters of a divergence-free kernel representation, producing continuous, mesh-free velocity fields that satisfy incompressibility exactly by construction rather than approximately through soft constraints or projection operators. Unlike existing divergence-free kernel approaches, which estimate kernel coefficients via a separate optimization for each field, DFK-Former predicts these coefficients directly in a single forward pass. This eliminates costly iterative fitting while providing a learned prior that enables accurate reconstruction even when observations are insufficient to uniquely determine the field. To enhance representational power, we introduce adaptive and anisotropic divergence-free kernels that preserve exact incompressibility guarantees while capturing more complex flow structures. Extensive experiments across varying levels of sparsity, noise, and occlusion, including transfer to real Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) turbulence data, demonstrate substantial gains in both accuracy and efficiency. DFK-Former reduces endpoint error by up to 4.6x compared to per-field divergence-free-kernel optimization, while reconstructing each field in 7.5 ms instead of 9.8 s, yielding a speedup of more than three orders of magnitude. These results establish direct, feed-forward prediction of divergence-free kernel parameters as a practical and effective paradigm for physically consistent velocity-field reconstruction from sparse observations.

title: One-Way Coupling via Patchwise Adaptive Normalization in Transformer Surrogates
authors: Emmanuel Gottlob, Hugo Thimonier, Ludovico Buizza, August Martens, Alexandre Gavaudan, Thiago Guzella
abstract: Many physical systems exhibit one-way coupling: exogenous fields such as medium density or obstacle geometry influence the dynamics without being affected by them. We investigate how explicitly representing these fields can improve the accuracy and computational efficiency of transformer-based PDE surrogates. Building on spatially adaptive normalization, we introduce Patchwise Adaptive Normalization (PAdaNorm), which partitions exogenous fields into patches aligned with the state tokenization. We evaluate PAdaNorm on datasets from three different domains, using a Walrus-inspired transformer architecture. Across the three PDE families, PAdaNorm is on par with or up to 16% better than parameter-matched baselines in mean long-horizon variance-scaled RMSE on 60-step autoregressive rollouts. We also find that PAdaNorm better maintains hard physical constraints over long rollouts, such as preventing flow into impenetrable solid regions in porous media. When the conditioning is static, PAdaNorm caches the conditioning embeddings once and reuses them across the entire rollout, reducing inference FLOPs per step by up to 36% compared with parameter-matched baselines. An ablation over eight conditioning variants shows that modulating a single attention axis (temporal or spatial) suffices and that a lightweight shared MLP across blocks remains competitive with per-block projections.

title: Dynamical-state switching controls active microrod navigation in porous media
authors: Ana Cazorla, María L. Jiménez, Raúl A. Rica, Carla Fernandez Rico, Laura Alvarez
abstract: Adaptive search and travel strategies enable biological swimmers to explore complex environments, but remain difficult to encode in minimal synthetic microswimmers. Here, we unveil multiple dynamical and orientational states of rod-like Janus microswimmers actuated via electric fields: planar active, oriented chiral and persistent rods. We discover a hidden dynamical state after pre-orienting them, which allows us to switch on demand from strong chiral to persistent motion. We harness this phenomenological orientation and chirality switch for exploration in microstructured porous arrays. Here, strong chirality promotes local scanning but drives circular trapping and poor net displacement, whereas the pre-aligned dynamical state enables efficient obstacle sorting, and trap escape. Comparing experiments with simulations of active Brownian particles in the very same experimentally-extracted obstacle geometries, we quantify navigation efficiency via first-passage time statistics, revealing how chirality tuning optimizes the trade-off between local exploration and long-range transport.

title: CFD Forge: A Physics-Constrained Agentic Framework for Autonomous CFD
authors: Aakash Shailesh Oza, Ryan F. Johnson, Amir Barati Farimani
abstract: Setting up, running, and assessing a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation requires substantial manual effort, from meshing and solver setup to diagnosis and interpretation, and repeating it across design variants slows engineering iteration. We present CFD Forge, an agentic framework built around OpenFOAM that carries an engineering request through case construction, meshing, solver execution, diagnostics, and reporting. A large language model interprets the request, reads the simulation evidence, identifies likely causes of problems, and proposes actions from a closed set. Automation is only useful if its results can be trusted, so acceptance is not left to the model: deterministic checks, registered for each type of flow, measure explicit criteria and decide. We demonstrate the framework on a converging-diverging nozzle and a two-dimensional forward-facing step, including geometry and operating changes requested in text. A turbulent cube, run outside the agent loop, shows why the checks matter: the solver completed and the mean drag settled, but the lateral-force oscillations were still growing, so a retrospective assessment withheld acceptance. To test this separation, we replayed 36 recorded simulation states, some with deliberately altered diagnostics, through the same model in two setups. Judging from the evidence without the check results, the model accepted 12 of the 13 detectable faults in all three repeats; with CFD Forge's checks deciding, none was accepted. The two setups also differ in prompting, and a fixed rule reached the same verdicts, so the model's value lies in the open-ended work rather than the verdict. Case files, recorded model calls, and decisions are retained for audit. A model that does the work, paired with checks that decide what is accepted, is a step toward automated CFD that can be trusted in high-throughput design and active-learning loops.

title: Learnable wavelet-enhanced localized Transformer for low-SNR wind turbine bearing fault diagnosis
authors: Yan Zhang, Yunfei Zhang, Xiaoqiang Zhao
abstract: Abstract Wind turbine bearing fault diagnosis under low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions remains challenging because vibration signals are often affected by rotational-speed fluctuations, load variations, and non-stationary background interference. These factors may weaken fault-related impulsive components, disturb time–frequency energy distributions, and reduce the discriminability of fault features. To address these issues, this paper proposes a learnable wavelet-enhanced localized Vision Transformer framework, termed LW-ViT. The proposed framework focuses on three core designs: adaptive time–frequency representation, localized token interaction, and noise-aware residual regulation. First, a learnable continuous wavelet transform (LCWT) module is developed to transform one-dimensional vibration signals into adaptive time–frequency representations. In this module, the scale and center frequency of the wavelet kernel are optimized during training, thereby reducing the dependence on manually predefined wavelet parameters. Second, a localized Transformer attention mechanism is introduced to restrict token interactions within neighboring time–frequency regions, which reduces unnecessary long-range noise propagation among time frequency tokens. Third, a noise-gated MLP block is incorporated to regulate the residual feed forward pathway and limit the propagation of noise-sensitive responses in deeper layers. Experiments are conducted on an in-house LUT wind turbine bearing dataset under different SNR levels, rotational speeds, and load conditions. The CWRU dataset is further used as a public benchmark for supplementary validation of the general applicability of the proposed framework. On the LUT dataset, LW-ViT achieves classification accuracies of 93.3% and 98.4% at −6 dB and −4 dB, respectively. Comparative experiments, ablation studies, and feature visualizations indicate that the proposed framework improves adaptive time–frequency representation, localized feature interaction, and fault classification under low-SNR conditions.

title: Machine learning-based analysis of heat and mass transfer in casson hybrid nanofluid flow over a variable porous riga plate
authors: Shajar Abbas, Syeda Farzeen Fatima Gilani, Imran Siddique, Rashid Jan, Mohammad Farooq Hakimi, Aiedh Mrisi Alharthi, Mamurakhon Toshpulatova, Ibrahim Mahariq
abstract: This study uses an artificial neural network (ANN) architecture in combination with the Levenberg-Marquardt backpropagation (LMBP) method to investigate the impact of heat radiation on the hybrid nanofluid flow through a variable porous medium beneath a stretchy Riga plate. The purpose of this work is driven by the increasing demand for accurately modeling complex nonlinear thermal systems involving electromagnetic control, porous media, and nanofluids, which are not sufficiently covered in the existing literature. Single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) and multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) are suspended in propylene glycol, which is regarded as the base fluid. The Riga plate is a plate composed of alternating electrodes as well as permanent magnets to form electromagnetic forces, which act significantly on the flow and the heat transfer properties. The governing nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) are transformed into ordinary differential equations (ODEs) via similarity transformations in order to provide datasets for ANN training. The finite difference technique (FDM) is then used to numerically solve these ODEs. Then the successive over relaxation method, executed through custom MATLAB code, is used to obtain the solutions of these equations. The novelty of the work is in the integrated evaluation of hybrid nanofluid flow over a Riga plate in a variable permeable media with radiative heat transfer, as well as the use of an ANN-LMBP predictive model, which is trained on high-fidelity numerical data. The numerical data show that the thermal radiation increases the temperature distribution by about 21% in the case of SWCNT-based nanofluid and 18% in the case of MWCNT-based nanofluid. The porosity parameter decreases the velocity of fluid by approximately 12%, whereas the modified Hartmann number increases the fluid velocity by 15–17%. Additionally, SWCNTs exhibit 8–10% higher thermal conductivity compared to MWCNTs. The ANN-LMBP model demonstrates excellent predictive performance with a coefficient of determination R 2 > 0.998 and a mean squared error on the order of 10 −4 . These results confirm that the proposed ANN-based framework is a fast, accurate, and computationally efficient tool for modeling nonlinear thermal fluid systems, with significant applications in thermal management, cooling technologies, energy systems, and industrial fluid flow processes. Clinical trial number not applicable.

title: An accurate low-order model of a fin-and-tube heat exchanger for the dynamic simulation of heat pumps
authors: Roberto Sedoni, Paolo  Emilio Santangelo, Diego Angeli
abstract: Dynamic modeling of heat exchangers is essential for the analysis, control, and optimization of vapor compression systems such as heat pumps and air conditioners. These technologies are increasingly relevant in the context of energy transition, where regulatory frameworks and climate goals demand improved energy efficiency and reduced greenhouse gas emissions. Accurate yet computationally efficient models are crucial for system-level simulation, control design, and digital twin development. Traditional low-order approaches, such as lumped parameter and moving boundary models, offer fast computation but often lack the fidelity needed to capture dynamic two-phase phenomena, especially under transient or off-design conditions. Finite volume models offer better accuracy but are often too computationally demanding for real-time applications. This work presents a segment-by-segment heat exchanger model that balances accuracy and efficiency, allowing for detailed prediction of dynamic behavior with limited computational cost. The model was implemented using the Simscape language within the Simulink environment and was validated in both condenser and evaporator configurations. Simulation results show good agreement with a higher-fidelity reference model developed in EVAP-COND 5.0 environment, with a maximum deviation of 2.7% for the sensible heat transfer in condenser mode, while the evaporator mode exhibited deviations of 6.8% for the latent heat transfer and -2.4% for the sensible heat transfer. The proposed approach supports the development of advanced, energy-efficient HVAC systems within increasingly stringent regulatory contexts.

title: Lumped modeling of bubbling fluidized beds for high‐temperature processes
authors: Ravi Ramesh, Elyas M. Moghaddam, Wiebren de Jong, Johan Tiemen Padding
abstract: Abstract Bubbling fluidized beds (BFBs) have been a source of study for multiple decades. Among other applications, they can be used as scalable reactors for the conversion of biomass and waste resources to fuels. Several experimental and computational studies have been devoted to correlating the interplay of hydrodynamics and heat and mass transfer in fluidized beds. Despite the existence of several direct correlations for full‐scale reactors, these are typically only applicable to cylindrical reactor geometries, fluidized through a homogeneous gas distributor plate at the bottom. Detailed Computational Fluid Dynamics models could, in theory, handle more complex geometries, but are still computationally too expensive for industrial‐scale equipment. Therefore, there is a need for relatively fast models that enable researchers to estimate performance parameters with reasonable accuracy for non‐standard fluidized‐bed geometries. An important role is played by so‐called lumped models, in which the various interactions between the transport phenomena are explicitly described. Although lumping is not a new concept in the literature—various authors have applied lumping for hydrodynamics and heat transfer in the past—it is not immediately clear how different kinds of lumping could be used for more complex designs for high‐temperature processes. Here, we discuss the various lumped models available in the literature for fluidized‐bed reactors and critically analyze the developments necessary to apply them to high‐temperature processes.

title: Learnable Hodge-Laplacian Driven Mixture of Experts for Steady-PDE Surrogates on Coarse Unstructured Meshes
authors: Stavros Nousias, Akis Nousias, Konstantinos Gkrispanis
abstract: Current approaches for steady partial differential equations surrogate models on unstructured meshes apply a single mixing mechanism to the whole solution. This paper proposes an architecture that partitions the solution among vanilla transformer experts, each focused on a different spectral scale. The partition is built from a discrete Hodge Laplacian $L_0=\star_0^{-1} d_0^{\top}\star_1 d_0$, that serves as a fitting layer measuring high-frequency content. A gating mechanism takes the mesh as input and produces the per-vertex weights that recombine the expert outputs. AirFRANS is a steady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) airfoil benchmark. We evaluate our approach in a reduced remeshed version of the benchmark with each unstructured mesh counting 9.6K faces and 4.9K vertices. We compare our approach with the Transolver on the same dataset and dataset slit. Our approach reduces relative $L_2$ error by 31% and interior mean squared error by 47%.

title: Physics-Guided Multi-Fidelity Surrogate Modeling for Natural Supercavity Geometry of an Axisymmetric Conical Cavitator
authors: Vinh Pham, Nguyen Van Tu, Warn-Gyu Park
abstract: Natural supercavitation behind conical cavitators generates a vapor-filled envelope that, when sustained over the full body of a high-speed underwater vehicles, reduces hydrodynamic skin-friction drag and enables performance levels unattainable in fully wetted flow. Accurate prediction of maximum cavity length and maximum cavity radius and local cavity profile as functions of cavitation number and cone half-angle is essential for both the static design and the real-time shape management of super-cavitating torpedo cavitators. Classical analytical models provide computationally inexpensive predictions but exhibit systematic disagreements in the practically important regime of moderate cavitation number and large angle, where slender-body assumptions begin to break down. Existing data-driven machine learning approaches offer higher accuracy but are constrained by the prohibitive cost of multiphase computational fluid dynamics (CFD) sweeps over the full design space. This study proposes a physics-guided multi-fidelity surrogate framework based on Extended Hierarchical Kriging (PG-EHK) that addresses this challenge by fusing the multiple competing analytical cavity formulas as non-level low-fidelity (LF) trend functions corrected by a sparse set of high-fidelity (HF) CFD data. It simultaneously incorporates the analytical models regardless of their local fidelity ordering, using Bayesian-estimated scaling factors to construct the trend function as physical baseline. The resulting surrogate maps operational condition inputs to cavity geometry responses using fewer than 20 high-fidelity CFD evaluations. Cross-validation on five independent hold-out CFD cases demonstrates that the proposed PG-EHK surrogate achieves 61% reduction in prediction error compared to the best-performing individual analytical approach.

title: Heat treatment of railway and heavy machinery grade mild steels: from conventional quenching to smart-nanofluid-assisted cooling
authors: Emmanuel O. Atofarati, Mathew Olurotimi Adeoti, Victor O. Adogbeji, Basiru Philip Aramide, Ayorinde E. Olatunde, T. A. Adegbola, Tamba Jamiru, Mohsen. Sharifpur
abstract: Abstract Railway-grade mild steel remains a cornerstone material in rail and heavy machinery infrastructure due to its cost-effectiveness and mechanical robustness. However, ensuring optimal hardness, toughness, and wear resistance under demanding service conditions requires intelligent heat treatment strategies. The transformative potential of integrating nanofluid-based quenching and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven optimization in the heat treatment of railway-grade mild steel was explored. We first summarize the influence of critical thermal parameters, such as austenitizing temperature, cooling rate, and quenching medium, on the steel’s microstructure and performance. Particular attention is given to emerging nanofluid quenchants, which enable tunable heat transfer characteristics and improved control over phase transformations. We then examine the role of machine learning (ML) and optimization algorithms in predicting mechanical outcomes, designing process parameters, and reducing trial and error in thermal processing. State-of-the-art applications of deep learning, surrogate modeling, and multi-objective optimization in heat treatment are critically reviewed. Finally, we propose future directions including hybrid intelligent systems, sustainable nanofluid design, and the deployment of digital twins for real-time control in smart manufacturing. This interdisciplinary synthesis provides a roadmap for materials engineers and AI practitioners to co-develop next-generation heat treatment workflows that are efficient, sustainable, and performance-driven, contributing to the evolution of smart railway infrastructure.

title: Pollutant Dispersion in and Around Buildings: A Critical Review of Modelling, Mitigation, and Future Opportunities
authors: Manash Jyoti Gogoi
abstract: Pollutant dispersion in and around buildings is governed by the coupled behavior of atmospheric flow, building aerodynamics, ventilation, source characteristics, and pollutant-specific transport processes. Openings, leakage, air intakes and exhausts cause an interaction between outdoor pollution and indoor emissions, resulting in spatially heterogeneous and time-dependent concentrations. This narrative review summarizes experimental and numerical studies on pollutant sources, transport, modelling, measurement and exposure mitigation. Additionally, it focuses on validation against wind-tunnel, tracer-gas, and field measurements. It compares Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS), large-eddy simulation (LES), and transport-based recurrence computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and it also compares URANS. The reviewed literature shows that the prediction accuracy depends on inflow turbulence, source representation, geometry, numerical resolution, atmospheric stability, validation targets and turbulence closure. While RANS provides an affordable alternative for engineering evaluation when necessary, LES can remove the effects of unsteady transport and concentration fluctuations; neither is dependable without application-specific validation and verification. The indoor-outdoor coupling concept is effective depending on facade concentration, wind direction and opening configuration and shows dilution of indoor emissions and increased intake of outdoor air pollution. These modelling limitations are connected to sensor placement, exposure assessment, and energy-air-quality trade-offs through the synthesis. The review does not provide complete coverage or combined effect estimates, as the literature collection was not achieved by a documented systematic search. Priorities include reproducible benchmarks, uncertainty-aware validation, indoor-outdoor models by pollutant, and ventilation and filtration controls based on occupant exposure, energy demand, and robustness of operations.

title: Size and geometry effects on the flow-rate–torque trade-off of a drainage impeller in a submerged mechanical defoamer
authors: Fan Wang, Youqiang Jiang, Youjie Qiu, Wei Liu, Yangyang Huai
abstract: Abstract Rotating drainage impellers must balance suction-driven flow against shaft loading, yet which geometric parameters govern this flow-rate–torque trade-off remains poorly established. This work addresses this question for the drainage impeller of a submerged mechanical defoamer, focusing on the single-phase hydrodynamics underlying froth capture rather than directly modelling foam rupture. Thirty configurations spanning four geometric parameters — blade number Z, impeller diameter D, impeller height H and blade outlet angle β — were generated by maximin orthogonal Latin hypercube sampling and evaluated by three-dimensional steady-state CFD for drainage flow rate and torque. Gaussian-process surrogates with leave-one-out cross-validation then supported conditional-response analysis, Sobol sensitivity indices and surrogate-based multi-objective Bayesian optimization. The results show that impeller diameter dominates the dimensional responses, with first-order Sobol indices of 0.91 for flow rate and 0.96 for torque. After dimensional normalization removes the leading size-scaling effects, diameter still governs the flow coefficient, whereas impeller height emerges as the principal secondary factor for the torque coefficient, indicating that size mainly sets the operating point while the residual geometry modulates the normalized loading. A representative Pareto compromise design (Z = 8, D = 81.11 mm, H = 30 mm, β = 120°) was verified by CFD within 6% of the surrogate predictions; relative to the original impeller it raises the flow rate by 25.5%, a gain attributable mainly to the enlarged diameter rather than to improve dimensionless flow capacity. Water experiments at 1000 rev/min confirmed the CFD predictions for both impellers, with flow-rate deviations within 5% and torque deviations within 10%. Flow-field analysis relates the higher throughput to an enlarged suction-related low-pressure region, smoother blade-passage flow and reduced local wake dissipation. The framework provides a practical basis for drainage-impeller design and, more generally, for separating size and geometry effects in CFD-based optimization under limited simulation budgets.

title: A Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM) for Physically-Interpretable Rainfall-Evapotranspiration-Runoff Simulation Across Diverse Hydroclimatic Regimes
authors: M Jawad, HV Gupta, MA Farmani, A Behrangi, GY Niu
abstract: Recent advances in machine learning have improved rainfall-runoff prediction, yet most data-driven models remain difficult to interpret and do not explicitly enforce physical conservation laws. We present the Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM), a mass-conserving architecture based on the Mass-Conserving Perceptron (MCP). GCHM uses five storage states representing canopy interception, snow, soil moisture, groundwater, and streamflow generation. Constrained gates govern precipitation partitioning, evapotranspiration, infiltration, seepage, runoff, and baseflow while learning context-dependent process relationships. We evaluate GCHM across 50 CAMELS catchments spanning snowmelt-dominated, recent-rainfall, historical-rainfall, and arid regimes, using NOAA AORC meteorological forcing and remotely sensed vegetation and land-surface data. Performance is assessed using the Jawad-Kling-Gupta Efficiency (JKGE) metric, which accounts for stationary and non-stationary hydrologic behavior. We compare the full architecture with ablated variants and recurrent neural network benchmarks. GCHM reproduces streamflow dynamics across diverse hydroclimatic regimes, including arid catchments, while maintaining interpretable states and fluxes. Ablation experiments show that simplified architectures may perform adequately under wet conditions but struggle to represent flow persistence and recession during dry periods, when groundwater storage sustains low flows. Learned gates recover hydrologically plausible relationships governing snowmelt, runoff, seepage, and evapotranspiration. GCHM combines competitive predictive performance with mass conservation and interpretability, providing a foundation for hydrologic modeling and counterfactual analysis.

title: Development and Integration of a Data-Driven Coarse-Grid Turbulence Model in the SCENES System Code
authors: Q Ma, H Zhang, Y Yang, M Zhao
abstract: Thermal-hydraulic phenomena in advanced reactors, such as natural circulation and thermal stratification, are intrinsically three-dimensional and cannot be adequately captured by conventional one-dimensional system codes. Although three-dimensional modules have been introduced into these codes, their predictive accuracy is limited by the lack of a reliable turbulence closure on coarse meshes. In this study, a data-driven coarse-grid turbulence model is developed and integrated into the system code SCENES. The model follows a high-to-low framework, in which a multilayer perceptron learns the mapping from six Galilean-invariant local flow features to the turbulent eddy viscosity using high-fidelity CFD data. The trained model is deployed in SCENES through the ONNX format, and the predicted turbulent eddy viscosity is used to evaluate the turbulent stress and heat flux in the momentum and energy equations. The model is assessed on a NuScale-like natural circulation loop using two SCENES meshes. With the validation mesh, the results reproduce the radial velocity and temperature distributions of the OpenFOAM reference, whereas the original SCENES simulation without the model produces non-physical profiles and erroneous radial temperature differences in the riser. With the generalization mesh, which uses a coarser radial discretization and a different channel partitioning, the results remain consistent with the reference, confirming that the trained model is not tied to the specific mesh used in training. The study demonstrates a computationally efficient pathway for embedding data-driven turbulence closures into system codes and improving their three-dimensional predictive capability.

title: CFD-Based Comparative Assessment of RANS Turbulence Model Under Inlet Angle Variation in Ranque-Hilsch Vortex Tube
authors: Pankaj Kumar Sagar, Akhilesh Arora
abstract: This study conducts a systematic numerical analysis of the two-equation Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS)turbulence model to predict flow behaviour within a Ranque-Hilsch vortex tube (RHVT). Six geometric configurations,defined by variation in inlet angle, are examined through three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD)simulations. The investigation compared the performance of three widely adopted turbulence models: the standard k-ε, standard k-ω and SST k-ω models formulations. The simulations are considered to resolve the complex flow phenomena within the RHVT, characterised by strong swirling motion, compressibility effects, and intense turbulence that drive temperature separation. To enhance solution accuracy, particular emphasis is placed on mesh quality and near-wall resolutions with careful control of the dimensionless wall distance (y+). Model evaluation is carried out by comparing predicted temperature fields, outlet temperature at both cold and hot ends, and the overall flow structures. The results demonstrate that the standard k-ω model shows closure agreement with experimental data, which can be attributed to its improved treatment of the near-wall regions and its ability to capture the adverse pressure gradient more effectively. Overall, the findings underscore the importance of appropriate turbulence model selection in RHVT simulations and provide a useful basis for future numerical studies aimed at improving RHVT performance.

title: Field2Form: A Geometry-First Framework for Symbolic Solutions of Differential Equations, with a Held-Out Residual Court Against Extrapolation Blindness
authors: ali madfa
abstract: Non-linear and complex differential equations govern physical phenomena across fluid dynamics, quantum mechan-ics, and astrophysics. While Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and conventional Symbolic Regression (SR)algorithms excel at fitting observational data within training domains, they systematically suffer from “extrapolationblindness”—failing catastrophically when deployed beyond training boundaries or near boundary tails. In this work,we present Field2Form, an autonomous geometry-first framework that eliminates extrapolation blindness by couplingangle-field direction geometry, anchored latent neural generation, and a novel Held-out Tail Residual Test governed byKarush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) convex sparsity optimization. We establish two distinct evaluation protocols: Protocol A(Selection Gate Validation), which verifies the court’s capacity to isolate true analytical closed forms when present in can-didate libraries, and Protocol B (Unbiased Symbolic Discovery), where the framework autonomously discovers symbolicexpressions for forced, non-linear, and second-order differential systems without human-crafted dictionaries. Empiricalevaluations on the Logistic equation (y′= 1.1y(1 − y)), Riccati non-linear ODE (y′= y2− 1), forced non-linear ODE(y′= 1.1y(1 − y) +0.2 sin(x)), and the second-order non-linear pendulum (y′′+ sin(y) = 0) demonstrate that Field2Formachieves near-zero tail residual errors (MSE ≤ 10−23for analytical forms and MSE ≈ 10−4for dynamic harmonic series),while completely exposing and rejecting spurious polynomial or rational approximations whose tail errors explode byup to 5–6 orders of magnitude. Field2Form provides an end-to-end, reproducible, and fully autonomous pipeline forverifiable scientific discovery in physical systems.

title: Numerical Investigation of Flow Direction and Inlet–Outlet Configuration Effects on Thermo-Hydraulic Performance in T-Junction Tubes
authors: Ali Gürcan
abstract: Direct comparisons of diverging and converging T-junction configurations under identical operating and boundary conditions remain limited, restricting the design-oriented selection of suitable flow arrangements. This study numerically investigates the effects of flow direction and inlet–outlet topology on the thermo-hydraulic performance of a symmetric equal-diameter T-junction with water as the working fluid. Four configurations were examined: axially fed and branch-fed diverging flows (K1 and K2) and opposing-stream and orthogonal-stream merging flows (K3 and K4). Three-dimensional steady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations were performed in ANSYS Fluent using the standard k"-" ε turbulence model with Enhanced Wall Treatment at Reynolds numbers of 5000, 10000, and 15000 and inlet temperatures of 313, 333, and 353 K. The configurations were compared under identical geometry, total mass flow rate, and wall-temperature conditions using the average Nusselt number, static pressure drop, and a common thermo-hydraulic performance criterion (PEC). K1 consistently provided the highest average Nusselt number and the lowest pressure drop, while K2 was the closest alternative. Relative to K1, the PEC values of K3 and K4 were lower by 43.3–53.4% and 45.0–53.5%, respectively. The results show that stronger local flow interaction in converging configurations does not necessarily yield superior overall performance and provide a quantitative basis for selecting equal-diameter T-junction topologies in water-based thermal and process-piping applications.

title: A Hybrid physics-informed digital twin for offshore wind-farm flow prediction: integrating CFD simulations with deep regression forest and probabilistic surrogate models
authors: Xu Wu, Liang-Kui Yin, Tao He
abstract: The marine-atmosphere dynamics are nonlinear and multiscale, which poses a computational challenge for accurately describing the flow field around offshore wind turbines. Using advanced data-driven surrogate models and CFD simulations, this study presents a hybrid physics-informed digital twin framework to predict wind farm behavior under stochastic environmental conditions with high accuracy. In this work, we propose a framework that simultaneously integrates spatiotemporal dependencies, physical constraints, and probabilistic uncertainties by combining Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), Deep-Gaussian Process Regression (Deep-GPR), Extreme Gradient Boosting Algorithm (XGBoost), and a transformer-based regression model called CFD-Former. PINNs incorporate Navier–Stokes equation residuals into the training process to ensure physical consistency, while XGBoost and Deep-GPR improve model generalizability to different inlet flow conditions. Hybrid surrogate models are trained on data from CFD calculations with different wind direction and speed conditions. The generated digital twin is able to predict the velocities measured at the meteorological tower within an uncertainty of 10% and reproduce the high resolution flow patterns due to CFD with a mean absolute deviation below 1%. This novel approach uses deterministic simulation and intelligent inference to predict offshore wind farm performance in a scalable and physically based manner, possibly enabling adaptive operation and reliability assessment.

title: Momentum and thermal transport in Casson fluid flow over an unsteady radially stretching sheet: A comparative study of unified and modular physics-informed neural networks
authors: Shravan Kumar Rudrabhatla
abstract: This study presents two artificial intelligence-based frameworks, unified physics-informed neural network (UPINN) and modular physics-informed neural network (MPINN), for analyzing boundary-layer flow and heat transfer of a Casson fluid over an unsteady radially stretching sheet. The governing partial differential equations are transformed into nonlinear similarity ordinary differential equations using similarity transformations. The resulting equations and boundary conditions are incorporated into the neural-network loss function through automatic differentiation, enabling a label-free solution strategy. UPINN employs a single network to predict the dependent variables, whereas MPINN uses separate subnetworks for the velocity and temperature fields, consistent with the one-way coupling structure of the governing system. A systematic hyperparameter analysis examines the effects of learning rate, network architecture, and collocation points. The predictions are validated against numerical solutions obtained using the BVP4C solver and show close agreement. Parametric studies investigate the effects of the unsteadiness parameter, Casson parameter, Prandtl number, and suction/injection parameter on the velocity and temperature profiles and wall transport quantities. The results demonstrate that both frameworks produce stable solutions and show close agreement with the reference BVP4C solutions, with differences in loss and relative error across the investigated configurations. The study provides a comparative assessment of unified and modular PINN architectures for the present nonlinear boundary-layer system.

title: Experiencing Mars Dust-Storm Electrostatic Discharge in Virtual Reality: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Predicting Electrostatic Discharge in Martian Dust Storms
authors: Emmanuel Mudaheranwa, Gilbert Masengo, Alphonse Blaise Bataringaya
abstract: The sustained deployment of human missions and permanent settlements on Mars will depend on highly reliable electrical power systems to support life-support facilities, habitats, scientific instruments, communication networks, in-situ resource utilization, transportation, and other mission-critical operations. The safety and uninterrupted operation of astronauts’ electrical and electronic equipment,including spacesuits, rovers, autonomous robots, sensing devices, and power electronics are equally essential for mission success. This is because, electrostatic discharge (ESD) generated during Martian dust storms may pose significant risks by affecting spacecraft electronics, communication systems, scientific instruments, and solar photovoltaic (PV) power systems through tribo electric charging, dust deposition, and electrical breakdown. Accurate prediction of these coupled phenomena remains challenging because conventional models do not simultaneously account for atmospheric flow, particle electrification, electric-field evolution, and dynamic gas breakdown under Martian environmental conditions. This research presents an integrated computational and experimental framework that combines Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD), a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN), and a novel Dynamic Mars Paschen Model (DMPM) to predict electrostatic discharge and assess its impact on Martian surface sys tems. The CFD model simulates airflow, dust transport, and pressure distribution within a Martian environmental chamber, while the PINN incorporates the governing equations of fluid flow, charge conservation, and electrostatic field evolution to efficiently predict triboelectric charge accumulation and electric-field intensity. The proposed DMPM extends the classical Paschen law by incorporating the effects of airflow velocity, dust concentration, atmospheric temperature, triboelectric charge density, and carbon dioxide frost coverage to estimate the dynamic breakdown voltage under realistic Martian conditions. Experimental validation con ducted in a purpose-built Martian environmental chamber demonstrated excellent agreement between numerical predictions and laboratory measurements, with coefficients of determination exceeding 0.98 and prediction errors generally below 3%. Beyond electrostatic discharge prediction, the developed laboratory provides a sustainable multidisciplinary research platform for investi gating dust-induced degradation of Martian solar PV systems, evaluating electrostatic mitigation technologies, validating planetary instrumentation, and supporting future Mars exploration research. The proposed CFD–PINN–DMPM framework therefore con tributes to improved mission safety, energy-system reliability, and the long-term sustainability of planetary surface operations.

title: Computational fluid dynamics for assessing nasal ventilation and virtual surgery in pediatric cleft patients
authors: Quentin Gouget, Lionel Meister, Nathalie Degardin, Richard Nicollas, Éric Moreddu
abstract: Abstract Background Cleft lip and/or palate causes complex nasal deformities that result in persistent obstruction. This study aimed to quantitatively assess nasal airflow and simulate virtual surgical interventions using CT-based Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) in pediatric cleft patients. Methods CT scans from two pediatric cleft patients (10 months and 5 years old) and age-matched controls were used to generate 3-dimensional nasal models. CFD simulations quantified mass flow rate, pressure drop, and nasal resistance during peak inspiration and expiration. Time-varying pressure–flow data allowed generation of virtual rhinomanometry curves. Virtual surgeries included isolated rhinoplasty, isolated septoplasty, and combined rhinoseptoplasty. Results Baseline cleft models exhibited markedly elevated nasal resistance and asymmetric airflow. The functional effects of virtual anatomical correction differed between patients. Septal correction accounted for most of the resistance reduction in the 10-month-old model, whereas combined correction of the septum and nasal framework produced the closest approximation to control airflow in the 5-year-old model. Conclusions CFD provides a quantitative, patient-specific characterization of the airflow mechanics underlying nasal obstruction in pediatric cleft patients. The magnitude of functional improvement produced by virtual anatomical correction varied markedly between the two patients, underscoring the patient-specific nature of nasal airflow mechanics across early childhood. Virtual surgery, coupled with CFD, offers a realistic framework for exploring the mechanical determinants of nasal obstruction in this population, with future automation potentially facilitating its integration into individualized, physiology-based assessment.

title: An energetically and thermodynamically consistent Boussinesq model
authors: Rémi Tailleux, Thomas Dubos, Benedict J. Hatton
abstract: The Boussinesq approximation is a cornerstone of geophysical fluid dynamics, yet its thermodynamic and energetic underpinnings have remained ambiguous. In standard formulations, the links with the fully compressible Navier–Stokes equations are obscured, internal energy is only implicit, and the representation of diffusion and irreversibility remains ad hoc. Here we derive a new Boussinesq model in a fully traceable way from the two-component compressible Navier–Stokes equations, ensuring exact energy conservation and consistent thermodynamics. Assuming a linear equation of state, our model treats density as a proxy for specific volume, distinguishes in situ temperature and potential temperature explicitly, and incorporates diffusive fluxes that homogenise the correct thermodynamic potentials, ensuring consistent non-negative entropy production. The resulting formulation makes gravitational and internal energy explicit, resolves the salinity – entropy coupling required for non-negative entropy production, and yields an exactly closed total energy budget. We also introduce a thermodynamically soundproof model that retains the compressible dynamical structure for the same simplified equation of state and therefore provides a reference for interpreting the Boussinesq approximation. The purpose of these models is primarily to improve structure rather than accuracy: they establish a transparent and thermodynamically admissible framework for energy budget analysis and for future studies of stratified mixing.
