title: Ensuring economic security of machine-building business in Ukraine amid economic turbulence
authors: Viktoriia Hnieusheva
abstract: Стаття присвячена формуванню нових наукових рішень щодо пошук шляхів забезпечення економічної безпеки машинобудівного бізнесу в Україні в умовах економічної турбулентності. Розкрита наукова та практична необхідність підвищення рівня економічної безпеки українських машинобудівних підприємств, як запоруки розвитку машинобудування та економіки країни в цілому у воєнний та пост воєнний період. Метою статті є пошук шляхів забезпечення економічної безпеки машинобудівного бізнесу в Україні в умовах економічної турбулентності. Методологія: використано комплекс загальних та спеціальних методів на емпіричному і теоретичному рівнях, таких як: історичний та логічного узагальнення – для ідентифікації хронологічних етапів розвитку машинобудівного бізнесу в Україні; кількісного аналізу – для дослідження розвитку машинобудування та машинобудівних підприємств в Україні у 2010-2024 роках; синтезу – для визначення ключових проблем забезпечення економічної безпеки на машинобудівних підприємствах країни; наукової абстракції – для визначення причин, що формують економічну турбулентність для машинобудування країни та українських підприємств - виробників машинобудівної продукції; системний – для розробки напрямів забезпечення економічної безпеки машинобудівного бізнесу в Україні в умовах економічної турбулентності. title: Deep Operator Learning for Interface Evolution and Uncertainty Quantification in Complex Multiphase Flow
authors: Yixin Xiao
abstract: Predicting moving interfaces in multiphase flow remains computationally demanding because topological changes, high curvature, and thin ligaments require fine spatial and temporal resolution. This study develops a Fourier-DeepONet surrogate that maps initial phase geometry, nondimensional flow parameters, and space-time coordinates to future volume-fraction fields while producing calibrated uncertainty. High-fidelity trajectories are generated with the adaptive volume-of-fluid solver in Basilisk for Rayleigh-Taylor instability and droplet deformation. The architecture combines convolutional branch encoding, Fourier coordinate features, global spectral mixing, physics-aware constraints, and a Normal-Inverse-Gamma evidential head. On the held-out benchmark, the model reaches an interface Dice score of 0.954 ± 0.006, an intersection-over-union score of 0.913 ± 0.009, and a volume-fraction MAE of 0.0187 ± 0.0014. Relative mass error remains 0.73 ± 0.12% over 50 frames, while uncertainty-error correlation reaches 0.812 ± 0.021 after calibration. Under unseen parameter combinations, Dice decreases by only 0.026 ± 0.007. These results support physics-constrained operator learning as a fast and reliability-aware approach to multiphase interface prediction.

title: Editorial: Advances in energy efficiency: design, technologies and policies
authors: Mouloud Azzedine Denai, Shady Khalil
abstract: Policy frameworks, regulatory incentives and financial mechanisms are essential in driving the transition to innovative technologies, shaping how societies manage their energy usage. These policies encompass a variety of tools and frameworks to overcome the key barriers and challenges and ensure that energy efficiency practices deliver widespread and lasting benefits.Energy efficiency is a broad and multidisciplinary field which spans a wide range of topics such as analysis and modeling, energy management and performance optimization, policies, innovative technologies. This special issue explores the latest advancement in energy efficient innovations, supportive energy policies, regulatory frameworks, public awareness and demand-side initiatives highlighting their contributions to lowering energy costs for consumers and businesses, reducing dependency on fossil fuels and minimizing greenhouse gas emissions.The contribution provides a comprehensive review of multi-objective optimization (MOO)-based design of cost-effective renovations and retrofit of buildings to achieve net-zero energy buildings (NZEB) or zero-energy buildings (i.e. buildings that consume as much energy as they produce locally from renewable sources) while maximizing indoor thermal comfort, air quality and natural light for occupants. The research aims to identify several building performance objectives that bridge the social, environmental and economic criteria of sustainability. In addition, this research aims to identify the key factors and their assessment criteria to enhance occupant well-being by maintaining a healthy and comfortable indoor environment. It also demonstrates the effectiveness of MOO and its potential for decisionmaking in NZEB development based on a wide range of design variables and under various conditions. The article presents a comparative study of various optimization algorithms, tools, and simulation software in terms of their reliability and computational effectiveness in solving building problems. Finally, this research proposes a four-step hierarchical framework based on MOO to guide building professionals in the design of NZEB. The research is validated through case studies developed for India context.The second contribution focuses on the cooling of photovoltaic (PV) systems in the Sub-Saharian Africa known for its intense solar irradiance and prolonged hours of high temperatures throughout the year which can reduce the efficiency of the PV panels. The article presents a comprehensive coverage of the recent literature on cooling techniques and their performance including active cooling such as photovoltaic-thermal (PV-T) systems which use heat exchangers and fluid circulation and passive cooling such as photovoltaic-phase change material (PV-PCM) which use special materials that melt and solidify at specific temperature without circulating fluids or heat exchangersThe PV-T integrated with phase change material (PV-T/PCM) uniformly regulates PV cell temperature to an optimal operating condition and is considered in this study. A critical design criterion for effective PCM integration in PV-T systems requires that the phasetransition temperature matches the optimal operating temperature range for photovoltaic cells, typically between 30°C and 45 °C. Shea butter, a bio-based PCM that is environmentally sustainable and eco-friendly as compared to the traditional paraffin wax, was selected for this study due to its latent heat characteristics and melting temperature (approximately 32 °C), which aligns exactly with the optimal temperature range.The PV-T/PCM computational models, developed using TRNSYS software, were used to simulate the electrical and thermal behaviour of the hybrid PV-T/PCM system, to analyse the heat-transfer mechanisms and assess the impact of the PCM on the efficiency of the PV system. The models were successfully validated against experimental and simulation studies from the literature. The modelling framework developed in this study can be adapted to a broad spectrum of bio-based PCMs possessing appropriate thermos-physical properties.The contribution focuses on thermal energy storage (TES) in packed granular beds considered as a highly efficient technology for high temperature solar thermal plants, industrial waste heat recovery and grid-scale energy management. This technology stores heat by passing a heated fluid through a stationary bed of solid particles like rocks, ceramics of manufactured sand (M-sand) during the storage phase and reversing the fluid flow to retrieve the heat during the release phase.This research developed a physics-informed neural network (PINN) for predicting the full three-dimensional (3D) temperature distribution inside an M-sand packed-bed thermal energy storage unit. The physical laws governing fluid dynamics and heat transfer are embedded into the NN model's cost function.The PINN was trained on temperature datasets collected from five thermocouples at three distinct volumetric flow rates (1.00, 1.88, and 2.66 LPM), with the governing threedimensional transient heat conduction equation enforced simultaneously through a physicsconstrained loss term evaluated at 300 collocation points.The continuous 3D temperature gradient predicted by the PINN revealed several internal thermal characteristics as compared to the five-sensor experiment which only captures localized temperature measurements. The PINN simultaneously inferred effective physical parameters-thermal conductivity, density-specific heat product, and heat transfer coefficient-from the training process, without separate calibration experiments. Traditionally, characterising materials to extract these key parameters requires setting up separate, often costly and time consuming laboratory experiments.The fourth contribution investigates the multiple energy benefits (MEBs) of energy efficiency (EE) measures implemented by small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) across five distinct European regions.The study uses a targeted survey questionnaire distributed across these five European regions to examine how local contextual factors influence organizational priorities regarding energy efficiency.The results reveal that having increased knowledge about the company energy use is the top overall MEB across the surveyed areas. However, individual regions show a distinct tendency to favour certain benefit categories over others even though all the investigated regions provide supportive energy policies; this suggests that policy availability is not the driving factor behind these observed disparities.The findings indicate that MEBs are socially constructed outcomes shaped by interactions between regional contexts and company practices. Therefore, the research emphasizes the need to analyse MEBs alongside EEMs rather than treating them as separate outcomes.When MEBs of energy efficiency are recognized not just a technical or economic calculation but a human-centric process shaped by social values, institutional structures and political priorities, this opens up a comprehensive understanding of how benefits emerge, are prioritized and valued across different contexts.The future of energy efficient technologies presents tremendous opportunities and is universally recognized as a cornerstone of global sustainability and decarbonization. The journey towards an energy-efficient future also present significant challenges which introduce several barriers. Policymakers worldwide must prioritize the integration of these technologies into existing frameworks, fostering innovation, and cultivating a lasting energy-conscious society.

title: Use of Machine Learning Methods to Predict the Unsteady Wind Pressure on Tall Buildings: An Integrated Approach
authors: D.P.P. Meddage
abstract: As buildings become taller, their natural frequencies decrease into a range where they may be susceptible to vibrations under unsteady wind loading. Traditional methods for estimating unsteady wind pressure include boundary layer wind tunnel experiments and Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations. Although these methods are reliable and accurate, their routine use in engineering practice is challenging due to resource, time and cost constraints. Design engineers require a fast and accurate complementary approach to assess unsteady wind pressures on generalised tall buildings. Machine learning has gained attention in wind engineering as a surrogate modelling approach. However, most existing applications focus on predicting static pressure. Accurate wind-resistant design requires reliable prediction of unsteady wind pressure, which governs the dynamic response of a tall building. This thesis addresses this gap by developing a machine learning-based surrogate model to reconstruct unsteady wind pressure on generalised rectangular tall buildings considering spatial coordinates, wind direction (0°-90°), slenderness ratios (6-10) and side ratios (1-2). Boundary layer wind tunnel experiments were conducted to obtain high-resolution wind pressure measurements. Validated CFD simulations incorporating Large Eddy Simulation (LES) generated an extensive dataset covering multiple wind directions, slenderness ratios and side ratios. Several ML approaches were implemented and evaluated, including tree-based algorithms and neural networks. The framework accurately reconstructed unsteady wind pressure, reproducing key flow features such as separation, reattachment, conical vortices, pressure gradients and extreme peak pressures. The final neural network-based surrogate model (TabNet) achieved high predictive performance (R² ≈ 0.98) and showed strong agreement with unseen CFD data and independent wind tunnel measurements for external validation. The surrogate model was further integrated with OpenSees and Python to obtain the dynamic response through a one-way (uncoupled) fluid-structure interaction analysis. The surrogate-predicted wind loads preserved a physically consistent dynamic response, including critical phenomena such as vortex-induced lock-in. This combined approach reduces computational time from hours or days to seconds or minutes, providing a fast, accurate and geometry-aware framework for early-stage design evaluation of wind loading on tall buildings.

title: Tropical Ocean Evaporation‐Temperature Sensitivity to Surface Radiative Property Perturbations in Fully Coupled CESM2
authors: Jian Wei, Ping Xian Yang, Ping Chang
abstract: Abstract Tropical ocean evaporation is the dominant source of moisture for global precipitation. However, the dependence of evaporation‐temperature sensitivity on ocean surface radiative properties has not been quantified in the fully coupled modeling framework. This study developed physically based ocean surface albedo (OSA) parameterizations that incorporate multiple governing processes, along with a spectrally resolved graybody effective ocean surface emissivity (OSE). These formulations were implemented as perturbation experiments within the fully coupled Community Earth System Model version 2 (CESM2), and the resulting fractional changes in evaporation‐temperature sensitivity were decomposed into individual contributions via the ocean surface energy budget framework. OSA perturbations drive the large increase in fractional evaporation–temperature sensitivity. The resulting surface warming and atmospheric moistening elevate downward longwave radiation, with enhanced low‐cloud coverage further amplifying this effect. These positive contributions are partially offset by stronger surface thermal‐emission damping and reduced incident solar flux associated with increased cloudiness. OSE modification alone produces negligible changes in sensitivity, as reduced emissivity largely compensates for the weakened thermal damping within the longwave budget. The contrasting responses reveal that OSA adjustments exert substantially greater influence on evaporation‐temperature sensitivity than OSE modifications, operating through both direct shortwave absorption and indirect atmospheric radiative feedbacks. These findings carry practical implications for future Earth system model development. Refined OSA treatments and the associated shortwave radiative budget will likely demand more extensive model retuning, whereas OSE improvements can be incorporated with comparatively less effort.

title: CIS-Transolver: A Cross-Layer Incremental-State Neural Operator for Fine-Scale Automotive Aerodynamic Flow Prediction
authors: Jiang-Long Liu, Zhi-Cheng Zhu, Jia Hao, Liang-Yue Jia
abstract: Neural operators offer an efficient data-driven approach to rapid prediction of complex automotive aerodynamic flows. However, spectral bias and other factors limit accurate reconstruction of fine-scale flow variations near complex geometries. Existing studies improve the representation and fitting of fine-scale information mainly through information extraction and training objectives. Further study is needed to determine how extracted local details can be used continually in subsequent operator computations and contribute effectively to the overall flow-field representation. We propose CIS-Transolver, a cross-layer incremental-state neural operator that extends fine-scale modeling from local information extraction to its use across layers. The method extracts fine-scale information through local multiscale analysis and encodes it as geometric moment states that are propagated and updated across layers. By combining information from previous layers with feedback to the value representations in Physics-Attention, the method allows local details to contribute continually to subsequent modeling of global physical correlations. We systematically evaluate CIS-Transolver on three public automotive aerodynamics benchmarks, ShapeNet-Car, AhmedML, and DrivAerNet++, covering surface pressure fields and volumetric pressure and velocity fields. CIS-Transolver achieves the lowest mean relative L2 error among the evaluated methods for all five prediction metrics across the three benchmarks. The relative error reductions average 8.72% across the five metrics compared with the best baseline for each metric, reaching 16.38% for ShapeNet-Car pressure prediction and 15.60% for AhmedML velocity prediction. These results provide a new approach to fine-scale flow prediction for complex geometries.

title: Image-Based Prediction of Lift and Drag Coefficients of a Circular Cylinder Using Convolutional Neural Networks and Flow Visualization
authors: Jing-Wen Hu, Waleed Khan, Zhi Wu
abstract: Force measurement is a fundamental diagnostic technique in experimental fluid mechanics. However, conventional instrumentation, such as mechanical balances and pressure taps, is often intrusive, geometry-dependent, and mechanically constrained. This study proposes a non-contact, image-driven force-estimation framework wherein convolutional neural networks (CNNs) infer the instantaneous lift and drag coefficients of a circular cylinder directly from wake streakline flow-visualization images. A comprehensive hybrid numerical–experimental dataset was established across laminar and turbulent regimes. Navier–Stokes simulations (DNS at Re=150; LES at Re=500 and 3900) were post-processed into synchronized streakline–force pairs, complemented by water-tunnel dye-visualization experiments at Re=500, 8000, and 12,000. Five CNN architectures, including lightweight custom networks and vision backbones (AlexNet, ResNet18), were trained and validated. For numerical datasets, all models show high prediction accuracy in lift and drag coefficients. In simulation-to-experiment transfer at Re=500, the models capture the dominant vortex-shedding Strouhal number within 12.0% (St=0.233 vs. 0.208), while CNNModel_v5 predicts the mean drag coefficient within 0.35%. On experimental datasets, ResNet18 achieved the best predictive performance among the models tested under random splitting. These results indicate that wake flow-visualization images contain rich physical representations for non-intrusive fluid force estimation.

title: Assisted Turbulence Modeling via Data Assimilation and Machine Learning for Turbomachinery Flows
authors: Tom Moussie, Pierric Joseph, Marcello Meldi
abstract: This work presents the development and assessment of a hybrid framework coupling numerical simulation, experimental samples, data assimilation (DA) and machine learning (ML) to investigate the flow within an axial compressor stage. The methodology first implements a Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter (MFEnKF) which integrates experimental PIV data with a two-fidelity numerical simulation setup, combining steady-state RANS on a fixed grid with unsteady hybrid RANS/LES simulations on a moving grid. This data assimilation step successfully reduces discrepancies between experiments and CFD realizations. Besides, it provides additional high fidelity samples when compared with the available PIV data. This enriched database is used to train machine learning (ML) tools, with the objective to obtain black-box forcing terms to be included in the discretized form of the Navier-Stokes equations. These models are expected to preserve the accuracy of the DA results while not longer requiring the input of experimental data. The neural network architecture used here maps local physical features such as the velocity, the velocity gradients and the turbulent viscosity, to obtain the volume forcing terms. The analysis of the performance of such ML models shows that global accuracy is preserved but localized increased errors in specific regions of the compressor, such as close to the blade tips, can exceed those observed from the baseline RANS simulations. To resolve this issue, a Mixture of Experts (MoE) method is employed, which classifies and combines the trained ML tools for different flow regions. The discrepancy with experimental data of this method is systematically lower than the one observed for the baseline RANS solution and very similar to the one obtained with the MFEnKF.

title: A Simple Empirical Method for Estimating Extreme Air Velocities from CFD Mean-Flow Statistics: Validation Using ISS Columbus and CASA Ventilation Data
authors: George Efthimiou
abstract: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations based on Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) models are widely used for spacecraft cabin ventilation design; however, they primarily provide mean-flow quantities and often underestimate velocity extremes relevant to crew comfort, ventilation effectiveness, and stagnation-zone assessment. This study presents a simple empirical post-processing framework for estimating extreme air velocities from CFD mean-flow statistics. The proposed approach expresses the upper velocity envelope as a function of the local mean velocity and standard deviation through a single empirical coefficient, Kc. Throughout this study, the upper velocity envelope is defined consistently as the 99th percentile of the velocity magnitude distribution, denoted p99, and the empirical peak factor is accordingly defined as Kc,p99 = (p99 − μ)/σ. This definition is applied uniformly to the calibration dataset and to all external validation datasets, so that the same target variable is used at every stage of the analysis. The method is calibrated using published velocity-field data from International Space Station (ISS) Crew Quarters studies and subsequently examined against independent ISS ventilation datasets, including the Columbus module and Crew Alternative Sleeping Area (CASA) configurations. Analysis of digitized experimental and CFD-derived velocity distributions yields a robust median coefficient of approximately Kc = 4.5, while external datasets indicate p99-equivalent values generally within the range Kc ≈ 4–6. Independent validation evidence from Columbus ventilation studies demonstrates that accounting for velocity fluctuations substantially improves agreement with experimental observations, reducing distribution mismatch by approximately 83% compared with uncorrected mean-velocity predictions. The external comparison should be understood as a retrospective consistency check rather than a prospective prediction: the peak factors reported for the Columbus and CASA datasets were derived from the same distributions against which they are compared, and they therefore describe the data rather than forecast it. Accordingly, the proposed framework is presented as an exploratory upper-envelope indicator whose transferability is suggested, but not yet demonstrated, by the observed clustering of independently derived peak factors. The results suggest that a simple statistical correction applied to standard CFD outputs can provide practical estimates of extreme ventilation velocities without the computational cost of Large Eddy Simulation (LES). While the proposed framework should be regarded as an exploratory upper-envelope indicator rather than a universal turbulence closure, and while it does not by itself provide a conservative bound or identify stagnation risk, the consistency observed across multiple ISS ventilation datasets indicates that it offers a useful preliminary screening tool for spacecraft cabin ventilation assessment and design.

title: A Hybrid Approach Using Lattice Boltzmann and Machine Learning for Predicting the Transient Dynamics of Slug Flow in Non-Newtonian Fluids
authors: H. Behrouzi, Ebrahim Goshtasbi-Rad
abstract: Slug flow is a prevalent and crucial flow regime in many industrial applications, such as petroleum and chemical processing, where accurate modeling and prediction are essential for optimizing system performance and ensuring operational stability. This study presents a comprehensive numerical investigation of two-phase slug flow (Newtonian and non-Newtonian) in a horizontal channel using the Lattice Boltzmann Method (LBM). A color-gradient model is employed to capture slug formation, and a non-Newtonian power-law model is used to represent the shear-thickening behavior of one of the fluids. The simulations explore the influence of key parameters, including the flow index (n) and inlet velocities, on slug formation, propagation, and pressure drop. Results show that increasing the power-law index (n)—indicating higher shear-thickening behavior—significantly modifies the velocity profile, reduces apparent viscosity near the wall, and leads to a positive pressure drop compared with Newtonian cases. Additionally, this study introduces a hybrid machine learning approach combining Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for predicting transient slug flow behavior. The POD method reduces the high-dimensional LBM data by capturing the dominant flow dynamics, while LSTM predicts the temporal evolution of these modes with minimal error. The POD+LSTM framework demonstrates significant reduction in computational cost for real-time prediction, with high accuracy, particularly when trained with larger datasets. Validation of the LBM simulations against benchmark tests, as well as comparisons with analytical and numerical solutions from the literature, confirms the reliability of the proposed LBM solver for simulating complex two-phase fluid flows. This research provides valuable insights for both fundamental understanding and practical applications of slug flow in multiphase systems, enabling real-time monitoring and optimization of two-phase flow systems.

title: Heat Transfer Enhancement in the Microscale: Optimization of Fluid Flow
authors: Md Atiqur Rahman, Abhinav Adarsh, Dharani Kurri, Aishwarya Gittoju, P. Paramasivam, S. M. Mozammil Hasnian, A. G. Ayanie
abstract: Microchannel heat sinks have emerged as a leading solution for high‐heat‐flux thermal management in electronics, aerospace, energy conversion and biomedical systems owing to their high surface‐to‐volume ratio and superior convective performance. As channel hydraulic diameters decrease to the microscale, however, fluid flow and heat transfer deviate markedly from classical continuum predictions. These deviations arise from pronounced scale effects, rarefaction, surface roughness, axial wall conduction and compressibility, together with the complex behavior of advanced working fluids such as nanofluids and phase‐change coolants. This review presents a systematic synthesis of microscale heat transfer and hydrodynamics from two complementary perspectives: (1) pure scale effects governing single‐phase convection, and (2) the coupled thermal–hydraulic phenomena that occur when microscale confinement interacts with advanced fluids. Key dimensionless parameters (Knudsen, Reynolds, Bond and Mach numbers) are examined in detail, and their influence on velocity slip, temperature jump, friction factor, Nusselt number, and two‐phase flow regimes is critically assessed. Emerging geometric strategies biomimetic fractal and leaf‐vein networks, shark‐skin and fish‐scale surfaces, honeycomb and raccoon‐type channels are evaluated with respect to heat‐transfer enhancement and pressure‐drop penalty. A comprehensive analysis of numerical methodologies is provided, spanning continuum Computational Fluid Dynamics, mesoscopic Lattice Boltzmann methods, molecular‐dynamics and direct‐simulation Monte Carlo techniques, as well as data‐driven optimization frameworks based on Genetic Algorithms, the Taguchi method, and Artificial Neural Networks (multi‐layer perceptrons, hybrid convolutional networks, and physics‐informed neural networks). Comparative performance metrics, unresolved modeling challenges, and practical selection criteria for each approach are identified. By integrating mechanistic insight with modern computational and optimization tools, this review establishes clear design guidelines and highlights priority research directions for the next generation of high‐performance microchannel heat sinks operating under extreme heat fluxes and compact spatial constraints.

title: Computational Fluid Dynamic Analysis in Tunnel Kiln, a Holistic Approach
authors: Konstantinos Tzikas, Dorothea Kasiteropoulou, Xenofon Spiliotis
abstract: In this research, we analyze the effect of the geometric characteristics of the ceramics as well as the effect of their placement at different distances on the temperature distribution of the furnace. The computational analysis and simulation aimed at producing results were carried out with the ANSYS-CFX computer package. The analysis was based on how these factors affect the backflow and specifically to what extent the temperature rises in the preheating zone and how well we can maintain better thermal uniformity. Specifically, reducing the height of the stacks as well as increasing their width gives a greater increase in the backflow. The thermal distribution shows great non-uniformity by modifying these parameters. However, these smaller stacking widths help in thermal homogeneity. In relation to flow velocity and turbulence, it was observed that we have higher values in the center of the oven than on the sides. There is also great sensitivity to the Reynolds number.

title: Particle-Unresolved CFD-DEM Simulations of Cluster-Induced Turbulence at scale L = 2048dp: From Filtered Drag Closures to In Situ Machine Learning
authors: , William Fullmer, , Aytekin Gel, Jordan Musser
abstract: Predictive scale-up of gas–solid multiphase flows remain a significant challenge in computational fluid dynamics (CFD) due to complex, multiscale fluid-particle interactions such as cluster-induced turbulence (CIT). Coarse-grained two-fluid models (TFMs) and discrete element method (DEM) simulations require accurate sub-grid closure models—particularly filtered drag laws—to account for unresolved mesoscale structures. This report presents the outcomes of a high-performance computing effort leveraging the exascale-capable CFD–DEM solver MFIX-Exa to generate high-fidelity training data and pioneer real-time, in situ machine learning (ML) workflows for sub-grid closure development.

title: Dynamics-informed deep learning for predicting extreme events
authors: Eirini Katsidoniotaki, Themistoklis P. Sapsis
abstract: Abstract Predicting extreme events in high-dimensional chaotic dynamical systems remains a fundamental challenge because these events are rare, intermittent and often driven by transient dynamical mechanisms that are difficult to identify from limited observations. We propose a fully data-driven framework for real-time forecasting of extreme events based on an interpretable, mechanism-aware precursor that tracks the transient instabilities preceding event onset. Specifically, we use the finite-time Lyapunov exponent (FTLE) as the precursor, computed directly from state snapshots through a reduced-order, equation-agnostic formulation. By restricting the instability dynamics to an adaptively evolving subspace spanned by optimal time-dependent (OTD) modes, the method substantially reduces the computational cost of classical FTLE evaluation while retaining the dominant transiently amplifying directions. The resulting FTLE sequence serves as input to a transformer-based model that forecasts the system observable at future lead times, enabling long-lead prediction of extreme events. We demonstrate the framework on Kolmogorov flow, a canonical model of intermittent turbulence. The results show that explicitly encoding transient instability mechanisms substantially extends extreme-event prediction horizons compared to baseline observable-based approaches.

title: Cerebrovascular flow field reconstruction method based on residual network of physical information
authors: Zhifan Teng, Yaochun Hou, Jianhua Liu, Q WANG
abstract: Introduction Accurate characterization of the hemodynamic environment within intracranial aneurysms is important for rupture‐risk assessment and interventional treatment planning. Although computational fluid dynamics (CFD) provides high‐fidelity flow‐field data, its computational cost limits parametric analyses across multiple vascular geometries and inlet flow conditions. Existing physics‐informed neural‐network surrogates are predominantly trained for individual geometries and single flow conditions. Systematic comparisons of performance degradation under geometric and flow‐rate distribution shifts across different architectures remain lacking, and the distinct roles of physics‐based constraints under in-distribution versus out‐of‐distribution conditions have not been thoroughly examined. Methods This study proposes PIReN, a physics‐informed residual network that decomposes the velocity‐pressure field into a learnable baseline field and a gated residual correction. The training objective incorporates continuity and steady, incompressible Navier‐Stokes momentum residuals. Training and in‐domain evaluation employ seven geometries; zero‐shot testing uses 16 fully held‐out geometries, and flow‐rate generalization is evaluated via five leave‐one‐flow‐rate‐out folds. These two protocols withhold complete geometries or flow conditions and avoid spatial-correlation leakage. Results In the pointwise‐random in‐domain test, PIReN achieves an aggregate relative L 2 error of 11.34% ± 0.65%, outperforming a standard PINN (16.57% ± 1.04%) and purely supervised MLP (14.74% ± 0.72%). These optimistic values describe spatial‐interpolation accuracy. Using a contiguous axial held‐out block while fixing model weights, PIReN still delivers superior accuracy: under the pooled configuration, its aggregate relative L 2 error is 30.35%± 2.55% versus 39.27%±2.85% for PINN. PIReN dominates across all four metrics, both partitions and five configurations, with a larger absolute performance margin under the stricter block partition. On geometry set B, the corresponding errors for PIReN and the PINN are 42.71% and 121.92%, respectively. Discussion Ablation studies show that removing the residual decoder produces the largest increase in prediction error, whereas the physics‐informed loss terms primarily reduce governing‐equation residuals. These results indicate that PIReN reduces performance degradation under changes in vascular geometry and inlet flow rate and provides a promising framework for steady‐state cerebrovascular flow‐field surrogate modeling.

title: Aerodynamic Optimisation in Car Exterior Design: Improving Energy Efficiency Through Formula 1 Design Principles
authors: Yuanchen Zhao
abstract: Exterior shape is one of the few levers a designer can pull to cut energy use without adding a single kilogram to the vehicle. Body contours govern how air attaches to the surface, where the boundary layer lets go, and how much static pressure is recovered before the flow leaves the tail. Those three behaviours set the drag area (CdA), and drag area sets power demand once speed climbs. This paper does not argue for transplanting racing hardware onto road cars. It uses Formula 1 aerodynamics, in particular the downforce-drag trade-off and adaptive devices such as the Drag Reduction System (DRS), as a conceptual template for condition-dependent flow control. Comparing passive shaping against active devices shows that the payoff is strongly speed-dependent: gains are modest in city traffic and substantial above roughly 100 km/h. Active hardware carries its own bill, though. Actuators add mass, draw current, complicate assembly and durability, and eat into cabin and luggage space. Morphing geometries and non-mechanical flow control look promising for the next generation of electric vehicles, but only where the fluidic gain outweighs the mass, energy and computational penalty they bring with them.

title: Surface Integrity Evolution in WEDM of Nickel-Based Superalloys: Formation and Implications of Recast Layer, Residual Stresses, and Microhardness—A Critical Review
authors: Gurnam Singh, Neel Kanth Grover, Vivek Aggarwal
abstract: Wire Electrical Discharge Machining (WEDM) is widely applied for machining nickel-based superalloys used in aerospace and high-temperature systems; however, thermally induced surface alterations strongly affect structural reliability. This review synthesizes recast layer thickness (RLT), microhardness evolution, residual stress development, and elemental redistribution in precipitation- and solid-solution-strengthened alloys. Discharge energy—mainly governed by pulse-on time and peak current and influenced by gap voltage—controls melt-pool behavior, resolidification, chemical modification, and stress evolution. Reported RLT values vary from ~1 to 50 µm depending on machining regime, while low-energy multi-trim strategies can restrict thickness below ~5–6 µm for aerospace requirements. High discharge energy promotes Cu–Zn electrode transfer, oxygen incorporation, and tensile residual stresses (~200–800 MPa), increasing crack susceptibility. Microhardness response is alloy-dependent, often showing subsurface softening under aggressive conditions. This review establishes an energy–microstructure–performance framework for improving surface integrity in critical applications.

title: Biomimetic Applications in the Aerodynamic Shape Design of Aviation and Automotive Vehicles
authors: Baichuan Song
abstract: Biomimetic aerodynamic design draws inspiration from biological structures and flow-control mechanisms to improve the aerodynamic performance of aircraft and automobiles. This paper reviews representative biomimetic concepts, including humpback-whale leading-edge tubercles, shark-skin riblets, boxfish-inspired body shapes, dragonfly-wing corrugations, and bird-inspired wingtip structures. The discussion focuses on how these designs influence drag reduction, lift enhancement, flow-separation control, and stability under specific operating conditions. A conditional cross-domain comparison is conducted between aviation and automotive applications in terms of Reynolds number, dominant drag source, operating conditions, scaling effects, manufacturing difficulty, surface durability, and engineering maturity. The review shows that the effectiveness of biomimetic structures is highly condition-dependent and that laboratory-scale benefits cannot be directly transferred to full-scale engineering systems. Supporting technologies, including computational fluid dynamics, advanced manufacturing, and machine learning, are also examined. Major challenges include scale mismatch, operating-condition migration, surface contamination, durability, manufacturability, and cost. Future research should move from direct form imitation toward mechanism-based biomimetic design, while integrating aerodynamic performance with structural, manufacturing, and economic constraints. More rigorous benchmarking and full-scale validation are required to bridge the gap between experimental studies and practical engineering applications.

title: Research Progress on Manifold Microchannel Technologies for Thermal Management of Microelectronic Chips
authors: Sicheng Zhou
abstract: As high-performance computing, artificial intelligence, and power-electronic devices continue to evolve toward higher integration and power density, localized chip hotspots impose increasingly severe thermal constraints. Conventional air cooling and heat-spreading-only solutions are becoming insufficient to simultaneously remove high heat fluxes and maintain temperature uniformity. Microchannel liquid cooling offers a large surface-area-to-volume ratio, short heat-transfer paths, and high volumetric heat-transfer capability. In particular, manifold microchannels shorten the effective flow length and reshape coolant distribution, providing a promising route for cooling chips under high and spatially non-uniform heat loads. Based on a thorough revision of the original manuscript, this review discusses the development of microchannel heat sinks, geometric parameters and flow-distribution mechanisms of manifold structures, hotspot-oriented cooling strategies, field-synergy and secondary-flow mechanisms, thermal response under dynamic boundary conditions, multiphysics simulation, and advanced manufacturing. Current studies indicate that manifold structures can reduce streamwise pressure losses while improving local heat transfer; however, their performance strongly depends on the coupled manifold-microchannel geometry, flow uniformity, and operating boundary conditions, and no universal optimum geometric parameter exists independently of the specific application. Future work should focus on adaptive flow control for dynamic hotspots, chip-cooler co-design, two-phase and advanced coolants, data-driven optimization, and integrated additive manufacturing to move manifold microchannel cooling from high-performance prototypes toward reliable and scalable engineering systems.

title: A Chemistry Integration Surrogate Model Based on Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks for Reacting-Flow CFD
authors: Chong Wu, Yu-Peng Liu, Jia-Jian Li, Jian An, Bing Liu, Shao-Hua Zhu, Hai-Feng Hu, Chen-Chuan Zhou
abstract: The accuracy and efficiency of reacting-flow computations in supersonic combustors directly influence the performance analysis and optimal design of hypersonic propulsion systems. To address the substantial cost of detailed chemistry integration, this work proposes a chemistry integration surrogate method based on Kolmogorov–Arnold networks (KANs). Through learnable univariate function structures and locally adjustable B-spline basis functions, the method achieves high-accuracy prediction of the complex nonlinear mapping between thermochemical states and species increments with fewer parameters, replacing the solution of the conventional chemical source term. The results show that, at comparable parameter counts, the KAN achieves lower test loss and lower ignition delay prediction error. Even with 10.5 times as many parameters as the KAN, the baseline multilayer perceptron has a higher test loss, indicating the parameter efficiency of the KAN. In the three-dimensional supersonic combustor case, both the KAN and the baseline model reproduce the spatial distribution of the temperature field and the major species fields. Compared with this multilayer perceptron, the KAN yields a lower domain-averaged absolute temperature error at each evaluation instant, together with smaller absolute errors and narrower error distributions for the major species. The KAN delivers a lower test loss, higher three-dimensional flow-field accuracy and satisfactory continuous integration stability with fewer parameters, which makes it suitable for efficient combustion chemistry computation.

title: Model Selection for Biological Blockage at Cooling Water Intakes: A Structured Critical Review of CFD, FSI, CFD–DEM, and Surrogate Models
authors: Xin-Shu Jiang, Wei Bai, Pei-Yan Pan, Jing-Fei Wang, Hui-Chao Li, Qian Huang, Li Dai, Wen-Jie Zhang, Qi Li, Rong-Yong Zhang
abstract: The biological blockage of cooling water intakes links regional transport, local hydraulics, barrier deformation, organism contact, and operational recovery. This structured critical review connects these physical subproblems to computational fluid dynamics (CFD), fluid–structure interaction (FSI), CFD–discrete element methods (CFD–DEM), resolved-interface methods, and surrogates. We distinguish contextual relevance from validation strength and compare reported numerical checks, experimental comparisons, and calibration dependence. Calibrated reduced-screen CFD provides a candidate starting point for flow and head loss within its tested regime. FSI becomes necessary when deformation or dynamic feedback changes a decision-relevant response; agreement in mean load alone cannot establish peak load credibility. CFD-DEM is restricted to populations whose quasi-rigid-body and unresolved flow assumptions are defensible. Soft-body passage and entanglement require additional constitutive and interaction evidence. Surrogates require separate assessment of approximation errors, source-model validity, and domain shift. Integrating established verification and validation principles, we present a quantity-first selection map and an explicitly hypothetical numerical example linking model enrichment, uncertainty, and an acceptance margin. The principal evidence gap remains independent intake-specific validation across hydraulic, structural, and object-level responses.

title: Load-Balanced Neural-Network-Aided Adaptive Tabulation of Phase Equilibria for Transcritical Multiphase Flows
authors: Navneeth Srinivasan, Po-Yu Lai, Suo Yang
abstract: Simulating high-pressure transcritical flows with phase change is critical for advanced propulsion, yet traditional first-principles approaches, vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE) calculations, consume most of the runtime and frequently fail to converge. Standalone machine learning models introduce heavy evaluation overhead across large grids, while dynamic tabulation still relies on fragile iterative solvers. To resolve these limitations, this study introduces a hybrid In-Situ Adaptive Tabulation and Artificial Neural Network (ISAT-ANN) framework. A pre-trained ANN replaces the iterative solver during table expansion to guarantee crash-free operation, while ISAT enables rapid data retrieval via local linear interpolation. To eliminate parallel load imbalances, an O(N) greedy load-balancing algorithm redistributes computational tasks across cores. Coupled with Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR), the framework was validated on a Mach 5 shock-droplet interaction benchmark. It accurately captured shock-interface dynamics without instability, achieving a 2.30 times speedup in thermodynamic calculations on a single core and 2.62 times in parallel over standalone ANNs, with AMR providing an additional 2.92 times overall efficiency boost. This plug-and-play framework offers a stable, scalable path for high-fidelity multiphase flow simulations.

title: Artificial intelligence-driven airfoil aerodynamic design via deep surrogate modeling and evolutionary algorithm
authors: M Li, J Wang, K Sun, F Han, C Lee
abstract: Airfoil aerodynamic design relies on computationally expensive flow solvers, while aerodynamic performance optimization and target pressure distribution inverse design are treated separately. This study develops a framework combining low-dimensional geometric representation, deep surrogate modeling, and evolutionary search for aerodynamic prediction, constrained optimization, and inverse design. A density-guided principal component analysis strategy constructs the airfoil design space, while a fully connected autoencoder provides a compact representation of the surface pressure distribution. A multi-branch residual surrogate network jointly predicts lift coefficient, drag coefficient, and surface pressure coefficient distribution from airfoil geometry, Mach number, and angle of attack; mean absolute errors are 3.765 × 10−3, 1.178 × 10−4, and 1.399 × 10−2, respectively. The surrogate maintains high accuracy for combinations of unseen airfoil geometries and interpolated inflow conditions, demonstrating predictive coverage within the training parameter range. Each inference requires 0.024 ms, and 6 × 104 aerodynamic evaluations are completed in 20.5 s. Coupled with the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy, the surrogate supports two constrained design tasks. Aerodynamic-efficiency optimization improves the lift-to-drag ratio in all 20 cases without reducing lift or increasing drag. Target pressure distribution inverse design reconstructs the prescribed suction peak, low-pressure region, and pressure-recovery process. Independent high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics recalculations of 40 optimized airfoils show close agreement with surrogate predictions. Flow-field analyses reveal localized velocity and pressure changes for efficiency-oriented optimization, whereas inverse design produces broader upper-surface acceleration, increased suction, and modified pressure recovery. These results demonstrate an efficient framework linking airfoil geometry, aerodynamic performance, and distributed flow responses.
